questions.question: S.E. is a 1-year-old boy (weight 10.8 kg) who presents to the emergency department (ED) with a 4-day history of fever, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, a diffuse maculopapular rash, and a cervical lymphadenopathy greater than 1.5 cm on the left side. According to his mother, his temperature has ranged from (38.8^C-40^C). He has been extremely irritable, especially when febrile, with no runny nose or cough but some mild congestion. In the ED, serum chemistries are within normal limits; white blood cell count (WBC) is 10.4times10^3cells/mm3, platelet count is 250,000/mm3, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are markedly elevated. A chest radiograph is normal, and cultures of blood and urine, as well as viral swabs, are collected. Because of the child's physical examination, laboratory values, and 4-day history of fever, an echocardiogram (ECHO) is obtained. It reveals normal ejection fraction without evidence of coronary artery aneurysms (CAAs) or valvular regurgitation. At this point, which is the best option for managing S.E.?
options: A. Immune globulin 20 g once with high-dose aspirin starting immediately.
B. Immune globulin 20 g once with high-dose aspirin after fever has persisted for 5 days or more.
C. No medications because this patient is not at risk of developing CAAs according to the results of the ECHO.
D. Immune globulin 4 g once daily for 4 days with high-dose aspirin starting immediately.
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of KD can be made on day 4 of illness in the presence of at least four principal criteria (i.e., nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, maculopapular rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy larger than 1.5 cm for this child). Initial ECHO serves only as a baseline for long-term management of patients with KD, so the lack of significant cardiac findings on ECHO does not rule out the need for treatment, making Answer C incorrect. Although CAA may be detected as early as 3 days from illness onset, CAAs more commonly develop in the subacute phase of illness (i.e., after fever resolves, but before resolution of all clinical features). Immune globulin is the standard of care to prevent CAA in children with KD; therefore, the AHA recommends that all children thought to have the diagnosis be treated with immune globulin. Treatment with immune globulin before the fifth day of illness, however, has been associated with persistent and recrudescent fever that requires retreatment. Therefore, Answer B is correct and Answer A is incorrect. A single high dose of immune globulin (2Cg/kg) is preferred to a low dose (500 mg/kg) over 4 days because two meta-analyses showed a significantly lower incidence of CAA in patients receiving high-dose therapy (Answer D is incorrect). At present, the AHA recommends adding high-dose aspirin therapy (80-100Cmg/kg/day) for 48-72 hours after the patient is afebrile and then continuing low-dose aspirin therapy (3-5Cmg/kg/day) for at least 6-8 weeks until repeat ECHO. However, use of aspirin (low, medium, or high dose) during the acute phase of illness is controversial and varies by practice site. Although high-dose aspirin may shorten the duration of fever, no studies have shown a reduction in CAA with either low- or high-dose aspirin regimens.

questions.question: C.P. is a 2-year-old boy (weight 12 kg) treated for a diagnosis of Kawasaki disease (KD) 8 weeks ago. He has a repeat ECHO that reveals an aneurysm greater than 8 mm in diameter in the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery. Which is the best treatment to initiate for C.P.?
options: A. Low-dose aspirin until the aneurysm regresses.
B. Clopidogrel until the aneurysm regresses.
C. Low-dose aspirin with clopidogrel until the aneurysm regresses.
D. Low-dose aspirin with warfarin indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The child has a giant CAA (larger than 8 mm in diameter), which places him at high risk of myocardial ischemia (AHA risk level IV). Antiplatelet therapy is recommended for all patients with small (less than 5 mm) or greater aneurysms on ECHO or angiogram. For small to medium aneurysms (at least 3 mm but smaller than 6 mm), one can consider discontinuing antiplatelet therapy when aneurysm regression is documented. For large aneurysms (larger than 6 mm), including giant aneurysms, antiplatelets should be used in combination with anticoagulants (either warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin) indefinitely, making Answer D correct and Answers A-C incorrect.

questions.question: L.E. is a 2-month-old girl (weight 4 kg) with a diagnosis of a ventricular septal defect (VSD) shortly after birth. She is now being admitted to the hospital for failure-to-thrive. Blood pressure is within normal limits for age and sex. Average heart rate is 170Cbeats/minute. Chest radiograph reveals pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Left ventricular ejection fraction is 0.6 on ECHO. Patch closure of her VSD is planned, but the earliest her surgery can be scheduled is 2 months from now. Which medication regimen would be most appropriate for L.E. until her cardiac surgery?
questions.explanation: This patient has CHF secondary to her VSD, as indicated by her failure-to-thrive, tachycardia, cardiomegaly, and pulmonary edema. Her left ventricular ejection fraction is normal, so this is probably right-sided failure, which is what would initially be expected with a left-to-right shunt lesion. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors reduce afterload and the workload on the heart, so captopril would be beneficial for this patient. A loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide) is a good first choice for reducing preload and pulmonary edema, Answer C is correct. Digoxin has not been shown to be of benefit in managing right-sided heart failure without concomitant left ventricular dysfunction, so it would not be useful for this patient (Answers A and B are incorrect). B-Blockers (e.g., propranolol) may be beneficial in the long-term management of patients with CHF to blunt sympathetic hyperactivity and cardiac remodeling; however, this patient is expected to have surgical correction of her underlying cause for heart failure in the near future. Given the need for a prolonged titration schedule, it is unlikely that propranolol would add benefit in the short term, making Answer D incorrect.

questions.question: D.P. is a 28 weeks' post-conceptional age boy (current weight 992 g) who remains ventilator-dependent. He was born at 26 weeks' gestational age (birth weight 770 g). He has a continuous murmur and bounding peripheral pulses, and his chest radiograph shows evidence of pulmonary over circulation with mild cardiomegaly consistent with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). He has no evidence of intraventricular hemorrhage on cranial ultrasonography. His most recent laboratory values are as follows: blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 15Cmg/dL, serum creatinine (SCr) 0.9Cmg/dL, hematocrit 40%, platelet count 160,000/mm^3, total bilirubin 5.4Cmg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.4Cmg/dL. Urine output during the past 24 hours was 4CmL/kg/hour. Which is the best treatment option for D.P. at this time?
options: A. Allow spontaneous closure of the PDA.
B. Give intravenous ibuprofen 8 mg, followed by 4 mg at 24 and 48 hours after the first dose.
C. Give intravenous indomethacin 0.2 mg, followed by 0.25 mg at 12 and 24 hours after the first dose.
D. Give intravenous indomethacin 0.2 mg once, with a second and third dose of 0.25 mg at 12-or 24-hour intervals, depending on urine output after the first dose.
questions.explanation: This patient has a hemodynamically significant PDA, as evidenced by his ventilator dependence and his chest radiograph revealing pulmonary overcirculation and cardiomegaly. Pharmacologic or surgical closure of his PDA should be considered versus waiting for possible spontaneous closure therefore, Answer A is incorrect. He is eligible for pharmacologic closure, given his higher likelihood of response (i.e.. he is a preterm infant) and lack of contraindications (i.e., no evidence of intraventricular hemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, bleeding, or hyperbilirubinemia). His SCr appears elevated, but his urine output is good. SCr may be reflective of his mother's SCr. Ibuprofen would be the first choice for pharmacologic therapy because a recent meta-analysis showed it to be as effective as indomethacin for ductal closure but with a lower risk of renal dysfunction and necrotizing enterocolitis, making Answer B correct and Answers C and D incorrect. If treating with indomethacin, the correct dose for this patient according to gestational and postnatal age would be 0.2Cmg/ kg once, followed by a second and third dose of 0.25Cmg/kg at either 12 or 24-hour intervals, depending on the urine output measured after the first dose.

questions.question:
Questions 5 and 6 pertain to the following case:
F.E. is a 14-year-old female adolescent who presents to the ED after her mother finds her unresponsive in the bathroom. She is currently awake and endorses chest pain and feeling like her heart is beating funny. On physical examination, she is tachycardic, but her other vital signs are stable. A complete metabolic panel is within normal limits, and a urine drug screen is negative. Electrocardiogram (ECG) reveals a corrected QT (QTc) of 580 milliseconds. According to F.E., she and her mother had been arguing just before the event. According to her mother, F.E. has a history of "fainting spells" when she gets upset and when she works out too much. Her mother says that F.E. is just being overly dramatic and not drinking enough water when she exercises. Cardiology is consulted to evaluate the patient.

5. Which medication is F.E. most likely to be prescribed?
options: A. No medication, but she is counseled to avoid emotional triggers.
questions.explanation: This patient has a history highly suggestive of long QT syndrome (i.e., syncope on exertion and with emotional triggers). In addition, she presents with chest pain, palpitations, and a QT interval longer than 460 milliseconds. Because she has a history of syncope with exertion, she is at high risk of developing VF and sudden death. Chronic prophylactic therapy is recommended; therefore, Answer B is correct and Answer A is incorrect. B-Blockers are first-line agents because they reduce mortality from 71% to 6% in patients with long QT syndrome; therefore, Answers C and D are incorrect.

questions.question: 6. Which potentially fatal arrhythmia is most likely to develop in F.E.?
questions.explanation: Torsades de pointes is the hallmark dysrhythmia associated with long QT syndrome; therefore, Answer D is correct and Answers A-C are incorrect. Because cardiac output is impaired during this polymorphic VT, the patient often develops syncope or seizures. Although spontaneous return of consciousness usually occurs after the syncopal episode, dysrhythmia still has the potential for fatal consequences.

questions.question: N.R. is a 10-year-old girl (weight 37 kg) with a history of congestive heart failure (CHF) who is admitted to the hospital for severe nausea, vomiting, and dehydration. She has a peripherally inserted central catheter placed for the administration of intravenous fluids because she keeps losing peripheral access. On day 5 of admission, she has arm swelling with pain and redness. Ultrasonography reveals an extensive thrombus. She is initiated on enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously twice daily. Initial platelet count is 125,000/mm^3. After 2 days of therapy, the clot is continuing to expand, despite an anti-factor Xa (anti-Xa) of 1.02Cunits/mL. Her platelet count has also dropped to 66,000/mm3. An anti-heparin antibody screen is positive. Which would be the best option for N.R.?
options: D. Continue enoxaparin at the same dose, and add warfarin.
questions.explanation: This patient has signs of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (i.e., extension of the clot despite a therapeutic anti-Xa level, decline in platelet count, and positive anti-heparin antibody screen). All heparin products (unfractionated heparin infusion, heparin flushes, and low-molecular-weight heparin) should be discontinued, making Answers A, B, and D incorrect. The patient should be initiated on a short-acting alternative anticoagulant therapy to treat her existing clot (e.g., argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux). Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that may be used to manage this patient, making Answer C correct.

questions.question: W.K. is a 13-year-old male adolescent (weight 47 kg) who received a bioprosthetic aortic valve because of aortic valve insufficiency. His last ECHO before valve placement revealed an ejection fraction of 70%. He has never experienced dysrhythmias, and he has no history of coagulopathy. Which would be the best anticoagulation option for W.K. after valve placement?
options: A. Warfarin with goal international normalized ratio (INR) 2.5-3.5 for 3 months, followed by low-dose aspirin for life.
B. Warfarin with goal INR 2.0-3.0 for 3 months, followed by low-dose aspirin for life.
C. Warfarin with goal INR 2.5-3.5 for life.
D. Warfarin with goal INR 2.0-3.0 for life.
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation with warfarin is appropriate for the first 3 months in left-sided valve placements. The goal INR for bioprosthetic (tissue) valves is lower (2.0-3.0) than for mechanical prosthetic valves (2.5-3.5): therefore, Answers A and C are incorrect. Because this patient has no risk factors for thrombosis (i.e., no left ventricular dysfunction, history of thrombosis, hypercoagulable disorder, or Afib), he may transition to low-dose aspirin after 3 months, making Answer B correct and Answer D incorrect. If he had risk factors, he would continue on warfarin therapy.

questions.question: G.S. is a 3-month-old girl (weight 3.4 kg, 32 weeks' gestational age, birth weight 1.5 kg) who received a diagnosis of truncus arteriosus and interrupted aortic arch. She went to the operating room for repair of the truncus arteriosus. Unfortunately, during surgery, she had a significant pulmonary hypertensive crisis with suprasystemic pulmonary artery (PA) pressures. She was initiated on inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm, given sodium bicarbonate, and briefly hyperventilated. Her PA pressures were lowered, and she was transported to the pediatric intensive care unit. During the first few hours in the intensive care unit, her PA pressures began to rise and became equal to her systemic pressures. Which would be the most appropriate adjustment to therapy for G.S. at this time?
options: A. Increase inhaled nitric oxide above 20 ppm indefinitely.
B. Discontinue inhaled nitric oxide, and initiate inhaled iloprost.
C. Continue inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm, and initiate sildenafil.
D. Continue inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm, and initiate epoprostenol.
questions.explanation: Inhaled nitric oxide is currently a first-line treatment to rapidly reduce PA pressure in patients with newly diagnosed severe PHN or in postoperative PHN, making Answer B incorrect. Initial dose may be 20 ppm with weaning once oxygenation improves. Doses should not exceed 20 ppm for prolonged periods because of the risk of methemoglobinemia and elevation in detoxic metabolite nitrogen dioxide; therefore, Answer A is incorrect. Because the patient had rising PA pressures despite inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm, additional therapy should be added versus maintaining high-dose, prolonged inhaled nitric oxide. Although inhaled iloprost is as beneficial as inhaled nitric oxide in the acute care setting, this medication requires a special delivery system that may be technically difficult to initiate in the immediate postoperative period after cardiac surgery. Similarly, oral therapy with sildenafil and bosentan would not be a good choice in the immediate post-cardiac surgery patient (Answer C is incorrect). Epoprostenol infusion is effective for managing PHN in the postoperative setting and can be quickly titrated to effect, making Answer D correct.

questions.question: K.W. is a 13-month-old boy (weight 9.4 kg) with a history significant for a previously repaired large VSD and pulmonary hypertension (PHN). He has been maintained on sildenafil 15 mg orally four times/day and bosentan 15.6 mg orally twice daily. Before starting sildenafil and bosentan therapy, his baseline alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 42 IU/L, and his aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 30 IU/L. Repeat ALT and AST values after 2 months of sildenafil and bosentan therapy are 304 IU/L and 500CIU/L, respectively. He has had no nausea, vomiting, jaundice, or fatigue. Which would be the best treatment option for K.W.?
options: A. Continue sildenafil and bosentan at the same doses.
B. Continue sildenafil at the same dose, and discontinue bosentan.
C. Reduce the sildenafil and bosentan doses.
D. Continue sildenafil at the same dose, and reduce the bosentan dose.
questions.explanation: Bosentan may cause hepatotoxicity, including acute liver failure. Monthly liver enzymes are required as part of the Tracleer Access Program (T.A.P.). Registration and compliance with T.A.P. requirements are necessary to receive bosentan on an outpatient basis from a specialty pharmacy. Even though this patient has not experienced clinical symptoms of hepatic dysfunction, bosentan should be discontinued and the patient further evaluated for liver dysfunction (Answer B is correct; Answers A, C, and D are incorrect). Ambrisentan, a selective endothelin A receptor antagonist, may be an option in the future. Although ambrisentan carries the same potential risk of hepatotoxicity as bosentan, it has not been shown to cause elevations in liver enzymes or clinical signs or symptoms of liver dysfunction in recent trials. More data will be required to determine whether this reduced risk of liver dysfunction continues.

questions.question:
Questions 11 and 12 pertain to the following case:
J.L is a 10-year-old boy (weight 33.2 kg) who presents with a history of fever for 5 days accompanied by a rash, conjunctivitis, and cherry-red lips. He continues to have a negative infectious workup. His CRP and ESR are mildly elevated. After 24 hours of remaining afebrile off antibiotics, he receives a diagnosis of a viral illness, and he is discharged home. Two days later, he returns because of recurrent fevers at home. Repeat CBC shows a platelet count of 100,000/mm^3. The following day, an ECHO is obtained that reveals mild dilatation of the left and right coronary arteries.

11. Which is the best option for initial management of J.L.?
options: A. Immune globulin with high-dose aspirin.
B. Immune globulin with high-dose aspirin plus corticosteroids.
questions.explanation: Immune globulin is the only proven therapy to reduce the incidence of CAA, so it should be part of initial therapy, making Answers C and D incorrect. However, this patient has several factors that place him at high risk of developing CAA and possibly immune globulin failure: age older than 9 years, male sex, incomplete KD presentation, and thrombocytopenia during the acute phase of illness. Corticosteroids should be considered as first-line therapy with immune globulin and high dose aspirin for this patient. The AHA now states that the addition of prednisolone to immune globulin for patients with severe KD appears to substantially reduce the incidence of coronary artery anomalies (Answer B is correct and Answer A is incorrect).

questions.question: 12. J.L. has a repeat ECHO at 6 weeks that reveals an aneurysm of 4-mm internal diameter in the left anterior descending artery and an aneurysm of 3 mm in the right coronary artery. Which is the best treatment option for J.L. at this time?
options: A. High-dose aspirin until the aneurysm regresses.
B. Low-dose aspirin until the aneurysm regresses.
C. Low-dose aspirin with clopidogrel until the aneurysm regresses.
D. Low-dose aspirin with warfarin indefinitely.
questions.explanation: This patient is AHA risk level III (i.e., medium aneurysms larger than 3 mm but less than 6 mm in at least one coronary artery), so it is recommended that he stay on low-dose aspirin therapy until the aneurysms regress (Answer B is correct). High-dose aspirin should only continue through the acute phase of illness until the patient is afebrile for about 48-72 hours, making Answer A incorrect. Adding clopidogrel would be considered if he had many or complex aneurysms in a single artery (i.e., AHA risk level IV), so Answer C is incorrect. Warfarin would be added to low-dose aspirin for large CAAs (i.e., AHA risk level IV); therefore, Answer D is incorrect.

questions.question:
Questions 13-15 pertain to the following case:
E.R. is a 6-month-old girl (weight 7.4 kg) who meets the diagnostic criteria for KD and has an initial ECHO that reveals an aneurysm of 5-mm internal diameter in the right coronary artery.

13. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment option for E.R.?
options: A. Immune globulin and high-dose aspirin followed by corticosteroids.
B. Immune globulin and high-dose aspirin followed by infliximab.
C. Immune globulin and high-dose aspirin followed by abciximab.
D. Immune globulin and high-dose aspirin followed by alteplase.
questions.explanation: This patient already has developed CAA during the acute phase of illness. Abciximab has been shown to aid in the regression of established CAA during the acute phase of illness, making Answer C correct. Another benefit of abciximab may include vascular remodeling, which may limit the long-term consequences of CAA (e.g., stenosis of the arteries, thrombotic occlusions, and vessel rupture). Corticosteroids or infliximab in combination with immune globulin and high-dose aspirin does not aid in regression of established CAAs, so Answers A and B are incorrect. Alteplase is a thrombolytic and would only be of benefit if the patient had an established thrombus (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question:
E.R. received treatment, but she remains febrile. Her temperature continues to range from 100.5 to 101.5^CF (38.1-38.6^CC) up to 40 hours after completion of her immune globulin-containing regimen. On her daily serum chemistries, her SCr has risen from 0.3m mg/dL pretreatment to 0.9C mg/dL posttreatment, and BUN has increased from 3Cmg/dL to 8Cmg/dL. Her urine output has decreased from 2.5CmL/kg/hour during the previous 24-hour period to 0.2CmL/kg/hour. She is maintaining good oral intake and otherwise appears well hydrated and well nourished.

14. Which would be the best regimen for managing E.R. at this time?
options: A. Repeat immune globulin, and continue high-dose aspirin until afebrile for 48 hours.
B. Repeat immune globulin, continue high-dose aspirin until afebrile for 48 hours, and add corticosteroids.
C. Repeat immune globulin, continue high-dose aspirin until afebrile for 48 hours, and add infliximab.
D. Give infliximab, and continue high-dose aspirin until afebrile for 48 hours.
questions.explanation: For patients who do not respond to the initial dose of immune globulin, the most common second-line therapy is to repeat the dose of immune globulin. However, this patient developed renal dysfunction after the initial immune globulin treatment. Because she experienced a significant adverse event that was probably related to immune globulin, it is recommended to use an alternative second-line agent, making Answers A & C incorrect. Although infliximab is now the most common third line agent for patients who have two doses of immune globulin, it also has been used successfully as a second line agent in place of a second dose of immune globulin (Answer D is correct).

questions.question: 15. E.R. now has received a second course of therapy, has remained afebrile, has a stable cardiac examination, and is ready for discharge. Because her admission occurred in October and she has a 2-year-old brother in day care, her mother asks if E.R. should receive the influenza vaccine before discharge. Which vaccination recommendation is best for E.R.?
options: A. Injectable influenza vaccine is not recommended for E.R. because it would not be effective after high dose immune globulin.
B. Injectable influenza vaccine is not recommended because E.R. will be taking long-term salicylates and is at high risk of developing Reye syndrome.
C. Injectable influenza vaccine is recommended because E.R. is at a higher risk of developing complications related to influenza infection than she is of developing Reye syndrome.
D. Injectable influenza vaccine is recommended because E.R. will not require long-term salicylates and is not at risk of developing Reye syndrome.
questions.explanation: It is recommended that this patient receive an annual influenza vaccine, regardless of her history of KD (Answers A and B are incorrect). For patients with KD specifically, both influenza and varicella vaccinations are recommended to limit the risk of developing Reye syndrome from an active viral illness during salicylate therapy. The patient will be committed to aspirin therapy until her aneurysm regresses, so she should be vaccinated, making Answer C correct and Answer D incorrect. Patients may not mount a complete immune response to live vaccines after high-dose immune globulin, so it is commended that they be revaccinated 11 months after immune globulin. Because injectable influenza vaccine is an inactivated virus, there are no restrictions with administering the vaccine in relation to immune globulin and need for repeat immunization other than the second dose of vaccine to complete the series for this 6-month-old infant.

questions.question: 16. B.P. is a 4-week-old term female (weight 4.2 kg) who was given a diagnosis of moderate CoA. She underwent an aortic balloon dilatation procedure in the cardiac catheterization laboratory and just returned to the intensive care unit. On arrival, her SBPs range from 65 to 70 mm Hg, and her diastolic blood pressures (DBPs) range from 55 to 60 mm Hg. In the past several hours, her blood pressures have begun to rise. Her SBPs are now 85-90 mm Hg, and DBPs are now 75-80 mm Hg. Which is the best option to manage B.P.'s blood pressure at this time?
questions.explanation: This patient has developed rebound hypertension after intervention for CoA. Manipulation of the aorta during catheter or surgical meedures may lead to stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system and RAAS causing the hypertension. Accordingly, hypertension in this setting esponds best to -blockers or ACEIs (or possibly ARBs), making Answer C contect and Answers A, B, and D incorrect. Esmolol would be an appropriate choice for managing this patient's hypertension.

questions.question: 17. W.P. is a 3-week-old boy (current weight 1890 g) who was born at 30 weeks' gestational age (birth weight 1309 g) and received a course of prostaglandin inhibitor to close a hemodynamically significant PDA. Repeat ECHO reveals that the ductus arteriosus remains open after initial treatment. On physical examination, he has a normal respiratory rate, slightly elevated heart rate and blood pressures, and normal peripheral pulses. He has abdominal distension and increased gastric residuals. His most recent stool is bloody. His current laboratory values are as follows: BUN 18Cmg/dL SCr 0.4Cmg/dL, hematocrit 28%, platelet count 150,000/mm^3, total bilirubin 0.5Cmg/dL, and direct bilirubin 0.3Cmg/dL. Urine output during the past 24 hours was 2.4 mL/kg/hour. An abdominal radiograph is obtained that reveals dilated loops of bowel with free air. Which would be the best option for managing W.P.'s PDA at this time?
options: A. Give intravenous ibuprofen 13 mg, followed by 6 mg at 24 and 48 hours after the first dose.
B. Give intravenous indomethacin 0.4 mg, followed by 0.3 mg at 12 and 24 hours after the first dose.
C. Do not provide additional pharmacologic intervention to close the ductus arteriosus.
D. Give intravenous indomethacin 0.4 mg once with a second and third dose of 0.3 mg at either 12- or 24-hour intervals, depending on the urine output after the first dose.
questions.explanation: This patient's ductus failed to close or reopened after initial herapy with a prostaglandin inhibitor, but he has developed signs and imptoms of necrotizing enterocolitis (abdominal distension, increased gastric residuals, bloody stools, low hematocrit, and abdominal radiograph with dilated sops of bowel and free air). It is uncertain whether the necrotizing enterocolitis developed as an adverse effect of prostaglandin therapy or as a consequence of prematurity. Regardless, prostaglandin inhibitors are contraindicated with necrotizing enterocolitis is currently the priority. In addition, this patient's PDA diagnosis, making Answers A, B, and D incorrect. Management of his hemodynamically insignificant, so no additional intervention is Warranted at this time, making Answer C correct.

questions.question: 18. L.D. is a 17-year-old male adolescent brought to the ED by ambulance after his friends found him on the floor shaking and sweating during a "rave" party. He was extremely agitated, shaking, grinding his teeth, and yelling at people who were not in the room. Vital signs were temperature 104^CF (40^CC), heart rate 140Cbeats/minute, respiratory rate 35Cbreaths/minute. and blood pressure 160/100 mm Hg. After initial stabilization, he was placed under a cooling blanket and given intravenous lorazepam 4 mg. Blood pressure remained on average 155/95 mm Hg. with a heart rate of 128 beats/minute. Which agent would be best for initial management of L.D.'s blood pressure?
questions.explanation: This patient is probably experiencing acute toxicity from thethamphetamine ingestion (i.e., "ecstasy"), including blood pressure above 120/80 mm Hg. Phentolamine is a non-selective a-adrenergic blocker that is preferred for managing hypertension secondary amphetamine/methamphetamine toxicity (Answer C is correct). It may be given and every 1-4 hours thereafter. Nitroprusside would be an alternative agent, but intermittent bolus doses every 5 minutes until blood pressure is controlled to cocaine or high doses or prolonged use were necessary (Answer A is incorrect). Esmolol is requires continuous intravenous infusion and might pose a risk of toxicity if contraindicated in amphetamine/methamphetamineinduced hypertension because it will worsen the crisis, given its unopposed action on a-adrenergic receptors, making Answer B incorrect. Oral therapy with enalapril would be inappropriate for an acutely intoxicated patient; therefore, Answer D is incorrect.

questions.question:
Questions 19-21 pertain to the following case:
S.B. is a 2-month-old boy who presents to the ED with a history of poor feeding, turning blue around the mouth during feeding, sweating while feeding and severe irritability. Vital signs are as follows: temperature 98.6^CF (37^CC) blood pressure 100/60 mm Hg, and heart rate 280Cbeats/minute. He is alert and active, does not appear to be in respiratory distress, is not mottled, and has a capillary refill of less than 2 seconds. An ECG is ordered immediately, which reveals a narrow QRS complex (less than 0.09 second) without discernible p waves and no variation in heart rate.

19. Which is the best option to initially manage S.B.'s tachycardia?
options: A. Ice water to the face.
questions.explanation: This patient has SVT (i.e., history of difficulty feeding and irritability, heart rate exceeding 220 beats/minute, ECG with narrow QRS complex without discernible P waves, and no variation in heart rate). He is hemodynamically stable with normal blood pressure, good perfusion, no altered mental status, and no may be tried initially to convert the patient to normal sinus rhythm (Answer A is correct); therefore, initial treatment with adenosine and/or synchronized cardioversion is unnecessary (Answers B and D are incorrect). Propranolol is not an appropriate option for acute management of SVT, making Answer C incorrect.

questions.question: 20. S.B. is successfully treated. He is admitted to the hospital for further workup that includes an ECHO, which reveals no structural abnormalities. A few hours after the test is completed, his mother calls the nurse because S.B. is not waking up to feed, and his color is dusky. When the nurse assesses him, she notes that he appears to have difficulty breathing, his heart rate is too fast to count, his pulses are weak and thready, and he has pale, cool extremities with a poor capillary refill. She calls the emergency response team. When you arrive, his ECG reveals a heart rate of 320Cbeats/minute with a narrow QRS complex. Which would be the most appropriate option for managing S.B. at this time?
options: A. Ice water to the face.
questions.explanation: The patient is now showing signs of poor perfusion related to SVT (i.e., lethargy, respiratory distress, weak pulse, and pale/cool extremities with poor capillary refill). Vagal maneuvers could be considered, but they should not delay adenosine or synchronized cardioversion in an unstable patient, making Answer A incorrect. Synchronized cardioversion should be considered for this patient, but adenosine may still be tried first if intravenous/ intraosseous access is readily available. Because the patient was previously treated for SVT and was admitted to the hospital, intravenous access is probably already established. Therefore, adenosine could be administered quickly (Answer D is correct and Answer B is incorrect). If adenosine therapy fails, synchronized cardioversion should be tried. Propranolol is not an appropriate option for acute management of SVT; therefore, Answer C is incorrect.

questions.question: 21. After S.B. receives the selected intervention, he has a shortened PR interval and delta wave (a slurred upstroke in the QRS complex or preexcitation) on ECG after conversion to normal sinus rhythm. Which first-line agent is most appropriate to chronically manage his arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: The patient has AVRT caused by pre-excitation (WPW syndrome), as indicated by the short PR interval and delta wave on ECG after adenosine. Digoxin, -blockers, and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil and diltiazem) may cause severe bradycardia and induce VF in WPW and are generally avoided unless the refractory period of the accessory pathway is longer than 0.3 second. Therefore, Answers A-C are incorrect. Flecainide is considered a first-line agent for WPW in patients with structurally normal hearts, and it would be a good choice for this patient in this scenario because the refractory period of his pathway is unknown, making Answer D correct. Propafenone, sotalol, and amiodarone are alternative agents.

questions.question: 22. G.A. is a 15-year-old male adolescent who presents to the cardiology clinic with a 2-day history of subjective fever, shortness of breath, and cough producing watery sputum. He has a medical history significant for idiopathic Afib, for which he takes propranolol and amiodarone. At the clinic, his temperature is 100.4°F (38^CC), and respiratory rate is 22 breaths/minute. Heart rate and blood pressure are within normal limits for age and sex. Overall, he appears well hydrated and is able to drink fluids. On physical examination, the only pertinent findings are crackles over his left lung field without wheezes. A chest radiograph is ordered, which reveals a left lower lobe consolidation. Which antibiotic would be the best option to treat G.A.'s pneumonia?
questions.explanation: The most likely pathogens for this patient's pneumonia are Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydophila pneumoniae, which are covered by doxycycline (Answer B is correct). Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is not covered well by doxycycline, is still a possibility. But given the patient's age and milder presentation, it is less likely. Azithromycin and levofloxacin are appropriate choices for atypical pathogens, but they should be avoided with amiodarone because of the potential for QT-interval prolongation, making Answers A and C incorrect. Cefdinir does not interact with amiodarone and is an appropriate empiric coverage for S. pneumoniae, but it does not cover atypical pathogens (Answer D is incorrect). A combination of doxycycline with cefdinir also would be appropriate to cover all of these organisms.

questions.question:
Questions 23-25 pertain to the following case:
G.E. is a 2-month-old girl (weight 4.2 kg) given a diagnosis of Tof with mild, intermittent right ventricular outflow tract obstruction at birth. She required admission to the pediatric intensive care unit for a significant hypertensive crisis, and a femoral central line was placed. The femoral central line remained in place for 2 days, until she was transferred to the intermediate medical unit. She now has a warm, red, swollen lower extremity, and Doppler ultrasonography confirms a venous thrombosis.

23. Which is the best option for managing G.E.'s clot?
questions.explanation: This patient has a clot that probably developed secondary to a femoral central line. Enoxaparin has ample data regarding safety, efficacy. monitoring, and dosing adjustment in infants, so it is appropriate first line therapy for treating clots in this patient, making Answer C correct. Fondaparinux is not a first-line option because of the limited data in infants and the lack of an appropriate dosage form for eventual outpatient therapy (ie, enoxaparin is available in a 300Cmg/3 mL multi dose vial, whereas fondaparinux is available only in prefilled syringes, with the smallest size being 2.5 mg), and most institutions do not have ready access to a fondaparinux based anti-Xa curve for monitoring therapy. Therefore, Answer B is incorrect Warfarin will not be effective immediately and is challenging to provide to infants, so Answer A is incorrect. Unfractionated heparin to achieve therapeutic aPTT values is not used on a general medical unit, so this patient will require transfer back to the pediatric intensive care unit if unfractionated heparin is selected. In addition, she will probably require anticoagulation for 3 months, depending on the size of the clot and her response to therapy, making Answer D incorrect.

questions.question: 24. Four months later. G.E. has another hypertensive crisis and is readmitted to the pediatric intensive care unit. She is scheduled for placement of a systemic-to-PA shunt during this hospital stay. After her surgery, which type of anticoagulation would be best for G.E. to receive?
options: A. Low-dose aspirin starting immediately postoperatively and continuing for long-term maintenance anticoagulation.
B. Unfractionated heparin starting immediately postoperatively and continuing for long-term maintenance anticoagulation.
C. Unfractionated heparin starting immediately postoperatively with transition to low-dose aspirin for long-term maintenance anticoagulation.
D. Unfractionated heparin starting immediately postoperatively with transition to warfarin for long-term maintenance anticoagulation.
questions.explanation: This patient should receive long-term anticoagulation with aspirin for her systemic-to-pulmonary shunt. Therefore. Answer C is correct, and Answers B and D are incorrect. Because she has a history of thrombosis, it is reasonable to place her on systemic heparinization in the immediate postoperative period (Answer A is incorrect).

questions.question: 25. G.E. presents to the ED pale, lethargic, and cyanotic 6 months after her systemic to PA shunt is placed. Her oxygen saturations are 70%. Thrombosis of her shunt is suspected. In addition to intubation and mechanical ventilation, which is the best option for emergently managing a clot in G.E.?
questions.explanation: Emergency systemic heparinization is indicated for suspected shunt thrombosis, making answer A correct. The inability to quickly titrate enoxaparin limits its usefulness in an emergency setting; therefore, Answer B is incorrect. Thrombolytic therapy is not recommended because of the high risk of bleeding in patients who will require further diagnostic procedures (e.g., cardiac catheterization) or procedures to restore patency of the shunt (e.g., surgical revision) or even cardiopulmonary support by ECMO, making Answer C incorrect. Bivalirudin would be expected to provide immediate, titratable anticoagulation; however, data in the pediatric population are still very limited. Bivalirudin is generally reserved for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia in the pediatric population at this time; therefore, Answer D is incorrect.

questions.question:
Questions 26 and 27 pertain to the following case:
A.V. is a 16-year-old female adolescent with no significant medical history who went to her primary care physician with ear pain. After receiving a diagnosis of acute otitis media, she was given an injection of ceftriaxone in her left hip. She had persistent pain in her left hip after the injection and had difficulty walking and bearing weight on her left leg. On the day of admission, she felt dizzy and nauseated, had double vision, and passed out. When she awoke, her mother took her to the ED, where a scan was positive for large bilateral pulmonary emboli with evidence of heart failure. She was given a bolus of heparin and initiated on a heparin infusion. After transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit, she remains hemodynamically stable on a heparin infusion. The results of an ECHO are within normal limits.

26. Which is the best option for managing A.V.'s anticoagulation at this time?
options: A. Continue heparin to complete 5 days of therapy.
B. Continue heparin, and transition to warfarin to complete 6 months of therapy.
C. Continue heparin, and initiate alteplase to complete 5 days of therapy.
D. Continue heparin, and transition to aspirin to complete 6 months of therapy.
questions.explanation: This patient has idiopathic pulmonary embolism, most likely as a result of deep venous thrombosis after her antibiotic injection. She is hemodynamically stable, so she should be treated with systemic heparinization and transitioned to warfarin or low-molecular-weight heparin to complete at least 6 months of therapy. Therefore, Answer B is correct, and Answers A and D are incorrect. She may require a longer duration of anticoagulation if it is determined that she has a coagulation disorder or another risk factor for recurrent thromboembolism. A thrombolytic is not indicated in a patient with cardiorespiratory stability, making Answer C incorrect.

questions.question: 27. Which would be the most appropriate treatment for A.V. if she presented with significantly increased work of breathing, tachypnea, tachycardia, and jugular venous distension and her ECHO revealed evidence of right heart failure?
options: A. Continue heparin for 5 days of therapy.
B. Continue heparin, and transition to warfarin to complete 6 months of therapy.
C. Continue heparin, and initiate alteplase to complete 5 days of therapy.
D. Continue heparin, and transition to aspirin to complete 6 months of therapy.
questions.explanation: The patient has signs of cardiorespiratory instability related to her pulmonary emboli (i.e., dyspnea, tachycardia, and right-sided heart failure with jugular venous distension), so she is a candidate for thrombolytic therapy. making Answer C correct. Life-threatening cardiorespiratory compromise may require thrombectomy or stent placement. Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are not appropriate options with cardiorespiratory instability; therefore, Answers A, B, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: 28. S.P. is a 16-year-old male adolescent (weight 95 kg) who underwent placement of a prosthetic mitral valve 2 years ago. He was maintained on low-dose aspirin, but he developed a thrombus 4 months after the valve surgery. He is currently receiving warfarin 12 mg on Monday, Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday and 9 mg on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, with INR values ranging from 2.02 to 2.44. He is visiting the anticoagulation clinic in preparation for knee surgery next week. Which is the most appropriate treatment plan for S.P.'s anticoagulation?
options: A. Discontinue warfarin 5 days before surgery, and resume warfarin at a higher dose on the day of surgery.
B. Discontinue warfarin 5 days before surgery, and resume warfarin at the former dose on the day of surgery.
C. Discontinue warfarin 5 days before surgery, bridge with enoxaparin, resume warfarin at the former dose on the day after surgery, and discontinue enoxaparin on the day after surgery.
D. Discontinue warfarin 5 days before surgery, bridge with enoxaparin, resume warfarin at the former dose on day 5 after surgery, and discontinue enoxaparin when INR is above 2.0.
questions.explanation: This patient is at high risk of thrombosis with a history of valvular thrombosis requiring long-term warfarin anticoagulation after his low-dose aspirin regimen has failed; thus, he should be bridged with alternative anticoagulation for his knee surgery, making Answer D correct and Answers A and B incorrect. A low-molecular weight heparin (e.g., enoxaparin), unfractionated heparin, or a combination of the two may be used while warfarin is being held. Although no standard bridging regimen exists (i.e., individual patient factors must be considered when assessing risks of clotting or bleeding), alternative anticoagulation should not be discontinued until a therapeutic INR has been achieved with warfarin (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: 29. L.L. is a 22-month-old girl (weight 12 kg) who just had tricuspid valve replacement. She does not have right ventricular dysfunction or other risk factors for clotting. It is anticipated that she will receive low-dose aspirin and warfarin therapy for 3-6 months after her procedure. Her baseline INR the day of surgery was 1.1. She received one dose of warfarin 1 mg, and the following day, her INR was 1.7. The medical resident ordered her next dose of warfarin as 1.5 mg because her INR had changed by only 0.6. Which is most appropriate for L.L.'s next dose of warfarin?
questions.explanation: This patient had a significant response to her initial warfarin dose (INR increased by 0.6). However, because it takes about 3 days to see the full response to warfarin at any given dose, she could become supratherapeutic if kept on the same loading dose. Therefore, Answer B is incorrect. According to the recommended American College of Chest Physicians dosing algorithm for warfarin in children, her dose on day 2 for an INR of 1.4-1.9 should be 50% of the initial loading dose, making Answer C correct and Answers A and D incorrect.

questions.question: 30. W.L. is a 4-year-old boy (weight 13.8 kg, height 38 inches [96 cm] [5th percentile for age and sex]) who "passed out" on the playground at day care. He has a 2-month history of being very despondent and tired, according to his mother, and he becomes "breathless" when playing with other children. He has cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion on chest radiography. An ECHO reveals a mean PA pressure/systemic artery pressure ratio of 0.9 and right ventricular hypertrophy but no CHD, so he is scheduled for cardiac catheterization as part of a workup for PHN. During catheterization, his PA pressure does not drop in response to inhaled nitric oxide. Which is the best option for W.L.?
questions.explanation: This patient is a "non-responder" to vasodilator testing; therefore, Answer A is incorrect. He is in a higher risk category (i.e., failure-to- thrive, syncope, WHO functional class IV, PA pressure/systemic pressure ratio greater than 0.75, and right heart failure). First-line therapy should be intravenous epoprostenol or intravenous/subcutaneous treprostinil, according to the World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension 2013 Consensus Pediatric IPAH/FPAH Treatment Algorithm (Answer C is correct; Answers B and D are incorrect). Combination therapy with a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor and/or endothelin receptor antagonist should be considered for initial therapy as well, particularly if the combination allows for reduced doses of prostacyclin analog.

questions.question: M.M. is a 14-year-old male adolescent (weight 63.2 kg, height 67 inches [171 cm] [75th percentile for age and sex]) with a history of dyspnea and fatigue with chest pain on physical exertion. An ECHO reveals a PA pressure of 75 mm Hg. Cardiac catheterization confirms a diagnosis of PHN. During vasodilator testing, his PA pressure decreases by 15 mm Hg. Which would be the best first-line treatment for M.M.'s PHN?
questions.explanation: Answer: A. This patient is a "responder" to vasodilator testing and is older than 1 year, so first-line treatment would be a calcium channel blocker on Pulmonary Hypertension 2013 according to the World Symposium Consensus Pediatric IPAH/FPAH Treatment Algorithm, making answer A correct and Answers B and D incorrect. Diltiazem and nifedipine are both options. Diltiazem, which may have a greater effect on the pulmonary vasculature than the systemic vasculature, has been shown to have a better reduction in PA pressure than nifedipine; therefore, Answer C is incorrect. However, these effects have not been studied sufficiently to make diltiazem the calcium channel blocker of choice. Twice-daily dosing, especially for an adolescent patient, is advantageous over thrice daily dosing. Thus, if nifedipine were selected, a better dosing option would be a 60-mg extended-release tablet given once daily.

questions.question: L.P. is a 2-year-old girl (weight 14 kg, height 36 inches [92 cm] [90th percentile for age and sex]) with idiopathic PHN (WHO functional class II) who has been taking oral sildenafil 25 mg four times/day for the past 2 months. Her mean PA/systemic artery pressure ratio was 0.6 at the beginning of therapy and is now 0.58. Which would be the most appropriate next step in managing L.P.?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient is lower risk, as evidenced by her WHO functional class, appropriate weight and height for age/ sex, baseline mean PA/systemic artery pressure ratio less than 0.75, and monotherapy with a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor. She has not responded to the maximum recommended dose of sildenafil (i.e., 2 mg/kg/dose four times/day); therefore, Answer A is incorrect. Adding an agent from another class (either an oral endothelin receptor antagonist or an inhaled prostacyclin analog) would be the next step after optimizing her sildenafil, making Answer B correct and Answer D incorrect. Given the technical requirements for a special inhalation delivery system for treprostinil and the frequency of four times/day inhalations, the better option would be oral therapy with bosentan (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: You are asked to develop an initial insulin treatment plan with 0.5 unit/kg/day The patient is an 11-year-old girl (weight 30 kg) with a recent diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus (DM). Her diet is fairly consistent. Which insulin regimen would be most appropriate to initiate in this patient?
options: A. Insulin glargine 15 units subcutaneously once daily in the morning and regular insulin 5 units 30 minutes before each meal.

B. Neutral protamine Hagedorn (NPH) insulin 7 units and insulin lispro 3 units subcutaneously 30 minutes before the morning meal and NPH 3 units and insulin lispro 1.5 units subcutaneously 30 minutes before the evening meal.
C. Insulin detemir 7.5 units subcutaneously once daily in the morning and 2.5 units insulin glulisine 15 minutes before each meal.
D. Insulin glargine 7.5 units subcutaneously once daily in the morning and insulin aspart 2.5 units 15 minutes before each meal.
questions.explanation: Answer: D. The patient is an 11-year-old girl (weight 30 kg) with newly diagnosed type 1 DM who requires insulin. Insulin glargine 7.5 units subcutaneously once daily in the morning and insulin aspart 2.5 units 15 minutes before each meal would be the most appropriate regimen for her, making Answer D correct. This combination of a long-acting basal insulin and a rapid-acting bolus insulin is appropriately dosed according to the patient's weight (15 units daily glargine/rapid-acting regimen but at a dose twice that of the correct answer, = about 0.5 unit/kg/day). Although option A also uses the once daily compared with the low-dose insulin detemir represented in option C, which should be dosed twice daily and, compared with the NPH dosing in regimen in Answer D is incorrect. option B, is associated with less hypoglycemia, making Answers B and C incorrect.

questions.question: H.M. is a 16-year-old male adolescent (body mass index [BMI] 32 kg/m2, greater than the 95th percentile for age) who received a diagnosis of type 2 DM 3 months ago, after which his primary care physician initiated lifestyle modifications and metformin 500 mg twice daily. At diagnosis, H.M.'s hemoglobin A1C level was 8.5%. Last week, his AIC level was 7.7%. He states that his fasting glucose concentrations during the past 1-2 weeks have ranged from 145 mg/dL to 190 mg/dL. He states that he is tolerating the metformin well. Which would be the most appropriate treatment option for H.M. at this time?
options: A. Add exenatide 5 mcg subcutaneously twice daily.
B. Increase metformin dose to 1000 mg twice daily.
C. Discontinue metformin and initiate pioglitazone 15 mg daily.
D. Add insulin aspart 5 units subcutaneously 15 minutes before meals.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. The most appropriate intervention at this time would be to increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily (Answer B), making this the correct answer. The AlC level is not at the target value, but the patient is not at the maximal daily metformin dosage (2000 mg daily in children 10 years or older). It would be more appropriate to maximize metformin monotherapy than to add another drug. Metformin is the initial therapy recommended by the ADA for adolescents. In addition, metformin is the only non-insulin DM drug labeled for use in children and adolescents. Although lack of an labeled indication is not always a reason not to use a medication, especially in pediatrics, metformin has the most literature supporting its use and superior efficacy compared with Answers A and C. Moreover, given the patient's mild degree of hyperglycemia, adding insulin at this time is unwarranted (Answer D), and a basal insulin would most likely be the choice when it is warranted.

questions.question: A 6-year-old (weight 17 kg, body surface area [BSA] 0.9 m2) is given a diagnosis of central diabetes insipidus (DI). Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: A. Desmopressin 0.05 mg orally twice daily.
B. Hydrocortisone 3 mg orally every 8 hours plus fludrocortisone 0.05mg orally once daily.
C. Water restriction of no more than 900 mL/day.
D. Sapropterin 170 mg orally once daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Answer A, desmopressin, is the first-line therapy for DI. It is typically dosed at 0.05 mg twice daily for children younger than 12 years. Answer C is incorrect because, although polyuria is an issue, it is not because of its extra fluid but because an inappropriate release of fluid and water restriction could lead to dehydration. Similarly, Answer B is incorrect; although steroids might affect water retention, they do not address the underlying problem, and central DI is not associated with steroid imbalances. Answer D is a synthetic cofactor BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) and would have no impact on this disease.

questions.question: A 4-year-old (weight 12 kg. BSA 0.8 m2) is given a diagnosis of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: A. Desmopressin 0.05 mg orally twice daily.
B. Hydrocortisone 2 mg orally every 8 hours plus fludrocortisone 0.05 mg orally once daily.
C. Water restriction of no more than 800 mL/day.
D. Furosemide 24 mg orally once daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. For SIADH, water restriction (Answer C) is first-line therapy. This is usually limited to no more than 1000 mL/m2/day. Answers A and B are not the best choices because the problem is with fluid retention, and these would make it worse. Answer D is a diuretic and would facilitate water removal but is usually instituted after water restriction has failed.

questions.question: A 10-year-old (weight 25 kg, BSA 1.4 m2) receives a diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: A. Desmopressin 0.05 mg orally twice daily.
B. Hydrocortisone 4 mg orally every 8 hours plus fludrocortisone 0.05 mg orally once daily.
C. Fluid replacement of more than 1400 mL/day.
D. Sapropterin 120 mg orally once daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. In adrenal insufficiency, replacement of steroids is paramount. The combination of hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone (Answer B) ensures both glucocorticoid and mineral corticoid replacement. Although dehydration is a problem, use of Answers A and C to retain fluid is not recommended, nor do they address the underlying problem. Answer D is a synthetic cofactor BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) and would have no impact on this disease.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl (weight 40 kg) has just been given a diagnosis of Hashimoto disease. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
options: A. Methimazole 20 mg orally once daily.
B. Liothyronine 25 mcg orally once daily on an empty stomach.
C. Levothyroxine 175 mcg orally once daily on an empty stomach.
D. Iodide 150 mg orally thrice daily in water or juice.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. Hashimoto disease is primary hypothyroidism for which the treatment of choice is levothyroxine at 4-5 mcg/kg/day (Answer C). Although Answer A, methimazole, and Answer B, liothyronine, replace T3, they are very expensive, have a shorter half-life and have an increased adverse effect profile. Answer D, iodide, are antithyroid drugs and do not address the underlying problem.

questions.question: A 12-year-old (weight 40 kg) has just been given a diagnosis of Graves disease. Which is the most appropriate initial therapy?
options: A. Methimazole 20 mg orally once daily.
B. Liothyronine 25 mcg orally once daily on an empty stomach.
C. Levothyroxine 175 mcg orally once daily on an empty stomach.
D. Iodide 150 mg orally three times daily in water or juice.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. For primary hyperthyroidism in children, antithyroid drugs are considered first line to check whether remission can be achieved without causing permanent hypothyroidism. Answer A, methimazole, is the preferred agent because of its better safety profile and once-daily dosing. Answers B and C are thyroid replacement therapies and are used in Graves disease only after permanent hypothyroidism has been induced by radiation or surgery. Answer D is used for short-term treatment, usually pre- or post-radiation or surgery, so it is not the best option.

questions.question: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA), which blood glucose (plasma) value most accurately depicts the targeted fasting goal for a 14-year-old with type 1 DM?
questions.explanation: Answer: D. The fasting goal for those 13-19 years of age is 90-130 mg/dL. Their bedtime goal is 90-150 mg/dL (Answer D is correct; Answer B and C are incorrect). Answer A, less than 180 mg/dL, is a postprandial range.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy (weight 12 kg, BSA 0.8 m2) has had a slow onset in his symptoms of DI. He did not have a prompt increase in osmolality to the water deprivation test. The patient is being treated for underlying conditions. He is on a diet that maximizes calories while limiting salt intake and is currently on hydrochlorothiazide. He is currently uncontrolled. Which is the most appropriate adjunctive treatment?
questions.explanation: Answer: D. Answer D, amiloride, is the preferred medication to be used with thiazide diuretics because of its safety profile and potassium-sparing effect. Answer B, indomethacin, could be used, but it has more safety concerns. Answer A, desmopressin, is not effective in nephrogenic DI because of the kidneys' resistance to it. The slow onset of symptoms and failure of the water deprivation test suggest nephrogenic DI. Chlorothiazide, Answer C, could be used as therapy, but because the patient is already on a thiazide, this would not be a good additive option.

questions.question: A patient with type 1 DM weighs 60 kg, and you want to initiate her on a new insulin regimen. You decide to use a 2-injection NPH/short-acting regimen. Which represents the most appropriate starting dose?
options: A. 7 units of NPH and 13 units of short acting in the morning plus 5 units of NPH and 5 units of short acting in the evening.
B. 7 units of NPH and 7 units of short acting in the morning plus 7 units of NPH and 7 units of short acting in the evening.
C. 13 units of NPH and 7 units of short acting in the morning plus 7 units of NPH and 3 units of short acting in the evening.
D. 27 units of NPH and 13 units of short acting in the morning plus 13 units of NPH and 6 units of short acting in the evening.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. Using 0.5 tnit/kg, the TDD is 30 units. For NPH, using the two-thirds morning and one-third evening method would yield 13 units of NPH and 7 units of short acting in the morning plus 7 units of NPH and 3 units of short acting in the evening (Answer C). Although Answer A has an appropriate evening dose, the morning dose is reversed. Answer B does not divide the doses appropriately. Answer D uses a starting dose of 1 unit/kg, which may be too aggressive.

questions.question: A patient with type 1 DM weighs 60 kg, and you want to initiate a new insulin regimen. You decide to use an intensive basal/bolus glargine/short- acting regimen. Which represents the most appropriate starting glargine dose?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Using 0.5 unit/kg, the TDD is 30 units. For this type of regimen, the basal dose is usually about 50% of TDD, which is 15 units (Answer B). Answer A would be 50% of a TDD that is less than 0.3 unit/kg or only about 25% of an appropriate TDD. Either way, it would not provide the best chance of lowering blood glucose to an appropriate level. Answers C and D both overestimate the patient's basal needs and would probably result in hypoglycemic periods.

questions.question: A patient with type 1 DM weighs 60 kg, and you want to initiate a new insulin regimen. You decide to use an intensive basal/bolus glargine/shon. acting regimen. Which represents the most appropriate starting I: CHO for dosing?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Using 0.5 unit/kg, the TDD is 30 units. One of the most common methods to calculate an I:CHO is the 500 method: 500/TDD = around 16. Answer B comes closest to this number. Answer A is twice as aggressive and might be calculated if 1 unit/kg were used for the TDD. Answers C and D are much smaller doses and might be calculated if using a TDD of 0.25 unit/kg or less. They also might be achieved if using the formula for ISF instead of I:CHO.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl presents with Graves disease. Her TSH is low, and her free T4 is 0.5 times higher than the upper limit of normal. She has been experiencing diarrhea, weight loss, and some vision changes. Which would be considered the best initial treatment for her?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. For primary hyperthyroidism in children, antithyroid drugs are considered first line to determine whether remission can be achieved without causing permanent hypothyroidism. Methimazole is the preferred agent because of its better safety profile and once-daily dosing (Answer B). Answer A is an option for treatment and is first line in adults. However, because of safety concerns in children, it is reserved for older children with lack of response to antithyroid medications. Answer C is a valid option because it is an antithyroid medication; however, it is not preferred to methimazole because of its adverse effect profile, including hepatotoxicity, and three-times-daily dosing. Answer D is used for short-term treatment usually pre- or post-radiation or surgery, so it is not the best option.

questions.question: A 15-year-old male adolescent with type 1 DM presents with hypothyroidism. His TSH is high, and his free T4 is 0.25 times lower than the lower limit of normal. He has been experiencing constipation, weight gain, and fatigue. Which would be considered the best initial treatment for him?
questions.explanation: Answer: C. The treatment of choice for hypothyroidism is levothyroxine (Answer C). Although Answers A and B are also replacement therapies, they are not preferred in children. Answer A, liothyronine, replaces T3 only, so it has a much shorter half-life. It is also very expensive and has an increased adverse effect profile with no demonstrated benefits. Answer B. desiccated thyroid, has a large degree of variability from dose to dose and carries the possibility of antigenicity. Answer D, Lugol's solution, is used for short-term treatment of hyperthyroidism, usually pre- or post-radiation or surgery, so this is not an option.

questions.question: A 15-year-old African American female adolescen (weight 51 kg) presents with a 2-month history of epigastric pain. She states that she likes to eat spicy food and that she drinks caffeinated beverages three times a day but that she does not feel she has changed her eating habits since the symptoms began. The pain is not relieved by eating, and she has tried over-the-counter (OTC) antacids without much relief. Which recommendation is best for this patient?
options: A. Have her eliminate spicy foods and carbonated beverages from diet.
B. Initiate ranitidine 75 mg twice daily.
C. Initiate omeprazole 20 mg twice daily.
D. Refer her to a gastroenterologist.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. In children and adolescents with recurrent heartburn, a 2- to 4- week trial of a PPI is warranted (Answer C). There is no evidence to support the elimination of a food from the diet, so Answer A is incorrect. Because this patient has tried OTC antacids and the patient's symptoms have lasted for 2 months, an H2RA (Answer B) would probably not be effective at this time. Therapy with an H2RA would be recommended for occasional heartburn symptoms. At this time, the patient's symptoms do not warrant referral to a gastroenterologist (Answer D). If, after 3 months, the heartburn persists on PPI or recurs after therapy is discontinued, a referral would be recommended.

questions.question: An 8-month-old girl with a 2-day history of diarrhea presents with decreased oral intake and "dry crying," and she has been more irritable. On physical examination, the mucosa is moderately dry, the eyes are slightly sunken, skin turgor is decreased, and the fontanelle is slightly reduced. Capillary refill is about 4 seconds. The mother states that she has not changed formulas (cow's milk formula) but wonders if her daughter could be allergic to milk. She has not introduced any new foods to her diet. There has been a recent family history of gastroenteritis. Which is the best initial management for this patient?
options: A. Recommend to change to a soy-based formula.
D. Initiate loperamide 1 mg with each loose stool.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient likely has diarrhea secondary to gastroenteritis. Answer A is incorrect; although there may be transient lactose intolerance with gastroenteritis, changing to a soy formula is not recommended. The patient's degree of dehydration seems to be moderate, and the patient is taking some oral feeds, making Answer B an appropriate choice. Intravenous fluid replacement (Answer C) would be indicated for severe dehydration, and oral replacement has been shown to be as effective as intravenous replacement in mild to moderate dehydration. Answer D is incorrect because an antidiarrheal would not be recommended for acute gastroenteritis or for an individual this age.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy with cerebral palsy and severe developmental delay presents to the clinic for a follow- up appointment from 3 months ago. On questioning, his parents state that he has only stooled an average of twice a week since his last clinic visit and that, when he does have a bowel movement (BM), the stools are very hard, and he seems to have pain with defecation. Which is the best initial management for this patient?
options: A. 1 infant glycerin suppository as needed for constipation.
B. Docusate sodium 10 mg four times daily.
C. Mineral oil 120 mL twice daily.
D. Polyethylene glycol 1.5 g/kg/day for 3-6 days.
questions.explanation: Answer: D. given this patient's clinical presentation, he meets the Rome III criteria for constipation. Treatment for impaction is needed, so glycerin (Answer A) would not be a good option (glycerin is good for maintenance/prevention). Answer B is incorrect because although docusate sodium would offer stool-softening properties, it is indicated for the prevention of constipation, not as a sole agent for the treatment of impaction. Although mineral oil (Answer C) would treat impaction, it would not be recommended in this age group or in the presence of neurologic dysfunction (risk of aspiration). Answer D, polyethylene glycol, is correct because this is the recommended first-line therapy for disimpaction. Polyethylene glycol has a relatively safe adverse effect profile; however, but its use would warrant electrolyte evaluation, and it would be contraindicated if this patient were to have a bowel obstruction.

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy with newly diagnosed Crohn disease (CD) is admitted to the hospital for induction of remission secondary to weight loss and concern for disease progression. His Pediatric Crohn's Disease Activity Index score is 45. Which is the best induction regimen for this patient?
options: B. Mesalamine 50 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. Answer A, exclusive enteral nutrition, although recommended by the European Society as potential first-line therapy, would not be the best therapy at this time because of the concern for disease progression. Most clinicians aim for a rapid remission induction, and it can take weeks to see the effects of exclusive enteral nutrition. Answer B is incorrect because, according to the Pediatric Crohn's Disease Activity Index score, this child has moderate to severe CD; therefore, mesalamine would not be recommended. Mercaptopurine (Answer D) is used in maintenance therapy, and prednisone is the drug of choice for induction in severe cases. If this patient were unable to tolerate an oral trial of prednisone (Answer C), intravenous methylprednisolone would be warranted.

questions.question: A 13-year-old presents with a history of moderate ulcerative colitis (UC) and has been treated with corticosteroids for week with a good response. The patient is able to swallow pills and has a documented reaction to Bactrim. Which agent would be best for maintenance therapy?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient with documented moderate disease has been responsive to steroids. Prednisone (Answer A) would be used for initial or induction therapy, not maintenance. An aminosalicylate agent would be the best therapy at this time. Mesalamine (Answer B) would be preferred to sulfasalazine (Answer C) because of the patient's possible allergy to sulfa (patient has a documented allergy to Bactrim). Answer D is incorrect because azathioprine is reserved for steroid-dependent disease.

questions.question: A 4-week-old, former 26 weeks' gestation, infant developed surgical necrotizing enterocolitis on day of life 7 and had 100 cm of small intestine removed and ileocecal valve removed. The patient, now 2 months of age, has achieved only moderate growth while on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) and has had an increased number and volume of stools since starting low-volume continuous enteral feeds. The patient has been on diphenoxylate and atropine at a dose of 0.3 mg/kg/day in four divided doses for 1 week with no improvement. Which recommendation is best for this patient?
options: A. Increase diphenoxylate/atropine to 0.5 mg/kg/day in four divided doses.
C. Initiate octreotide 10 mcg/kg/dose intravenously every 12 hours.
D. Initiate ursodiol 10 mg/kg/dose orally every 8 hours.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient has diarrhea secondary to SBS, probably caused by initiation of feeds, and is refractory to starting low-volume, continuous feeds. Discontinuing diphenoxylate/ atropine (Answer B) is correct because if no improvement occurs after around 48 hours of use, it should be discontinued because the medication will unlikely effective. Answer A is incorrect because increasing the dose above the recommended range would potentially cause additional adverse effects with little change in efficacy. Octreotide (Answer C) is incorrect because it is generally reserved for patients with diarrhea secondary to graft-vs.-host disease and has few data supporting routine use. The option to use ursodiol (Answer D) is incorrect because the patient is not reported to have cholestasis, and the patient is only on low-volume feeds. Ursodiol should not be initiated for PNALD until the patient is on full, or close to full, feeds (hyperosmolar solution).

questions.question: A patient with a history of short bowel syndrome (SBS) with only a few centimeters of the terminal ileum remaining recently underwent an anastomosis and ostomy takedown. The patient has been maintaining growth with increased enteral feeds and has weaned to 30% of total daily nutrition requirements given parenterally. However, the patient has been experiencing diarrhea and has skin breakdown in the diaper area. Which recommendation is best for this patient at this time?
options: A. Decrease enteral feeds and increase TPN until diarrhea resolves.
B. Draw B12 levels and initiate B12 replacement, if necessary.
C. Initiate cholestyramine 240 mg/kg/day in three divided doses.
D. Initiate loperamide 0.08 mg/kg/day in two or three divided doses.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. This patient's diarrhea with irritation is likely a result of decreased bile acid absorption from extensive ileal resection. Answer A is incorrect because the patient has been able to tolerate progress of enteral feeds, and unless she is losing weight, increasing TPN will not be beneficial. Answer B is incorrect; although vitamin B12 can be deficient in this population, the acute issue is the diarrhea and resulting malabsorption. Answer C, adding cholestyramine, would help decrease the diarrhea associated with increased bile acids, which is also likely causing skin irritation. Loperamide (Answer D) would be an option for diarrhea if it becomes chronic, but more information on the patient's age and clinical status is needed. Loperamide can also cause bacterial overgrowth, which may worsen malabsorption.

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl presents to the emergency department for right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, and inability to walk. Imaging and surgery confirm perforated appendicitis. Which postoperative antibiotic regimen is most appropriate for this patient?
options: A. One dose of metronidazole postoperatively.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. because this patient has perforated appendicitis, antibiotics should be continued postoperatively, making Answer A incorrect. Answer B is incorrect because clindamycin should be avoided given increasing resistance. Although single-agent therapy (Answer D) has been used, this patient appears to have no risk factors for resistance that would warrant use of a carbapenem. The best choice for this patient would be ceftriaxone and metronidazole (Answer C), which would provide coverage for the gram-negative and anaerobic organisms involved (similar to the recommendations in the IDSA guidelines for community-acquired intraabdominal infections).

questions.question: A previously healthy 4-year-old girl presents with a history of intermittent vomiting occurring at least once a month for the past year. Each time this occurs, she will vomit about 10 times for a 24- to 48-hour period. Some of the episodes have also occurred with an upper respiratory tract infection or otitis media, but each episode begins with complaints of nausea in the morning. followed by vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia, and dizziness. Her mother has a history of migraine headaches. The child's medical history is otherwise negative, and on physical examination, her growth, neurologic examination, and vital signs are all normal. A basic metabolic panel is ordered, which is within normal limits, and her upper GI series was normal. In addition to lifestyle modification, such as sleep hygiene, which is the most appropriate next step for this child?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient has cyclic vomiting, for which prophylactic therapy is recommended if symptoms occur more than once every other month, patients are hospitalized, or quality of life is affected. Tricyclic antidepressants are generally recommended as recommended for patients younger than 5 years, whereas amitriptyline is first-line therapy. Cyproheptadine is recommended for those older than 5 years. This patient is 4 years old, so amitriptyline (Answer A) would not be the best choice, making cyproheptadine the best answer (Answer B). Diphenhydramine (Answer C) has been used for sedation during acute episodes, but it would not be used for prophylactic therapy. Answer D is incorrect because ketorolac would also be used during an acute episode for severe abdominal pain, not for prophylaxis.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and a positive rapid urease test. He has a history of iron-deficiency anemia and a family history of gastric cancer. The patient has no known drug allergies. Which is best for this child?
options: A. Treatment not recommended until positive biopsy results.
B. Amoxicillin plus clarithromycin plus proton pump inhibitor (PPI).
C. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole plus sucralfate.
D. Metronidazole plus bismuth subsalicylate plus PPI.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Answer A is incorrect because eradication therapy is recommended for a patient with pediatric ulcer disease and a family history of gastric cancer. A three-agent regimen is recommended, which should always include amoxicillin, making Answer D incorrect. Answer C is incorrect because a PPI is recommended (or bismuth salt), not sucralfate. Sucralfate may also inhibit nutrient absorption. When choosing between clarithromycin and metronidazole, metronidazole is the better choice if the suspected resistance to clarithromycin is greater than 20%. Answer B is correct because it include three agents, amoxcillin, a PPI, and there is no indication for clarithromycin resistance.

questions.question: A 3-month-old boy presents to the clinic with a 1-month history of spitting up after at least two feedings per day. The patient is otherwise healthy and has been able to finish all of his bottles (breast milk), despite spitting up. At this visit, he is at the 75th percentile for weight and height. Which is the best recommendation for this patient?
options: A. Parental education, reassurance, anticipatory guidance.
B. 2-week trial of extensively hydrolyzed formula.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. This patient would be considered a healthy infant with uncomplicated recurrent regurgitation. Because he had adequate weight gain and nutrition status, changing formula (Answer B) would not be recommended but parental education and encouragement would be appropriate for this patient (Answer A).
