Answers C and D are incorrect because antisecretory therapy is not recommended unless other complications occur from symptoms. In addition, PPIs are not approved for use in GERD in patients younger than 1 year.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy with functional constipation has been treated successfully for impaction. The patient, a former 26 weeks gestation NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) graduate, has a history of some developmental delay secondary to small, bilateral intraventricular hemorrhages and chronic lung disease managed with inhaled corticosteroids and occasional diuretic therapy. He is currently on a regular diet supplemented with PediaSure. His bowel regimen before this recent impaction included docusate sodium 20 ml. twice daily and polyethylene glycol daily. The caregiver, who reports no adherence issues, asks for recommendations to avoid impaction in the future Which is best for this patient?
options: A. Bisacodyl 5 mg by mouth daily.
B. Lactulose 7.5 mL by mouth daily.
C. Magnesium citrate 100 mL by mouth daily.
D. Senna 10 mL by mouth daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. According to this patient's history, he has been unable to be maintained on polyethylene glycol (first-line therapy for maintenance therapy). Lactulose (Answer B), the recommended second-line therapy, is generally well tolerated in children. Answer A is incorrect because bisacodyl is not recommended for daily use. Magnesium citrate (Answer C) would not be used for maintenance therapy. Answer D is incorrect; although senna may be used as a second-line agent, the dosing is incorrect for this patient's age.

questions.question: A 4-month-old boy presents with a history of spitting up three times per day for the past 3 weeks. His mother reports no apnea or posturing, and the patient has met all developmental milestones and maintained good growth velocity during the past few months. In fact, his mother states that he is taking bottles every 3 hours and is sometimes hungry between feedings, for which the mother may give another half bottle. However, the patient does have some irritability with these episodes. Which is best for this patient?
options: A. Educate the parents on overfeeding and warning signs.
B. Change to an anti-regurgitation formula.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. This patient is a "happy spitter." Although he has some irritability, no warning signs are present, and the patient is maintaining adequate growth. Overfeeding may be an issue, so patient education and correction of feeding practices would be the best recommendation at this time (Answer A is correct). An anti-regurgitation formula (Answer B is incorrect) might be warranted if the child continued to have symptoms after adjusting volume Answers C and D are incorrect because neither antisecretory nor promotility agents are recommended for physiologic infant regurgitation.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy (weight 50 kg) presents to the clinic with a recent history of heartburn and epigastric pain. He reports an increase in frequency during the past month and states that symptoms are present most days. Which is best for this patient?
options: A. Initiate lifestyle change addressing obesity.
B. Initiate lifestyle change addressing obesity, and start omeprazole 20 mg/day for 2-4 weeks.
C. Initiate lansoprazole 30 mg/day for 2-4 weeks.
D. Initiate ranitidine 75 mg with meals.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Obesity, which is likely a contributing factor to this patient's reflux, should be managed; moreover, because of the increasing frequency and pain associated with the patient's episodes, a 2- to 4-week trial of a PPI is warranted (Answer B is correct). Either therapy alone would not be as effective: therefore, the combination would be the most appropriate answer, making Answers A and C incorrect. Ranitidine (Answer D) is recommended for occasional heartburn, but because this patient is having recurrent symptoms, ranitidine is not the best therapy for him.

questions.question: A 14-year-old white male adolescent with cystic fibrosis is admitted to the hospital for a second course of intravenous antibiotic therapy in a 1-month period. After 10 days of the current antibiotic therapy, the patient begins to have profuse, watery diarrhea. He is also having severe abdominal pain, with abdominal fullness and fever. Testing is positive for C. difficile. Which is the best initial therapy for him?
options: B. Initiate metronidazole 30 mg/kg/day orally divided every 6 hours.
C. Initiate vancomycin 40 mg/kg/day orally divided every 6 hours.
D. Initiate fidaxomicin 200 mg orally twice daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Patients with cystic fibrosis are at an increased risk of C. difficile, and this patient has had recent (and current) antibiotic exposure. Answer A is incorrect because discontinuing antibiotics would not be optimal in and vancomycin are options, metronidazole is the better option because this is the patient's first case of C. difficile,nidazole ironidazole has been shown to be more cost-effective. making Answer B correct and Answer C incorrect. Answer D is incorrect because fidaxomicin is generally reserved for toxic megacolon and refractory cases after several trials with oral metronidazole and vancomycin.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy with constipation is not adhering to his laxative regimen and has fecal impaction. Which is the best treatment for stool evacuation?
questions.explanation: Answer: C. For disimpaction therapy, polyethylene glycol is recommended first line (Answer C). Bisacodyl suppositories (Answer A), although a second- line agent, would not be recommended for disimpaction because the rectal formulation might be inserted into the middle of the stool, preventing it from coming into contact with the mucosa. Magnesium hydroxide (Answer B) is used for maintenance therapy, and contrast enemas (Answer D) are only recommended for intractable constipation..

questions.question: A 14-year-old presents with a 6-month history of abdominal pain, headache, and occasional back pain. These symptoms occur before stooling, and when stooling occurs, it is soft and mushy. No constipation has been reported during this time. The episodes have been occurring about five times a month. Dietary changes, involving avoidance of milk and caffeine, have not resulted in symptom improvement. Which describes the best treatment option for this patient?
options: A. Initiate a trial of a gluten-free diet.
questions.explanation: Answer: D. In a patient with IBS, the goals of therapy include a return to a normal bowel function, elimination of symptoms, and improvement in quality of life. Unfortunately, this is often unachievable by medications alone. Answer A is incorrect because avoiding gluten in the absence of celiac markers is not helpful. Ibuprofen (Answer B), which may aggravate symptoms, should not be used for pain in patients with IBS. Answer C is incorrect; although fluoxetine would help with regulation of GI motility, it is often used in IBS-C because the adverse effect can be diarrhea. Amitriptyline (Answer D) would be a reasonable choice because it has been shown effective in IBS-D and would help with the patient's other symptoms as well.

questions.question: A 15-year-old male adolescent received a diagnosis of CD of the colon 6 months ago. He has had active disease, despite 5 months of mercaptopurine therapy and two courses of corticosteroid therapy. Which is most likely to induce remission?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient would be considered refractory because maintenance therapy did not prevent two courses of corticosteroid therapy. Azathioprine (Answer A) is used for maintenance therapy, not induction. Answer C is incorrect because mesalamine would be used for induction in mild to moderate, not severe, disease. Answer D is incorrect because methotrexate is generally used for maintenance therapy, and there are data on infliximab (Answer B) use for both induction and maintenance.

questions.question: A 17-year-old female adolescent presents with an 8-week history of new. onset abdominal pain and 3-4 bloody stools per day. She reports an allergy to "sulfa"-containing medications (documented as wheezing). Colonoscopy reveals a diagnosis of UC, with lesions extending beyond the rectum. Which is best for this patient?
questions.explanation: Answer: B. According to this patient's symptoms, she has mild disease. disease extends beyond the rectum. Oral mesalamine is used for initial treatment with mild disease (Answer B). Because of the patient's sulfa allergy, not be appropriate Answer C, using sulfasalazine, would not be recommended, although it would otherwise be a choice for initial treatment. Answer D is incorrect because intravenous corticosteroids would be indicated for initial therapy in severe disease.

questions.question: A 16-year-old, previously healthy patient presents with nausea and periumbilical pain that has radiated to right lower quadrant pain during the past 24 hours. She has been unable to eat since the onset of these symptoms. She currently has a temperature of 38.1^CC(100.6^CF), and on physical examination she has positive rebound tenderness. When asked to cough, she winces in pain. Her CBC has a WBC of 15times10^3cells/mm^3 Which is best for this patient?
options: A. Admit patient for monitoring; no antibiotics are required at this time.
B. Admit patient for monitoring, and initiate piperacillin/tazobactam.
C. Consult surgery, and initiate ceftriaxone and metronidazole.
D. Consult surgery, and initiate cefotaxime and clindamycin.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. According to the Pediatric Appendicitis Scoring Tool, this patient is considered at high risk of appendicitis, and admission with surgical consult is warranted. The need for appendectomy would be assessed with further diagnostic imaging and clinical response. Antibiotic therapy would need to be initiated because of the patient's high-risk status, making Answer A incorrect. The IDSA guidelines report the success of single, dual, and triple therapy. However, this patient was previously healthy and would not need pseudomonal coverage with piperacillin/ tazobactam (too broad) at this time (Answer B). Answer D is incorrect; although cefotaxime is considered appropriate, clindamycin should be avoided because of resistance. However, ceftriaxone and metronidazole would be an appropriate initial antibiotic regimen.

questions.question: A 9-year-old African American boy (weight 30 kg) presents with a 2-month history of epigastric abdominal pain, weight loss, and chronic heartburn. He has been taking OTC calcium carbonate 500 mg with each meal and famotidine 40 mg/day, but with only temporary relief. Eating does not seem to help relieve the pain or heartburn. Which is best for this patient?
options: A. Ranitidine 75 mg orally twice daily.
C. Sucralfate 500 mg orally four times daily.
D. Ranitidine 75 mg orally twice daily plus imipramine 25 mg at bedtim.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient, whose OTC therapy has failed, meets the criteria for dyspepsia. Because his pain is not relieved by eating, a gastric ulcer is likely. Answer A is incorrect because the patient has already tried an H2RA and the dose was maximized, so switching to another H2RA would not be beneficial. Without imaging to see whether lesions are present, sucralfate (Answer C) would not be the initial therapy choice. Answer D is incorrect; although the combination of an anticholinergic and an H2RA has been studied in adults, benefit has only been shown in treating duodenal ulcers. After no response to H2RAs, a PPI is second line (Answer B). This patient would also benefit from referral to a gastroenterologist for further workup.

questions.question: D.S. is a 7-year-old boy on week 6 of prednisone therapy for minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS). His dose has been tapered to 40Cmg/m2/ day on alternate days. He has had resolution of his proteinuria but has persistent hypertension in the 95th percentile for age. He has been on both salt and water restriction since the diagnosis. Which is the best approach when initiating antihypertensive medication therapy?
options: A. Enalapril 0.1Cmg/kg/dose by mouth twice daily.
B. Atenolol 0.5 mg/kg/dose by mouth twice daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Enalapril 0.2-0.6Cmg/kg/day has been shown to decrease proteinuria in children with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (Answer A is correct). B-Blockers and calcium channel blockers will not prevent proteinuria, and they have not been studied in children with nephrotic syndrome (Answers B and C are incorrect). The starting dose of lisinopril given is likely too aggressive (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A.N. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who has frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome (FRNS). She has been on intravenous cyclophosphamide plus steroids for the past 6 months, but her family is requesting an oral medication because they are finding it difficult to get to the clinic for her infusions. A.N. is also experiencing alopecia, which she is very self-conscious about. The physician decides to try mycophenolate mofetil because of its potential for less cosmetic adverse effects. Which is the most important counseling point to make to her?
options: A. She should shake the suspension well before taking her doses.
B. She will need to use two forms of oral contraception while on mycophenolate mofetil.
C. She should make sure to take her capsules with a full glass of water.
D. If nausea and vomiting occur, she should contact her physician for an ondansetron prescription.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. An older patient would not likely be using the suspension form of mycophenolate mofetil (Answer A is incorrect). Counseling on oral contraceptive use for an adolescent female that is of childbearing age is the most important counseling point to make of the provided choices. Mycophenolate mofetil is pregnancy category D and has a black box warning stating that women of childbearing age should start on two forms of contraception, ideally 4 weeks before starting mycophenolate mofetil therapy and for 6 weeks after it has been discontinued (Answer B is correct). Although the patient should take her capsules with a full glass of water, this is not the most important counseling point to make (Answer C is incorrect). Nausea/vomiting may occur as an adverse effect of mycophenolate mofetil; however, it is doubtful that ondansetron would prevent it (Answer D is correct).

questions.question: Which patient would be most appropriate to receive antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: A. A 2-week-old boy with unilateral low-grade hydronephrosis.
B. A 1-day-old boy with antenatal hydronephrosis now with neonatal oliguria.
C. An 11-day-old girl with renal bladder ultrasonography showing grade II hydronephrosis.
D. A 6-week-old girl with antenatal hydronephrosis now with voiding cystourethrography showing grade IV vesicoureteral reflux.
questions.explanation: Answer: D. The risk of UTI increases with increasing grade of hydronephrosis and peaks at 40% in children with grade IV hydronephrosis. Antibiotic prophylaxis remains controversial. Epidemiologic-focused studies have weakly recommended that children with mild hydronephrosis receive no prophylaxis, whereas children with more severe disease may benefit (Answers A and C are incorrect). Vesicoureteric reflux occurs in 10%-20% of children with antenatal hydronephrosis; however, a 1-day-old boy with antenatal hydronephrosis now with neonatal oliguria has not yet been confirmed to have VUR (Answer B is incorrect). Many had hoped the RIVUR study would answer these questions definitively; however, the authors made no strong conclusions regarding the role of antimicrobial prophylaxis in children with VUR, but instead, stated that their data support reduced recurrence in treated children. If antibiotic prophylaxis must be done, a 6-week-old girl with antenatal hydronephrosis now with voiding cystourethrography showing grade IV vesicoureteral reflux would be expected to have the most benefit, according to a 2013 meta-analysis, which showed that children with high-grade hydronephrosis who received prophylaxis had a significantly lower UTI rate than those not receiving prophylaxis (Answer D is correct).

questions.question: You stop in a room to visit a mother with a 4-month-old male infant (weight 3.5 kg). The child has presented for failure to thrive, weakness, and polyuria. He is given a diagnosis of type I distal renal tubular acidosis (RTA) according to the following laboratory values: urine pH 6.5; urine sodium 30CmEq/L, potassium 40CmEq/L; urine chloride 20CmEq/L serum sodium 142 mEq potassium 2.8CmEq/L; and sodium bicarbonate 9CmEq/L Ultrasonography reveals the presence of nephrocalcinosis. Which medication would mon accurately be considered first-line therapy in correcting the above laboratory values?
options: A. Hydrochlorothiazide 1Cmg/kg/dose by mouth twice daily.
B. Spironolactone 2Cmg/kg/dose by mouth once daily.
C. Sodium bicarbonate 1-mEq/mL solution 4CmEq/kg/dose by mouth four times daily.
D. Potassium citrate and citric acid (Cytra-K) crystals 2CmEq/kg/doseCb mouth twice daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: D. Hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone are not recommended as first-line treatment of distal RTA (Answers A and B are incorrect). Sodium bicarbonate could be used; however, there is a risk of promoting hypercalciuria because of increased sodium intake, which could increase the risk of renal calculi, and this infant already has nephrocalcinosis (Answer C is incorrect). First-line therapy for distal RTA is potassium citrate, and the usual starting dose is 2-4CmEq/kg/day, which corrects urinary abnormalities while minimizing the risk of calcium oxalate stones.

questions.question: J.W. is a 9-year-old boy with CKD. He is admitted to your unit to rule out urinary tract infection (UTI). He has been febrile for the past 2 days, and his mother notes that his urine has been darker and cloudy. On admission, you note that his serum phosphorous level is 6.2Cmg/dL, and his serum calcium level is 10.8Cmg/dL. You screen his profile and note that he is taking calcium carbonate 500 mg 3 tablets by mouth three times daily with meals. Which is the best intervention for this patient?
options: A. It appears that J.W. does not like the taste of calcium carbonate and is nonadherent to his treatment; suggest changing to calcium acetate capsules.
B. J.W.'s calcium phosphorous product is greater than 65CmgC2/dL2. and he should be changed to a non-calcium-based phosphorous binder like sevelamer hydrochloride.
C. Once J.W.'s serum calcium level is corrected for his chronic low albumin, his calcium phosphorous product will be at goal; no change in therapy is needed.
D. Decrease J.W.'s calcium carbonate to 2 tablets by mouth three times daily with meals because his calcium level is mildly elevated.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. A switch to calcium acetate might increase adherence if that is a problem, but it would not address the high calcium phosphorous product (Answer A is incorrect). No serum albumin is provided; however, CKD serum albumin is typically normal or low. Doing the adjusted equation for calcium that is based on albumin would only yield a higher calcium value, which would still require a change in therapy because the calcium phosphorous product would still be elevated beyond 65CmgC2/dL2 (Answer C is incorrect). Decreasing the calcium carbonate daily dose would address the patient's elevated serum calcium level, but it would not address the elevated serum phosphorous (Answer D is incorrect). The calcium phosphorous product is elevated for this patient, and avoiding a calcium-based phosphate binder is recommended (Answer B is correct).

questions.question: M.M. is a 1-year-old, former 26 weeks' gestational age, boy (weight 9 kg) awaiting a liver transplant for total parenteral nutrition cholestasis/short bowel syndrome secondary to severe necrotizing enterocolitis. During the past 3 months, his renal function has declined. He is currently admitted for peritoneal dialysis (PD) catheter placement and initiation of outpatient PD. The nephrologist drew a serum 25(OH)D level, which was low at 28Cnmol/L She recommendation for this patient? Which product is the best
options: A. Calcitriol 1Cmcg/mL because it does not require renal or hepatic activation.
B. Ergocalciferol 8000 international units/mL because it is affordable and easy to find.
C. Paricalcitol 1-meg capsules because it causes less hypercalcemia and less increase in calcium phosphorous product.
D. Cholecalciferol 400 international units/mL because it tastes better.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Calcitriol is an optimal choice in this infant because of his chronic hepatorenal dysfunction (Answer A is correct). It is unlikely that he would be able to use ergocalciferol to correct his vitamin D levels in a timely manner (Answer B is incorrect). Paricalcitol is currently available only in capsule form, and there is not yet an FDA indication for children. In addition. there is only limited study information for pediatric patients (Answer C is Incorrect). Cholecalciferol may be an option if this patient's insurance will not cover calcitriol or the family cannot afford calcitriol, but it remains less optimal because it still requires renal activation for function (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question:
Questions 74 and 75 pertain to the following case: Team members in the nephrology department call you about an outpatient they are seeing. E.W. is a 7-year-old girl who has been on PD for the past 6 months because of bilateral Wilms tumor. She has a Broviac catheter for her chemotherapy and a future planned bone marrow transplant. She has a history of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection in her Broviac catheter but has not previously had a PD catheter infection. She has cloudy effluent from the PD catheter drainage today, and it is being sent for culture.
74. Which empiric regimen given intraperitoneally is best for her?
options: A. Give cefepime intraperitoneally: 125-mg/L loading dose.
B. Give cefazolin intraperitoneally: 500-mg/L loading dose plus gentamicin intraperitoneal 8-mg/L loading dose.
C. Give vancomycin intraperitoneally: 1000-mg/L loading dose plus cefepime intraperitoneally: 500-mg/L loading dose.
D. Hold off on antibiotics and wait for culture results.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. This child likely has many health care exposures because of her oncology diagnosis. She also possibly has a permanent indwelling central line in addition to her PD catheter for chemotherapy, and she is likely at a high risk of MRSA infection (Answer C is correct). Cefepime intraperitoneally at a 125- mg/L loading dose is incorrect and assumes she has no risk factors for MRSA (Answer A is incorrect). Delaying antibiotics while waiting for culture results is not recommended in the ISPD guidelines for patients with cloudy PD effluent and is likely inappropriate for a presumed immunocompromised patient (Answer D is incorrect). Cefazolin and an aminoglycoside do not address her health care exposure-related risk factors (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: 75. The nephrologist also comments to you that E.W.'s serum calcium has been trending upward, with today's value at 10.2Cmg/dL. She is on a standard PD fluid as well as sevelamer carbonate 800 mg by mouth three times daily with meals as her phosphate binder. Which is the best suggestion?
options: A. Start outpatient pamidronate in the infusion clinic every month.
B. Shorten her dwell time to prevent calcium from absorbing as much.
C. Change her to a low calcium PD solution, and repeat serum phosphorous and calcium in 2 weeks.
D. Increase the frequency of her PD exchanges to remove more solute.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. although a pamidronate infusion may address the serum calcium level, it is unclear whether it is truly necessary in this patient. There are few data on pamidronate use in pediatric patients with stage 4 or 5 CKD, and the benefit may not outweigh the risk (Answer A is incorrect). Shortening the dwell time for PD exchanges will increase the degree of ultrafiltration and urea removal, but typically, it will not increase the removal of phosphorous and will not address mildly elevated serum calcium levels (Answer B is incorrect). The simplest solution would be to change the PD solution to one that contains a lower amount of calcium and repeat electrolyte analysis in 1-2 weeks (Answer C is correct). Increasing the frequency of PD exchanges may increase solute clearance, but a greater proportion of the time is spent draining and filling, and it may be less effective than using a larger dwell volume (if possible, depending on patient size) (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: J.T. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who was initiated on amoxicillin 500 mg by mouth three times daily as an outpatient for strep throat. After a few days of antibiotic, she began to have acute flank pain and urinary urgency, and she noted that her urine had turned darker with a pink tint to it. She is also on drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol (Yasmin) oral contraceptive and loratadine 10 mg by mouth daily and uses topical azelaic acid (Azelex) for acne. The emergene department (ED) has discontinued her amoxicillin for presumes tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN). Which is the most effective way to treat her strep throat?
questions.explanation: Answer: C. Although azithromycin and clarithromycin both have coverage against group A Streptococcus, they have both been associated with the development of TIN (Answers A and D are incorrect). Only clindamycin is not a possible cause of TIN and therefore is the safest drug to prescribe to complete therapy in a patient with acute TIN (Answer C is correct). Cefuroxime lacks adequate coverage against group A Streptococcus, and cephalosporins have been implicated in TIN (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: T.M. is a 12-year-old girl with FSGS that was diagnosed when she was 1 years of age. She had been in a long-term remission for the previous 3 years, but about 6 months ago, she had severe disease reoccurrence that resulted in an episode of acute renal failure. Since then, she has been treated with high-dose prednisone 2Cmg/kg/day and cyclosporine 2.5Cmg/kg/dose by mouth twice daily. Her cyclosporine A trough level with her laboratory tests done at this appointment is 184 ng/mL. She is concerned about weight gain and insomnia Her mother states that she eats healthy but notes that she has gained about 15 lb in the past 6 months. T.M. is being teased at school because of her weight gain and "moon face." Which is the best solution to address this?
options: B. Begin a prednisone taper while monitoring carefully for symptom flare.
C. Suggest dietary modification, keeping fats less than 30% of her total caloric intake.
D. Switch cyclosporine to tacrolimus, which causes less weight gain.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient appears to have had a good response to cyclosporine therapy with additional steroids. She has been in a prolonged remission and is experiencing steroid-driven adverse effects. At this time, a trial of steroid withdrawal would be appropriate to minimize adverse effects (Answer B is correct). Discontinuing cyclosporine would not address this patient's current physical and psychosocial issues (Answer A is incorrect). Further dietary modifications will likely yield little benefit because the patient's mother has stated that the child already eats healthily, and it will not address the patient's insomnia (Answer C is incorrect). Switching from cyclosporine to tacrolimus will have minimal effect on the patient's weight gain because it is driven by the steroid exposure, not the calcineurin inhibitor (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A nurse from the outpatient infusion clinic calls you about T.S., a 10-year- old boy being treated in an outpatient infusion clinic who is scheduled to receive a rituximab infusion today. The nurse asks whether pretreatment is necessary, and if so, which would be best to pretreat with?
options: A. Yes, pretreatment is recommended with methylprednisolone, acetaminophen, and diphenhydramine.
B. Yes, pretreatment is recommended with a saline fluid bolus, acetaminophen. and diphenhydramine.
C. No, pretreatment is unnecessary unless the child has experienced a reaction in the past.
D. No, pretreatment is unnecessary; infusion-related reactions are uncommon with rituximab.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Rituximab (Rituxan) is FDA labeled to be administered after pretreatment with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine to minimize the risk of infusion reactions (Answer C is incorrect). Rituximab carries a black box warning stating the risk for fatal infusion reactions (Answer D is incorrect). Rituximab is not FDA indicated for the treatment of nephrotic syndrome, and the use of a corticosteroid as a premedication is not mandated. Most studies involving rituximab for the treatment of nephrotic syndrome have used pretreatment with intravenous methylprednisolone 30 minutes before the rituximab infusion. Pretreatment with methylprednisolone, acetaminophen, and diphenhydramine meets the rituximab package insert requirements and adds additional coverage as extrapolated from other indications (Answer A is correct). Pretreatment with crystalloids may help prevent hypotension, but crystalloids are not formally recommended, and use should be reserved for patients who experience symptomatic hypotension during infusion (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: A urologist is consulting on a newborn in the neonatal ICU that you cover. The infant is a 2-month-old born at 34 weeks. The infant was noted to have antenatal hydronephrosis, and ultrasonography today reveals grade IV hydronephrosis. The nephrologist would like a recommendation for an antibiotic to initiate. Which recommendation do you believe is best?
options: A. Give sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim 3 mg trimethoprim per kilogram per day.
C. Currently, the risk of antibiotic therapy in a newborn outweighs the benefit.
D. CAP is not recommended because of the risk of antibiotic resistance.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. The recommendation from a large meta-analysis published in 2013 was to use CAP in patients with high-grade hydronephrosis; however, the meta-analysis was based on low-quality evidence. A subsequent randomized placebo-controlled trial in 2014 (RIVUR) compared children treated with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim suspension 3 mg of trimethoprim per kilogram per day with placebo. The authors found that the risk of febrile or symptomatic recurrence of UTI was reduced by half among children who received prophylaxis compared with those who received placebo (Answer C is Incorrect). Despite this finding, the authors stated that cost-effectiveners and decision analysis studies were needed to further clarify the role of antimicrobial prophylaxis. The nephrologist has already chosen to initiate therapy according to the evidence available. The best choice would be initiating therapy with the agent and dosing according to the RIVUR study because the trial included the same age group this patient represents and has the most objective data supporting it (Answer A is correct). Nitrofurantoin has not been studied in a The relative risk of antibiotic therapy has not been adequately clarified to state controlled manner for the prevention of UTI in VUR (Answer B is incorrect) that it is unsafe. Antimicrobial resistance is a concern, but it has not been well studied (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl (weight 13 kg) presents with failure to thrive. She has no history of diarrhea or vomiting. Serum electrolyte values are sodium 136 mEq/L, chloride 111 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 13CmEq/L Urine electrolyte values are sodium 30CmEq/L, chloride 40CmEq/L, and potassium 20CmEq/L. Urine pH is 6.5. Which best depicts the plasma anion gap?
questions.explanation: Answer: A. Plasma anion gap is calculated by [serum sodium (serum Olcarbonate])+[chloride]) or [136CmEq/L]-(113CmEq/L)+[111CmEqL])=12 mEq/L (Answer A is correct; Answers B-D are incorrect).

questions.question: C.J. is a 12-day-old girl (weight 3.2 kg) admitted to the ED with severe dehydration, vomiting, jaundice, and failure to thrive. She is noted to have a urine pH of 5.0, serum sodium of 130CmEq/L potassium of 6.4CmEq/L; and bicarbonate of 18CmEq/L. Her SCr is 0.6Cmg/dL The ED physician administers intravenous fluids and gives intravenous sodium bicarbonate, with minimal resolution of her acid-base imbalance. Hypoaldosteronism is suspected with type 4 RTA. Which is the next best treatment for the physician to give in an effort to combat the persistent hyperkalemia?
options: C. Normal saline bolus 10CmL/kg over 1 hour.
D. Spironolactone 2Cmg/kg by mouth once daily.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. This patient has the classic symptoms of type 4 RTA. inchading hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, with a plasma bicarbonate of 15CmEq/L or greater and a mild decrease in GFR. Treatment with sodium bicarbonate alone may help correct the acid-base imbalance acutely but does not address the underlying cause, which is aldosterone deficiency or resistance. Lowering the infant's potassium level is a long-term solution, but it would not help acutely in the ED setting (Answer A is incorrect). Intravenous sodium chloride may help replace sodium and fluid deficit but will likely not fully correct the patient's hyperkalemia (Answer C is incorrect). Spironolactone may exacerbate hyperkalemia and hyponatremia because spironolactone is an aldosterone blocker that competes with aldosterone for receptor sites in the distal renal tubule (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: M.M. is a 16-year-old male HD-dependent patient (weight 82 kg) who ha had ESRD for 2 years. He is awaiting a possible kidney transplant. He has history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and anemia. Lately, the nephrologisth have been struggling to get M.M.'s serum phosphorous level under control, and adherence is an issue. Medications are as follows: epoetin 20,000 units thre times weekly at dialysis; B-complex with C multivitamin once daily pravastatin 20Cmg/day; ramipril 5Cmg/day amlodipine 10Cmg/day; and calcium acetate 1334 mg three times daily with meals. Laboratory values are as follows hemoglobin 9.8Cg/L; iPTH 800Cpg/mL sodium 142 mEq/L potassium 4.3 mEq/L; SCr 4.1Cmg/dL calcium 10.8Cmg/dL; albumin 2.5Cg/L and phosphoruy 6.9Cmg/dL. In addition to enforcing adherence to both medications and diet which is the best approach to managing this patient's hyperparathyroidism and renal osteodystrophy?
options: B. Add ergocalciferol 50,000-unit capsule by mouth once weekly.
C. Change calcium acetate to sevelamer carbonate, and add cinacalcet.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. This patient has an elevated iPTH (800Cpg/dL), which increases his risk of renal osteodystrophy, and high serum phosphorous and serum calcium levels. He is already taking a large dose of calcium acetate and has an elevated calcium phosphorous product of 74CmgC2/dL2 (goal less than 55 mg2/dL2). Increasing the calcium acetate dose may not add much benefit and may further increase his risk of calcium deposition in soft tissue (Answer A is incorrect). Ergocalciferol may be beneficial for this patient, but because of his ESRD, he may be unable to properly convert ergocalciferol to activated vitamin D, which could worsen his hypercalcemia (Answer B is incorrect). Calcitriol would not address the patient's elevated serum phosphorous and could worsen his hypercalcemia (Answer D is incorrect). The correct choice would be to change him to a non-calcium-based phosphorous binder like sevelamer and add cinacalcet to lower iPTH (Answer C is correct). Cinacalcet has not been studied in pediatric patients, but for this patient, who is 16 years of age with a weight of 82 kg, it would be appropriate. However, because of the recent clinical hold on cinacalcet, it would be prudent to alert caregivers to the risks and benefits associated with cinacalcet therapy and ensure proper monitoring.

questions.question:
Questions 83 and 84 pertain to the following case: T.B. is a 2-month-old girl (weight 4.23 kg) with CKD caused by autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. She is being seen urgently in the nephrology clinic today because her mother reports increased fussiness, fever, and increased abdominal girth. The nephrologist notes that the peritoneal effluent is cloudy, and the fluid is sent for cell count, differential count, and culture. Because of the infant's poor feeding and agitation, she is admitted to the inpatient unit for monitoring. This infant has a history of MRSA infection from a line while she was in the neonatal ICU. You note that she was just released 2 weeks ago from the neonatal ICU after a prolonged stay after birth for 6 weeks.
83. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is the best empiric recommendation?
questions.explanation: Answer: A. The ISPD recommends initial empiric therapy for PD patients with cloudy effluent while awaiting culture results. The guidelines state that cefepime monotherapy is the first-line recommendation. However, in this case, cefepime monotherapy is not appropriate because of the patient's history of MRSA (Answer C is incorrect). A second-line choice is a first-generation cephalosporin combined with either ceftazidime or an aminoglycoside. However, this option is inappropriate for the patient in the case because it lacks MRSA coverage (Answers B and D are incorrect). A glycopeptide should be added to cefepime, or it should replace the first-generation cephalosporin if the patient has a history of MRSA infection (Answer A is correct). However, some centers may choose coverage with vancomycin plus cefepime or vancomycin plus an aminoglycoside instead.

questions.question: 84. Two days later, the effluent culture returns with E. coli that is resistant to third-generation cephalosporins. Which changes would be best to make to the current therapy?
options: A. Continue previous regimen and add levofloxacin.
B. Discontinue all antibiotics and initiate gentamicin monotherapy.
D. Change therapy to double coverage with meropenem and gentamicin.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. Following the ISPD guidelines for PD infections, coverage can be narrowed once the bacteria is known. When the organism is gram-negative bacteria, the guidelines recommend discontinuing vancomycin (Answer A is incorrect). For E. coli, Proteus spp., or Klebsiella spp., the guidelines recommend cefepime, cefazolin, or ceftazidime, depending on susceptibilities, for 2 weeks. Discontinuing all antibiotics and initiating gentamicin monotherapy is incorrect because monotherapy with aminoglycosides is not recommended by the guidelines (Answer B is incorrect). Double coverage is not necessary for E. coli and is not recommended by the guidelines (Answer D is incorrect). Cefepime monotherapy is the best given choice provided for single coverage of E. coli (Answer C is correct).

questions.question: K.L. is a 10-year-old boy (weight 36 kg) admitted to the pediatric ICU on a Friday evening with community-acquired pneumonia and high suspicion of MRSA according to his medical history. He was initiated on vancomycin 720 mg (20Cmg/kg) intravenously every 6 hours plus ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously every 24 hours for empiric coverage. A fourth-dose vancomycin trough level was in the goal range at 17.7Cmcg/mL on Saturday. On Monday, the team notes on his daily basic metabolic panel that his SCr has increased to 1.4Cmg/dL from his baseline of 0.5Cmg/dL. You suspend his vancomycin therapy and draw a trough before what would have been his next dose. The vancomycin trough is 34.2Cmcg/mL His nurse notes that his urine appears dark, and an emergency renal ultrasonography reveals echogenic kidneys. Urine analysis shows 1+ proteinuria and the presence of eosinophils. He is given a diagnosis of TIN secondary to vancomycin. Which most accurately depicts the antibiotic regimen with a lower risk of TIN?
options: A. Clindamycin 360 mg intravenously every 8 hours plus ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously every 24 hours.
B. Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily plus ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously every 24 hours.
C. Levofloxacin 360 mg intravenously every 24 hours.
D. Continue ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously every 24 hours as monotherapy.
questions.explanation: Answer: A. In the setting of acute TIN for a patient who was concomitantly exposed to both vancomycin and a cephalosporin, which are known to cause TIN, the clinician must use judgment when deciding how to alter the regimen to address ongoing infectious coverage while removing a possible offending agent. In this example, Answers B and C are incorrect because Answer B adds a drug that is on the possible TIN list, which might further exacerbate the problem, and Answer C does not address the concern for MRSA coverage. Answer D is incorrect because, like Answer C. it does not allow for MRSA coverage. Answer A is correct because it introduces a drug that is not implicated in TIN but that also covers MRSA, which will allow the clinician to further distinguish whether vancomycin or ceftriaxone caused the TIN.

questions.question: T.G. is a 10-month-old boy (weight 10 kg) who presents to the clinic with a 3-day history of fever (temperature 38.5^CC, increased fussiness, decreased appetite, and increased lethargy. He has also been pulling on his right ear. An examination of both ears reveals that each has a bulging, erythematous, nonmobile tympanic membrane (TM). He is cooperative with the examination and does not seem to experience pain on manipulation of his ears, just discomfort. His medical history is noncontributory. He has no history of antibiotic use and no drug allergies. He does have two older siblings and attends day care 3 days a week. Which treatment option is most important to recommend for T.G.?
options: A. Augmentin ES 400 mg orally twice daily.
B. Amoxicillin 450 mg orally twice daily.
C. Ceftriaxone 750 mg intramuscularly x 1 dose.
D. Observation plus pain management x 48 hours.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Antibiotic therapy is appropriate for this patient because he is younger than 24 months and has bilateral signs and symptoms. Therefore, observation should not be considered (Answer D is incorrect). First-line therapy for a first-time AOM infection is high-dose amoxicillin (80-90Cmg/kg^{prime} day divided twice daily) (Answer B is correct). Adding clavulanate to amoxicillin is an alternative treatment option if patients do not respond to initial therapy or if symptoms are more severe. Adding clavulanate increases the risk of diarrhea (Answer A is incorrect). Ceftriaxone is an alternative for patients with a B- lactam allergy or if a patient does not respond to first-line antibiotic treatment within 48-72 hours. However, the dose is 50Cmg/kg/dose, not 75Cmg/kg/dose as listed (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl (weight 50 kg) presents to the emergency department (ED) 2 days after someone kicked her in the shin while playing soccer. Her lower leg is red and erythematous, and she has limited mobility of her toes and is unable to bear weight on her leg. She also has a temperature of 40^CC Radiography reveals soft tissue swelling consistent with cellulitis. Which antibiotic regimen should be initiated empirically in the ED?
options: A. Doxycycline 100 mg intravenously every 12 hours.
B. Nafcillin 2 g intravenously every 6 hours.
C. Ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5 g intravenously every 6 hours.
D. Meropenem 1 g intravenously every 8 hours.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. A penicillinase-penicillin such as nafcillin should be considered first line in patients with cellulitis because the most common organism is S. aureus (Answer B is correct). Depending on the geographic incidence of MRSA, empiric therapy should consist of clindamycin or possibly vancomycin. Doxycycline can be considered an option for this patient for the definitive treatment of a cellulitis caused by MRSA once sensitivities are known, but it should not be used empirically (Answer A is incorrect). Meropenem or ampicillin/sulbactam are considered broad-spectrum antibiotics and would be used if anaerobic bacteria were suspected (Answers C and D are incorrect).

questions.question: B.B. is a 2-year-old girl (weight 15 kg) with a history of reactive airway disease who presents to the ED with a 2-day history of wheezing, cough, and runny nose. Today, she is noted to have increased work of breathing and continued wheeze that did not respond to albuterol at home; she says that her "muscles hurt." A respiratory viral panel is positive for influenza A. The patient is to be admitted for treatment of the asthma exacerbation. Which agent would also be best to initiate on admission?
questions.explanation: Answer: D. The only recommended agent for treatment of influenza in this 2-year-old patient is oseltamivir (Answer D is correct). Zanamivir is indicated for patients 7 years and older (Answer A is incorrect). Ribavirin is not indicated for the treatment of influenza A, but it has been used in the treatment of RSV (Answer C is incorrect). Amantadine and rimantadine are FDA label approved for a 2-year-old for the treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A. However, they are not currently recommended by the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) because of the increased resistance that occurs with these agents (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question:
K.M. is a 21-month-old girl admitted to the hospital with a 3-day history of fussiness, decreased appetite, and high temperature (40^CC). Meningitis is suspected, and a lumbar puncture is performed with the following results: white blood cell count (WBC) 8times10^3cells/mm3 (72 s egs, 15 bands, 11 lymphs), g lucose 22Cmg/dL, and protein 95Cmg/dL. The Gram stain also reveals the presence of gram-positive cocci. The patient is placed on empiric therapy with vancomycin and ceftriaxone. Three days later, her cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) grows Streptococcus pneumoniae with the following sensitivities:
Penicillin R 2Cmcg/mL
Cefotaxime S 1mcg/mL
Ceftriaxone 12Cmcg/mL
Vancomycin S 1Cmcg/mL
Which would be the best changes to K.M.'s antibiotic regimen, given these culture and sensitivity results?
options: B. Discontinue ceftriaxone, continue vancomycin, and add rifampin.
C. Change ceftriaxone to cefotaxime, and continue vancomycin.
D. Discontinue vancomycin, continue ceftriaxone, and add rifampin.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. For the treatment of bacterial meningitis caused by ceftriaxone- intermediate S. pneumoniae, two treatment options are recommended by the guidelines. Rifampin can be added to vancomycin and ceftriaxone, or vancomycin can be combined with another third-generation cephalosporin. In this patient, the organism is sensitive to an alternative third-generation cephalosporin, so changing to that agent is the best choice, given the culture and sensitivity results (Answer C is correct). If rifampin is added, ceftriaxone should be continued (Answer B is incorrect). It is not appropriate to continue ceftriaxone and vancomycin because of the intermediate sensitivity and potential for treatment failure and complications (Answer A is incorrect). Vancomycin should be used together with a third-generation cephalosporin for all penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae; therefore, it is not appropriate to discontinue vancomycin and use ceftriaxone and rifampin (Answer Dis incorrect).

questions.question: A.C. is a 6-year-old boy (weight 30 kg) who presents to a local ED (local community-acquired methicillin- resistant Staphylococcus aureus [CA-MRSA] resistance 15%, local clindamycin resistance 5%) with left lower leg pain and swelling and the inability to bear weight for the past week, together with acute onset of fever and malaise during the past 3 days. His medical history is also significant for the upper respiratory symptoms of rhinorrhea, cough, and postnasal drip. On examination, there is diffuse tenderness and limitation in movement. The patient has had no recent trauma. Which empiric antibiotic regimen would best be initiated on admission?
options: A. Cefazolin 750 mg intravenously every 8 hours plus clindamycin 300 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
B. Ceftriaxone 1500 mg intravenously every 24 hours plus clindamycin 300 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
C. Ceftriaxone 1500 mg intravenously every 24 hours plus vancomycin 450 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
D. Cefazolin 750 mg intravenously every 8 hours plus vancomycin 450 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Geographic resistance patterns are important to consider when selecting empiric treatment of possible osteomyelitis. First-line agents in a geographic area with a high MRSA resistance rate include clindamycin and vancomycin. Vancomycin is not necessary in this patient because the local clindamycin resistance is less than 10% (Answer C is incorrect). Therefore, clindamycin should be the empiric agent of choice. Ceftriaxone is appropriate to add for this patient because of the suspicion of K. kingae (given the presence of upper respiratory symptoms). Clindamycin does not provide coverage against that organism (Answer B is correct). Cefazolin would be an appropriate first- line empiric agent if the local MRSA resistance pattern were less than 10%, but it is not recommended to be combined with clindamycin (Answer A is incorrect). Cefazolin may be added to vancomycin for empiric treatment of possible S. aureus bacteremia; however, this combination does not provide coverage against K. kingae (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: B.F. is a 16-year-old patient admitted for management of worsening lower leg cellulitis. Three days ago, he slammed his leg in a car door, and during the past 12 hours, it has become much worse. His leg is warm, erythematous, edematous, and painful to the touch. There is concern for necrotizing fasciitis because the area of cellulitis is also firm on palpation and appears to have an area of necrosis. He undergoes surgery for debridement of the necrotic area. A Gram stain of the skin tissue is performed, which shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which antibiotic therapy would be best to initiate in this patient?
questions.explanation: Necrotizing fasciitis caused by S. pyogenes should be treated with a combination of penicillin G and clindamycin. Combination therapy with clindamycin is recommended because it can neutralize the exotoxin produced by streptococcal species and decrease exotoxin production (Answer C is correct). Vancomycin can be considered an alternative in a patient with β-lactam allergy (Answer A is incorrect). Penicillin monotherapy would provide inadequate coverage against all possible toxin production (Answer B is incorrect). Clindamycin monotherapy would provide inadequate coverage against possible GAS resistant strains (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: E.P. is an 18-month-old girl who presents to the ED in respiratory distress She has a 3-day history of fever, rhinorrhea, and a "barky" cough. Inspiratory stridor is heard on examination. Which treatment regimen is mon appropriate for this patient in the ED?
options: A. Humidified O2, racemic epinephrine, and nebulized budesonide.
B. Humidified 02, racemic epinephrine, dexamethasone, and nebulize budesonide.
C. Humidified O2, racemic epinephrine, and dexamethasone.
D. Humidified O2 and racemic epinephrine.
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with laryngotracheitis, or croup. First-line treatment is a combination of non pharmacologic management (humidified O2) and a combination of two pharmacologic agents to decrease the airway edema (Answer D is incorrect). Racemic epinephrine acts as a potent anti inflammatory and causes local vasoconstriction. Dexamethasone acts as a potent antiinflammatory agent that reduces tissue edema (Answer C is correct). Dexamethasone has been shown superior to nebulized budesonide and has a faster onset of action and longer duration of action (Answer A is incorrect).

questions.question: K.D. is a 9-month-old boy, born prematurely at 32 weeks' gestation, with a medical history significant for necrotizing enterocolitis resulting in short gu syndrome and chronic total parenteral nutrition use. He currently has a Broviac catheter that has been in place for 4 months. Today, he presents with a 2-day history of fever, fussiness, and lethargy. Blood and urine cultures are drawn in the ED, and he is admitted for a sepsis workup. The blood cultures from both the central catheter and a peripheral line drawn in the ED reveal gram-positive cocci in clusters about 12 hours after obtaining the cultures. A transthoracic echocardiogram reveals a vegetation on the tricuspid valve. Which would be the most appropriate empiric regimen for K.D.?
options: A. Penicillin G with or without gentamicin.
B. Vancomycin with or without gentamicin.
C. Ampicillin with or without gentamicin.
D. Ceftriaxone with or without gentamicin.
questions.explanation: Answer: B. Empiric management of a patient with possible S. aureus endocarditis is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin with or without gentamicin for synergy. Vancomycin is an alternative for a patient with prosthetic material and if there is high suspicion of MRSA. The patient's medical history and the presence of the Broviac catheter place him at higher risk of MRSA (Answer B is correct). Penicillin G with or without gentamicin is appropriate for the treatment of streptococcal species (Answer A is incorrect). Ampicillin and ceftriaxone in combination with gentamicin are used in the management of endocarditis caused by the HACEK organisms (Answers C and D are incorrect).

questions.question: L.M. is a 5-month-old girl, born prematurely at 29 weeks' gestation, with a medical history significant for necrotizing enterocolitis, several bowel resections, and jejunostomy reversal. She is currently receiving total parenteral nutrition through a Broviac catheter and takes enteral feedings. She presents to the ED with fever (temperature 39.6^CC, irritability, and increased work of breathing. She is to be admitted for a sepsis workup and initiated empirically on ceftriaxone 50Cmg/kg/day. On hospital day 2, the culture from her Broviac catheter is growing coagulase- negative Staphylococcus. Peripheral cultures have remained negative. Which is the most appropriate regimen for L.M.?
options: A. Vancomycin for 5-7 days plus catheter removal.
B. Vancomycin plus rifampin for 5-7 days.
C. Vancomycin plus vancomycin antibiotic lock for 10-14 days.
D. Vancomycin plus gentamicin for 10-14 days plus catheter removal.
questions.explanation: Answer: C. The best management of a central venous catheter infection caused by coagulase-negative S. aureus is vancomycin in combination with an antibiotic lock for 10-14 days if the infection is uncomplicated for short- or long-term catheter types OR if the catheter is needed long term and the infection is uncomplicated (Answer C is correct). An alternative regimen would be removal of the catheter and systemic antibiotics for 5-7 days if the catheter were only needed short term. Because of the patient's complicated history and the need for the continuation of the catheter for parenteral nutrition, it is not recommended to remove the catheter at this time (Answer D is incorrect). Vancomycin with or without rifampin for 5-7 days can be considered if the catheter is only needed short term and is to be removed (Answers A and B are incorrect).

questions.question: T.B. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who presents to her primary care physician's office with recurrent cough during the past month and new onset of fever, chills, and night sweats. She is not sexually active and has no recent history of international travel. She lives at home with her mother, stepfather (who was recently released from prison), and four siblings. A chest radiograph is performed that shows a cavitary nlesion in the right upper lobe. A tuberculin skin test (purified protein derivative [PPD]) is placed, which becomes positive (15 mm) in 24 hours. Which regimen should be initiated in T.B.?
options: B. Rifampin plus isoniazid plus pyrazinamide plus ethambutol.
D. Isoniazid plus rifampin plus clarithromycin.
questions.explanation: Management of active TB disease is a four-drug combination for 2 months with rifampin, pyrazinamide, isoniazid, and ethambutol (Answer B is correct); a two drug regimen (isoniazid and rifampin) is considered for latent TB; however, this patient has active signs and symptoms (Answer A is incorrect). Rifampin plus pyrazinamide is an alternative two drug combination for latent TB (Answer C is incorrect). There is no role for clarithromycin in the management of TB; however, it does have coverage against atypical mycobacteria (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: C.A. is a 13-year-old female adolescent (weight 56 kg) who presents to the ED with a 1-day history of fever and severe lower right quadrant pain. On examination, she is tearful and reports a pain score of 9 of 10. She has rebound tenderness when palpating her abdomen. Her temperature is 39.5^CC. She has no significant medical history but did begin her menses 3 days ago for the first time. Which is the best initial empiric antibiotic regimen to begin?
options: A. Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours and metronidazole 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours.
B. Ampicillin 2 g intravenously every 8 hours and gentamicin 5Cmg/kg/day intravenously every 24 hours.
C. Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously every 24 hours and tobramycin 5Cmg/kg/day every 24 hours.
D. Clindamycin 600 mg intravenously every 8 hours and gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day intravenously every 24 hours.
questions.explanation: This patient has a possible intra-abdominal infection; the first-line empiric regimen should provide coverage against gram-positive streptococci, enteric gram-negative bacilli, and anaerobes; cefazolin and metronidazole does not provide adequate gram-negative coverage (Answer A is incorrect); ampicillin plus gentamicin does not provide adequate anaerobic coverage (Answer B is incorrect); ceftriaxone plus tobramycin does not provide adequate anaerobic coverage (Answer C is incorrect); clindamycin plus gentamicin provides coverage for streptococci and anaerobes (clindamycin) and enteric gram-negative organisms (gentamicin) (Answer D is correct).

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy (weight 30 kg) presents to the clinic with irritability, a temperature of 38.5^CC, and mild ear pain. On examination, his ear is erythematous with a copious amount of cerumen throughout the ear canal. He has had two previous episodes of AOM at 18 months and 2 years. For treatment of his latest episode, he received amoxicillin and developed a rash on his trunk im ma after 5 days of therapy. According to the AOM guidelines, which therap would be best for this patient?
options: A. Cefdinir 420 mg orally every 12 hours x 10 days.
B. Observation and pain management for 48-72 hours.
C. Azithromycin 300 mg orally x 1: then 150 mg orally once daily x 4 days.
D. Ceftriaxone 1000 mg intramuscularly x 3 doses.
questions.explanation: Because viruses are the cause of between 40% and 75% of AOM cases, the clinical practice guidelines for the diagnosis and management of AOM recommend observation and pain management for certain individuals (patients with mild symptoms and mild symptoms and unilateral age 6-23 months of age); this patient is 3 years old and has mild ear pain and a low-grade fever; therefore, observation and pain management are appropriate (Answer B is correct); if antibiotic therapy were to be used, cefdinir would be an appropriate choice because of the patient’s history of allergy to amoxicillin; however, this patient should only be observed and not treated (Answer A is incorrect); azithromycin is no longer recommended in the latest guidelines (Answer C is incorrect); ceftriaxone intramuscular therapy is an alternative treatment option for patients who do not respond to first-line antibiotic therapy after 48–72 hours; therefore, this patient is not a candidate for ceftriaxone (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: Questions 98 and 99 pertain to the following case: T.P. is a 16-month-old boy (weight 12 kg) admitted to the hospital for worsening abscess on his right lower inguinal area. The abscess, whis appeared 3 days ago, was initially treated at the physician's office with inci and drainage. The area around the abscess is warm and erythematousThe patient currently has a temperature of 39.2 C a WBC of ( segs, 15 bands), and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 12.8 (normal is less the 0.1). The patient has also been receiving oral cephalexin for the past 48 hour 20times10^3cells per mm^2 The wound culture from the physician's office is growing MRSA with the following sensitivities. Sensitive: Clindamycin (positive D-test), levofloxac linezolid, vancomycin, doxycycline, sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim. Resistant Erythromycin, oxacillin, tetracycline.98. Which antibiotic would be best to initiate in the hospital, given these sensitivities?
options: A. Cefazolin 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours.
B. Clindamycin 120 mg intravenously every 8 hours.
C. Vancomycin 180 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
D. Linezolid 120 mg intravenously twice daily.
questions.explanation: Vancomycin would be the first-line agent for this patient whose outpatient therapy failed and who is growing MRSA from his culture (Answer C is correct); clindamycin is not appropriate because the sensitivities show a positive D-test, which could result in inducible bacterial resistance and possible treatment failure (Answer B is incorrect); cefazolin is the agent of choice for empiric therapy when there is low suspicion for MRSA and for treatment of confirmed MSSA (Answer A is incorrect); linezolid is an alternative to vancomycin for MRSA; however, it would be less cost-effective than vancomycin (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: 99. Which oral antibiotic therapy would you most likely recommend fue T.P. on discharge?
options: A. Clindamycin 150 mg orally every 8 hours.
B. Doxycycline 24 mg orally every 12 hours.
C. Linezolid 120 mg orally twice daily.
D. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim 60 mg orally every 12 hours.
questions.explanation: Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim is the best oral treatment option for this patient because the organism is sensitive to this agent, the agent can safely be used for patients of this age, and the agent is cost-effective (Answer D is correct); clindamycin cannot be used because the D-test was positive (Answer A is incorrect); doxycycline could be a treatment option for an older pediatric patient (older than 8 years); however, this patient is only 16 months old and doxycycline is not indicated in this age group (Answer B is incorrect); linezolid could be a treatment option for MRSA and other multidrug-resistant gram positive organisms; however, it is costly and therefore not the first choice if other alternatives are available (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: M.L. is a 14-year-old male adolescent (weight 82 kg) who presents to the clinic today with right knee pain and swelling for the past week and new onset of fever and malaise during the past 3 days. On examination, there is diffuse tenderness of the affected area and limitation in flexion and extension secondary to the pain. The patient has no significant past medical problems and does not recall any recent trauma. M.L. is to be admitted to the hospital for possible osteomyelitis. Which is the best empiric therapy for M.L.?
options: A. Ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously every 12 hours.
B. Ciprofloxacin 400 mg intravenously every 12 hours.
C. Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours.
D. Vancomycin 1 g intravenously every 12 hours.
questions.explanation: The most common microorganisms for osteomyelitis in this age group are S. aureus and S. pyogenes. A penicillinase-resistant penicillin or first-generation cephalosporin is the first-line treatment option if the risk of MRSA is low. Cefazolin is the best option for this patient because he has no significant medical history or risk factors for MRSA (Answer C is correct). Ceftriaxone is not a first-line monotherapy agent unless Salmonella osteomyelitis (presence of sickle cell disease) or infectious arthritis caused by N. gonorrhoeae is suspected (Answer A is incorrect). Ceftriaxone can be used in combination with clindamycin when K. kingae is suspected (usually in younger children with concomitant respiratory tract infection symptoms). Ciprofloxacin is an alternative agent for patients with a penicillin allergy and a suspected Salmonella infection (Answer B is incorrect). Vancomycin is indicated empirically if there is a high suspicion of a resistant gram-positive organism or a positive patient or family history of MRSA (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: M.L. undergoes aspiration of the knee on admission. The fluid is positive for MSSA. The patient is hospitalized for 7 days to receive intravenous antibiotics. Which would be most appropriate for oral therapy, which will continue for another 3-4 weeks?
options: A. No appropriate oral agent for the organism.
B. Cephalexin 500 mg orally every 6 hours.
C. Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally twice daily.
D. Linezolid 600 mg orally twice daily.
questions.explanation: The length of therapy for osteomyelitis caused by MSSA should be 4-6 weeks and can be completed with a combination of intravenous and oral therapy in patients without a complicated course or resistant organism (Answer A is incorrect). First-line treatment of MSSA osteomyelitis would be an oral penicillinase-resistant penicillin (dicloxacillin) or a first-generation cephalosporin (cephalexin) (Answer B is correct). Ciprofloxacin can be used to continue treatment of Salmonella osteomyelitis (Answer C is incorrect). Linezolid should be reserved for the treatment of osteomyelitis caused by resistant gram positive organisms (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: P.E. is a 16-year-old male adolescent admitted to the hospital with fever, neck stiffness, and new-onset petechiae. His lumbar puncture in the ED reveals the following: CSF cloudy, WBC 2.5x10^3 cells/mm^3 (80 segs, 10 bands, 10 lymphs), glucose 38 mg/dL, and protein 130 mg/dL. He is initially placed on empiric therapy with vancomycin plus ceftriaxone. Twenty-four hours after admission, a Gram stain performed on the CSF fluid reveals gram-negative cocci. Which changes would be best to P.E.'s antibiotic regimen, given these culture results?
options: B. Discontinue vancomycin and continue ceftriaxone.
C. Discontinue vancomycin, continue ceftriaxone, and add rifampin.
D. Change ceftriaxone and vancomycin to penicillin and rifampin.
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy for bacterial meningitis in this age group includes vancomycin and a third-generation cephalosporin. The presence of gram-negative cocci in the CSF fluid of this patient indicates likely infection secondary to N. meningitidis. Therefore, it is appropriate to discontinue vancomycin and continue ceftriaxone (Answer B is correct). Vancomycin should only be continued for definitive treatment of a resistant gram positive organism (Answer A is incorrect). Rifampin can be used in combination with ceftriaxone and vancomycin for the treatment of S. pneumoniae meningitis when the ceftriaxone MIC is intermediate (Answer C is incorrect). Penicillin is first line for the treatment of proven S. pneumoniae with a penicillin MIC less than 0.1 mcg/mL and is usually not used in combination with rifampin (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: Which would be best to initiate for the household contacts of P.E.?
options: A. Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone x 7 days.
B. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg/dose intravenously every 6 hours x 2 days.
C. 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (Pneumovax) intramuscularly x 1 dose.
D. Rifampin 600 mg orally every 12 hours x 2 days.
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for individuals in close contact with patients who have N. meningitides meningitis. Appropriate agents are rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone (Answer D is correct). Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is used for empiric treatment of suspected meningitis (Answer A is incorrect). Dexamethasone can be used in combination with antimicrobial therapy for 2 days to help with inflammation of the meninges (Answer B is incorrect). The 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is a preventive strategy against S. pneumoniae that is currently recommended for patients 2 years and older and adolescents with certain underlying medical conditions (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: D.M. is a 14-month-old girl (weight 10 kg) who presents to the physician's office with reports that she has been fussy, with rectal temperatures of 39.8°C for 2 days. Her medical history is unremarkable, and her immunizations are up to date. She has had a decreased appetite for the past 24 hours but has not had any nausea or vomiting. On examination, she appears well, with no apparent source of the fever. A urinalysis is performed (bag collection) that shows the presence of leukocyte esterase, trace blood, WBC, and moderate bacteria. Nitrites are negative. Which is the best empiric therapy for D.M.?
options: A. Ciprofloxacin 150 mg orally every 12 hours.
B. Nitrofurantoin 20 mg orally every 24 hours.
C. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim 40 mg of trimethoprim orally every 12 hours.
D. Amoxicillin 450 mg orally every 12 hours.
questions.explanation: This patient can receive oral antimicrobial therapy as an outpatient. First-line empiric therapy for a presumed UTI includes sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim, amoxicillin/ clavulanate, or a cephalosporin. The agent of choice should be based on local susceptibility patterns to these agents (Answer C is correct). Nitrofurantoin should not be used for empiric treatment of a UTI because it does not maintain therapeutic serum concentrations in the blood. It is used for UTI prophylaxis (Answer B is incorrect). Ciprofloxacin is reserved for oral treatment of complicated UTIs secondary to P. aeruginosa (Answer A is incorrect). Amoxicillin/clavulanate is preferred to amoxicillin because of the potential for β-lactamase- producing gram-negative organisms. In addition, the high dose listed (80 mg/kg/day) is not required for treating a UTI (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: D.M. received a prescription for an oral antibiotic that she has been taking for 3 days. She returns to the clinic today with continued fever and new onset of nausea and vomiting and severe lower back pain. She is to be admitted to the hospital for treatment of presumed pyelonephritis. Which is most appropriate to initiate at this time?
options: A. Ciprofloxacin 30 mg/kg/day divided twice daily.
C. Ampicillin 50 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day.
D. Piperacillin/tazobactam 300 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours.
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone (or another third-generation cephalosporin) is considered first-line therapy for the management of pyelonephritis. It also has the advantage of being given once daily (Answer B is correct). Aminoglycosides are also recommended, but not in combination with ampicillin (Answer C is incorrect). Ciprofloxacin and piperacillin/tazobactam should be reserved for resistant organisms (Answers A and D are incorrect).

questions.question: G.T. is a 5-year-old white boy (weight 21.6 kg) with a medical history significant for hypoplastic left heart syndrome and recurrent otitis media. He presents after two surgical procedures to correct the congenital heart defect and is admitted today for his third procedure (Fontan). His medications are as follows: furosemide 10 mg orally twice daily and chlorothiazide 25 mg orally twice daily. He is allergic to amoxicillin (urticaria). Which surgical prophylactic strategy is most appropriate for G.T. before his surgery?
options: A. Administer cefazolin 650 mg intravenously within 60 minutes of first incision.
B. Administer cefoxitin 650 mg intravenously within 60 minutes of first incision.
C. Administer clindamycin 220 mg intravenously within 120 minutes of first incision.
D. Administer vancomycin 320 mg intravenously within 120 minutes of first incision.
questions.explanation: Cefazolin is the first-line agent recommended before cardiac surgical procedures. However, this patient has an allergic reaction to amoxicillin (urticaria). Cephalosporins (cefazolin and cefoxitin) should not be used in patients with type I, immunoglobulin (Ig)E-mediated allergic reactions to penicillin (Answer A is incorrect). In addition, cefoxitin is not recommended before a cardiac procedure (Answer B is incorrect). Alternative agents recommended for patients with a β-lactam allergy include clindamycin and vancomycin. Vancomycin is the correct choice for this patient because it should be administered 120 minutes before incision given its prolonged infusion time (Answer D is correct). Clindamycin can be given within 60 minutes (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question: During the Fontan procedure, G.T. had difficulty being transitioned off cardiopulmonary bypass. Therefore, the surgery took 6 hours rather than 3 hours. Which best describes when the antibiotic should be redosed intraoperatively in this patient?
options: A. Does not need to be redosed.
B. 2 hours after initial preoperative dose.
C. 4 hours after initial preoperative dose.
D. 6 hours after initial preoperative dose.
questions.explanation: Because of its long elimination half-life, vancomycin does not need to be redosed during surgical procedures that take longer than expected (Answer A is correct). Cefazolin would need to be redosed 4 hours after the initial preoperative dose (Answer C is incorrect). Like vancomycin, clindamycin would not need to be redosed if the surgery took 6 hours because it is not recommended to re-dose until 6 hours after the original dose (Answer D is incorrect). There is no recommendation to re-dose antibiotics within 2 hours (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: E.B., a 16-year-old female adolescent (weight 61.3 kg), presents in the ED after a snowboarding accident with severe hypotension (BP 65/45 mm Hg). She is disoriented, and her laboratory values point toward intravascular dehydration. Which is the most appropriate fluid to recommend for initial resuscitation?
options: B. Administer dextrose 5% in 0.225% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 95 mL/hour.
questions.explanation: The patient presents with a severe intravascular deficit, as evidenced by the patient's hypotension and disorientation. During the emergency phase of resuscitation, the most appropriate first-line therapy is to administer a normal saline bolus at a dose of 10-20 mL/kg. This will restore intravascular volume and perfusion. Although providing albumin and blood (colloids) may be useful, these would not be first-line therapies without a clear source of bleeding. In addition, when volume expansion is desired, 5%, rather than 25%, albumin should be used, making answer A incorrect. Furthermore, the dose of albumin provided in Answer D is above what would typically be indicated, making Answer D incorrect. Answer B provides maintenance fluids. In the setting of severe hypotension, it is first necessary to restore intravascular volume with a bolus; thus, Answer B is incorrect.

questions.question: E.B. does not respond to the initial therapy given in the ED. An hour after her initial presentation, her abdomen is rigid, and an emergency computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a liver laceration. Repeat laboratory tests show a hematocrit of 17% (previously 26%). Which is the most appropriate fluid to recommend?
options: B. Administer dextrose 5% in 0.225% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 95 mL/hour.
questions.explanation: This patient has not responded to the normal saline bolus that was given in the ED, and now, the patient has a clear sign of intra-abdominal bleeding. Administering blood will expand the intravascular volume while increasing hematocrit and the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, which is necessary to continue perfusing vital organs, especially during an acute trauma. Answer A is incorrect because there is now a clear source of bleeding. In addition, a dose of 10 mL/kg in the setting of severe hypotension would be insufficient to restore intravascular volume. Answer B is incorrect; this maintenance fluid would be needed after correcting the acute phase of dehydration. Similar to Answer A, simply increasing the volume of the normal saline bolus will not help correct this acute issue because there is a clear source of bleeding.

questions.question: E.H. is a 19-month-old boy with a 3-day history of vomiting, diarrhea, and dehydration. His current weight is 10 kg (previous weight 10.45 kg). His BP is stable on admission. He has decreased urine output. He is given a diagnosis of gastroenteritis. Which set of physical signs and symptoms would be most expected for his severity of dehydration?
options: A. Anuria, absent tears, capillary refill greater than 8 seconds.
B. Decreased skin turgor, capillary refill greater than 5 seconds, slightly increased HR.
C. Normal HR, slightly dry mucosa, capillary refill 2 seconds.
D. Normal skin turgor, capillary refill greater than 8 seconds, dry mucosa.
questions.explanation: The percentage of dehydration is calculated as 4.3% [% dehydration = (10.45 kg - 10 kg)/10.45 kg x 100 = 4.3%]. Therefore, this patient would be classified as having moderate dehydration (i.e., 4%-6% dehydration for children). Signs and symptoms typically associated with moderate dehydration include slightly increased HR, normal-low systolic BP, markedly decreased urine output, 6%-10% weight loss, dry mucosa, reduced tears, deep-set eyes, decreased skin turgor, cool skin, reduced fontanelle, capillary refill of greater than 5 seconds, and irritability. Answer A is incorrect because these symptoms would be more consistent with severe dehydration. Answer C is incorrect because these symptoms would be more consistent with mild dehydration. Answer D is incorrect because the symptoms of dehydration are mixed between mild, moderate, and severe.

questions.question: Which is the best recommendation for correcting E.H.'s dehydration at this time?
options: A. Dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 70 mL/hour x 8 hours, followed by dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 56 mL/hour x 16 hours.
B. Dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 19 mL/hour x 24 hours.
C. 200 mL 0.9% normal saline bolus, followed by dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 43 mL/hour x 16 hours.
D. 450 mL 0.9% normal saline bolus, followed by dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 43 mL/hour x 24 hours.
questions.explanation: Based on 4.3% dehydration, this patient's fluid deficit is around 450 mL (fluid deficit = 4.3% x 10.45 kg/100 = 449 mL). In addition, using the Holliday-Segar method for maintenance needs, the patient requires 1023 mL/day for maintenance. The most appropriate way to administer this is to provide one-half of the deficit over the first 8 hours and one-half over the next 16 hours.
