Likewise, the maintenance needs should be replaced by one-third over the first 8 hours and by two-thirds over the next 16 hours. Answer B is incorrect because this would only replace the deficit; it would not also provide maintenance requirements. Answer C is incorrect because a bolus is not indicated at this time (i.e., BP stable). In addition, this patient will require maintenance fluids for 24 hours rather than 16. Answer D is incorrect because a bolus is not indicated at this time (i.e., BP stable).

questions.question: B.B. is a 6-month-old boy (weight 6 kg) with short bowel syndrome who is parenteral nutrition (PN)- dependent. On admission, his direct bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, and he is found to have scleral icterus. Which is the best approach to managing B.B. at this time?
options: B. Add cysteine 40 mg per gram of amino acid.
C. Decrease soybean oil-based intravenous fat emulsion (IVFE) dose to 1 g/kg/day or less.
questions.explanation: Elevated bilirubin greater than 2 mg/dL in PN-dependent children is most likely caused by the development of PNALD. The exact cause of PNALD is unknown; however, it is multifactorial and is associated with prolonged use, lack of enteral nutrition, recurrent episodes of infection/sepsis, and low birth weight/gestational age. Although many of these factors depend on one another, an independent risk factor for developing PNALD is the administration of soybean oil-based IVFE because of the presence of proinflammatory mediators, phytosterols, and omega-6 fatty acids. Although this has not been conclusively determined, expert consensus agrees that the reduction of soybean oil-based IVFE to doses of 1 g/kg/day or less may prevent and/or treat the development of PNALD. Answer A is incorrect because this patient is PN-dependent (i.e., short bowel syndrome); further, holding PN for 48 hours will unlikely result in normalization of direct bilirubin/PNALD. Answer B is incorrect because cysteine is added to neonatal PN to increase the calcium-phosphorus solubility. Answer D is incorrect because heparin is added to neonatal PN solutions to maintain line patency.

questions.question: A 1-day-old neonate (weight 800 g), 27 weeks' gestational age, will receive PN. However, because of difficulty securing central venous access, she will receive nutrition through a peripheral venous catheter. Which most accurately reflects what the PN must be compounded to be?
questions.explanation: The maximum osmolarity for PN infused through a peripheral catheter is 900 mOsm/L. Parenteral nutrition above this must be infused through a central venous catheter to prevent phlebitis, making all other answers incorrect.

questions.question: J.G., a 5-year-old boy with a history of bilateral renal artery stenosis complicated by renovascular hypertension and fibromuscular dysplasia, underwent bilateral renal artery-reimplantation, superior mesenteric artery bypass, and patch aortoplasty. He presents to the ED today and is admitted for concern about possible bowel obstruction secondary to poor appetite, no stools x 48 hours, and nausea/vomiting x 3 days. A nasogastric tube is placed, and on placement, copious bilious fluid is suctioned from his stomach. Which choice of fluids is best to replace J.G.'s ongoing losses?
options: B. 0.9% normal saline plus potassium chloride 10 mEq/L.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B; the patient's ongoing loss of bile/gastric fluid is best replaced by 0.9% normal saline plus potassium chloride 10 mEq/L because of the electrolyte composition of bile/gastric fluid. Dextrose is unnecessary when choosing a fluid for replacing losses, and 0.45% normal saline does not contain sufficient sodium content to adequately replace the sodium that would be lost in the output of bile (Answers A, C, and D). As a reminder, replacement of ongoing losses should be considered separately from normal maintenance requirements. In clinical practice, replacement fluids are often administered in a 0.5 mL/1 mL or 1 mL/1 mL fashion.

questions.question: K.K. is a 3-year-old girl admitted to the hospital with a 3-day history of severe diarrhea. On admission, her weight is 15 kg; however, her caregiver reports that she usually weighs 15.8 kg. Which best describes K.K.'s percentage of dehydration and her classification of dehydration?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A; the percentage of dehydration is 5% [% dehydration = (15.8 kg - 15 kg)/15.8 kg x 100]. For a 3-year-old child, this would be classified as moderate dehydration. Answers B and C are incorrect because of mathematical miscalculation. Answer D is incorrect: for a 3-year-old child, 5% dehydration is considered moderate, whereas 5% would be considered mild if this patient were an infant.

questions.question: Which best describes K.K.'s fluid deficit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 0.79 L (790 mL). The fluid deficit is calculated by multiplying the percentage of dehydration by the pre-illness weight. Therefore, 0.05 x 15.8 kg = 0.79 L. Answers B, C, and D are incorrect because of mathematical miscalculations.

questions.question: S.B., a 13-year-old girl (weight 55 kg) who presents to the ED after a motor vehicle accident, has severe hypotension (60/40 mm Hg). She is lethargic and has the following signs on physical examination: rapid HR (180 beats/minute) and delayed capillary refill (10 seconds). Which is the best initial therapy to provide S.B.?
options: A. Dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 92 mL/hour.
B. Dextrose 5% in 0.45% normal saline plus potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 1000 mL/hour x 1 hour.
D. 0.9% normal saline at 2000 mL/hour x 30 minutes.
questions.explanation: Answer D is correct. This patient presents with severe hypotension and is in the emergency phase of intravenous fluid replacement. The most appropriate first-line therapy is the administration of a normal saline bolus to reestablish intravascular volume, maintain hemodynamics, and prevent tissue damage. The most appropriate first-line option is normal saline or lactated Ringer solution. Answers A and B are incorrect because of the fluid choice. Answer A provides maintenance fluid requirements, but it will not correct the acute phase of resuscitation/restore BP. Answer B is incorrect because it uses maintenance fluids at a bolus dose. When administering a bolus, normal saline or lactated Ringer solution is more appropriate. Answer C is incorrect; although 92 mL/hour is the maintenance rate needed, the patient requires a bolus for initial therapy.

questions.question: S.B. is unresponsive to two normal saline boluses, and her abdomen is then found to be rigid. An emergency CT scan reveals a large hematoma in her abdomen. Subsequently, her hematocrit is 19%, and her BP remains at 60/40 mm Hg. Which therapy would be best to recommend at this time?
options: A. 0.9% normal saline at 1000 mL/hour x 1 hour.
D. Lactated Ringer solution at 92 mL/hour.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. With a falling hematocrit value and obvious signs of bleeding, the most appropriate fluid is blood. This will expand the intravascular volume while increasing the hematocrit and oxygen-carrying capacity of the bloodstream. Answer A is incorrect because providing an additional bolus is unlikely to result in efficacy at this point. Answers C and D are incorrect because providing maintenance fluids at a rate of 92 mL/hour will not acutely correct the patient's hypotension.

questions.question: A 2-month-old (weight 3.4 kg) is receiving PN with the following : DIR 14 mg/kg/minute, amino acids 3.2 g/kg/day, and IVFE 3 g/kg/day (51 mL). Which most accurately reflects the infant's caloric intake for the day?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. To solve this question, dextrose and amino acid must first be converting into grams per day: 68.5 g/day and 10.9 g/day, respectively. Then, calculate the caloric contribution from each macronutrient: 68.5 g x 3.4 kcal/g + 10.9 g x 4 kcal/g + 51 mL x 2 kcal/mL = 378.5 kcal/day = 111 kcal/kg/day. For those who like to use more streamline calculations, the answer can also be determined in a simpler way, without accounting for weight, as follows: glucose 14 mg/kg/minute = 20.16 g/kg/day x 3.4 kcal/g = 68.54 kcal/kg/day + amino acids 3.2 g/kg/day x 4 kcal/g = 12.8 kcal/kg/day + IVFE 3 g/kg/day x 9 kcal/g = 27 kcal/kg/day, for a total of around 111 kcal/kg/day. Answers B, C, and D are incorrect because of mathematical miscalculations.

questions.question: K.T. is a previously healthy 8-year-old girl who was admitted to the hospital with pneumonia. She is febrile and requiring oxygen. K.T. attends school, her immunizations are up to date, and she lives at home with her two older siblings. Which is the best empiric treatment for K.T.'s pneumonia?
questions.explanation: The Infectious Diseases Society of America CAP guidelines recommend ampicillin (Answer B) as first-line treatment for CAP in fully immunized hospitalized patients. Amoxicillin (Answer A) is the recommended outpatient treatment, and the patient should be transitioned to amoxicillin once she shows clinical improvement. Ceftriaxone (Answer C) is recommended first line if the patient is not fully immunized. Clindamycin (Answer D) is a recommended addition to ampicillin if the patient has risk factors for MRSA.

questions.question: J.S. is a 5-year-old boy (15 kg) with cystic fibrosis (CF) who was admitted to the hospital for an acute pulmonary exacerbation. He is allergic to penicillins hives and his previous respiratory cultures have grown Pseudomonas aeruginosa, methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), and Haemophilus influenzae. Which is the best antibiotic regimen for empiric coverage?
options: A. Piperacillin/tazobactam 2250 mg intravenously every 8 hours and tobramycin 150 mg intravenously every 24 hours.
B. Meropenem 600 mg intravenously every 8 hours alone.
C. Cefepime 750 mg intravenously every 8 hours and tobramycin 150 mg intravenously every 24 hours.
D. Ceftriaxone 750 mg intravenously every 24 hours and tobramycin 150 mg intravenously every 24 hours.
questions.explanation: This patient has grown P. aeruginosa, which the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation recommends to double-cover while treating an exacerbation. This eliminates Answer B, because only one antibiotic is included, and Answer D, because ceftriaxone does not cover P. aeruginosa. Answer D contains only single coverage for Pseudomonas. Answer A is not the best option for this patient because of his allergy to penicillin, and piperacillin is a penicillin. In addition, the piperacillin dose is 120 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours, and the recommended dose for piperacillin in patients with CF at standard infusion times is at least 100 mg/kg/dose every 6 hours.

questions.question: P.L. is a 15-year-old, previously healthy female adolescent admitted to the hospital yesterday for nausea and vomiting. Today, she spikes a fever, and chest radiography is done. After she has a desaturation, she is placed on 0.5 L of oxygen by nasal canula. Her chest radiography reveals an infiltrate consistent with pneumonia. Which best classifies her pneumonia?
questions.explanation: The patient has CAP (Answer A) because her symptoms began less than 48 hours into her hospitalization. If the symptoms had occurred more than 48 hours into her hospitalization or if you had had previous contact with the hospital, her pneumonia would have been hospital acquired (Answer B). It is not ventilator associated because she is on non-invasive respiratory support (Answer C), and her symptoms are not consistent with a necrotizing pneumonia (Answer D).

questions.question: J.E. is a 9-year-old boy (weight 32 kg) with asthma who presents to the emergency department (ED) with an asthma exacerbation. J.E. has a history of many ED visits for his asthma and is currently living in a homeless shelter with his mother. After receiving three back-to-back albuterol treatments, he was initiated on every-4-hour albuterol treatments. His last treatment was 4 hours ago, and he is now doing well. Which is the best oral corticosteroid regimen for him?
options: A. Prednisolone 60 mg orally daily for a 5-day course.
B. Methylprednisolone 32 mg orally three times daily for a 7-day course.
C. Dexamethasone 18 mg orally daily for a 2-day course.
questions.explanation: From the patient's history, he has a difficult social situation that will make adherence to medications challenging. Dexamethasone (Answer C) 1- to 2-day courses was shown in a meta-analysis to be as effective as a 5-day course of prednisolone (Answer A) in preventing return visits for patients with asthma leaving the ED. The dexamethasone 2-day option is the best option for this patient given its ease of adherence and long half-life. The maximum dose of dexamethasone per day is 15-18 mg. Hydrocortisone (Answer D) is not recommended for treatment in asthma exacerbations. Given his history, it is unlikely that he will be adherent to a 7-day course of methylprednisolone (Answer B).

questions.question: K.D. is a 3-year-old girl who presents to her pediatrician with wheezing and shortness of breath. Her mother reports that K.D. has been given a diagnosis of pneumonia twice in the past year. Her mother also reports that she awakens coughing 1 night a month and that, the last time she received a diagnosis of pneumonia, she has had to use the albuterol inhaler she was given about three times weekly. The pediatrician gives K.D. a diagnosis of asthma. Which is the best treatment for K.D.?
options: A. Continue albuterol as needed for symptoms.
B. Add budesonide 0.5 mg nebulized twice daily.
C. Add beclomethasone hydrofluoroalkane (HFA) 80 mcg 2 puffs twice daily.
D. Add fluticasone 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily.
questions.explanation: According to the asthma guidelines, the patient's asthma would be classified as mild persistent. Mild persistent asthma should be treated with step 2 of the asthma treatment. Options in step 2 for 0- to 4-year-olds that are preferred are as follows: low-dose ICS, with the alternative being montelukast. Answer D is a low-dose ICS. Answer A is not the best answer because a controller medication is needed for persistent asthma. Answer B is incorrect because the dose is higher than low dose and is less convenient for the patient because it is nebulized, which will take longer to administer. Beclomethasone is not U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label approved for patients younger than 5 years, and the dosing is higher than low dose.

questions.question: R.Y., a 7-year-old previously healthy boy who presents to his pediatrician with fever and cough for the past 2 days, is given a diagnosis of pneumonia. His immunizations are up to date. Which is the most common cause of bacterial pneumonia in this patient?
questions.explanation: This patient was previously healthy and has no risk factors for community-acquired MRSA (Answer A). S. pneumoniae (Answer D) is the most common pathogen for CAP in children. The patient is fully immunized, so H. influenzae (Answer C) is unlikely. C. trachomatis (Answer B) can cause pneumonia in infants of mothers infected with C. trachomatis, but it is unlikely to occur in this age group.

questions.question: E.E. is a 10-year-old girl (weight 27 kg) with CF who presents for her regular CF clinic visit. Her home medications include the following: albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled twice daily; dornase alfa 2.5 mg nebulized daily; a multivitamin with extra vitamin A, D, E, K 1 tablet by mouth daily; pancrelipase 12,000-unit capsules: 2 capsules with meals and 1 capsule with snacks; and fluticasone nasal spray 1 spray in each nostril daily. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) today is 81% (baseline 95%). She reports a good appetite, having 2 stools a day that sink and no complaints of abdominal pain. Which is the best plan for her treatment regimen?
options: B. Increase pancrelipase 12,000-unit capsules to 3 with meals and 1 with snacks.
C. Add 7% hypertonic saline 4 mL inhaled twice daily.
D. Add fluticasone 110 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
questions.explanation: Although this patient does not report any symptoms, her FEV1 is decreased from baseline, which is of concern and should be treated. She is older than 6 years, so hypertonic saline (Answer C) is recommended as maintenance therapy, which may help increase her FEV1 back to baseline. Increasing pancrelipase (Answer B) is not necessary because this patient has no GI symptoms and is stooling well. Answer D is incorrect because inhaled ICS are not recommended by the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation for treating patients with CF.

questions.question: C.S. is a 15-year-old male teenager with CF who has his vitamin levels drawn at today's clinic visit. His home medications include albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled twice daily; dornase alfa 2.5 mg nebulized daily; pancrelipase 20,000-unit capsules 3 with meals and 2 with snacks; 7% hypertonic saline 4 mL nebulized daily; a multivitamin with extra vitamin A, D, E, K 1 tablet orally daily; and cyproheptadine 4 mg orally twice daily. Allergies include sulfa drugs - rash. C.S. states that he is adherent to all of his medications. Laboratory values are as follows: 25 OH vitamin D 23 ng/mL; vitamin A 33.1 mcg/dL; vitamin E 1.2 mg/dL; and international normalized ratio (INR) 1.1. Which medication would be most appropriate to initiate?
options: A. Vitamin D3 2000 units orally daily.
B. Vitamin A 10,000 units orally weekly.
C. Vitamin E 1000 units orally daily.
D. Vitamin K 5 mg orally daily.
questions.explanation: This patient's vitamin D level is below the goal of 30 ng/mL recommended by the CF vitamin D guidelines. With a level of 23 ng/mL, the guidelines recommend assessing adherence to current vitamins and, if the patient is adherent, to increase vitamin D by 1600-6000 units/day (Answer A is correct). This patient's vitamin A and E levels were normal (Answers B and C are incorrect), as was his INR (Answer D is incorrect); hence, the other vitamins do not need to be added to his treatment regimen.

questions.question: G.H. is a 13-year-old female adolescent with asthma who was admitted to the hospital for treatment of an asthma exacerbation. Her home medications include mometasone/formoterol 100/5 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily, albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing, omeprazole 20 mg orally daily, and a multivitamin 1 tablet orally daily. G.H. reports that she has been on her current controller medication for 3 months and that she occasionally misses a dose. She uses her albuterol inhaler about twice weekly and wakes up 4 or 5 days a week coughing. She has had one other hospital admission this year and three other courses of oral steroids. Which is the best option for G.H.'s controller therapy?
options: A. Mometasone/formoterol 200/5 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
B. Fluticasone 220 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
C. Fluticasone/salmeterol 45/21 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
D. Mometasone/formoterol 200/5 mcg 3 puffs inhaled twice daily.
questions.explanation: This patient's asthma is classified as very poorly controlled because of nighttime awakening, exacerbations, and SABA use. The recommendation is to increase 1 or 2 steps. She is currently on step 3 of therapy with a low-dose ICS and LABA combination. Step 4 options include a medium-dose ICS plus a LABA or a medium-dose ICS plus montelukast. Step 5 options include a high-dose ICS plus a LABA. Answer A is a medium-dose ICS plus LABA options. Answer B is not the best option because this is just a high-dose ICS with no additional agent. Answer C is a low-dose ICS plus a LABA. Answer D is a high-dose ICS; however, the LABA component in the combination product is above the recommended dose.

questions.question: K.N. is a 5-year-old girl (weight 19 kg) with asthma who is being seen in her pediatrician's office. K.N.'s current medications include albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing, beclomethasone 80 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily, montelukast 4 mg orally daily, and a multivitamin 1 tablet orally daily. K.N.'s mother reports that K.N. has not needed to use her albuterol inhaler since her last visit 6 months ago. She has had no nighttime awakenings or asthma symptoms. K.N.'s last course of oral corticosteroids was 2 years ago. Which is inhaled controller therapy is best for K.N.?
options: A. Beclomethasone 80 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
B. Beclomethasone 40 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
C. Beclomethasone 40 mcg 1 puff inhaled twice daily.
D. Fluticasone/salmeterol 230/21 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
questions.explanation: This patient is currently on a high-dose ICS plus montelukast, and her asthma is classified as well controlled. Because her asthma has been controlled for at least 3 months, her therapy can be stepped down by 1 step. The next step is step 4, which gives the options of a medium-dose ICS plus a LABA or a medium-dose ICS plus montelukast. Answer A is no change in current therapy, making it incorrect. Answer B is the correct answer because it decreases her ICS to medium dose, Answer C is incorrect because this is a low-dose ICS, and Answer D is incorrect because this is a high-dose ICS plus a LABA.

questions.question: B.L. is an 11-year-old girl with CF who presents to her regular clinic appointment. Her current medications include albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled twice daily, dornase alfa 2.5 mg nebulized daily, 7% hypertonic saline 4 mL nebulized twice daily, inhaled tobramycin solution 300 mg nebulized twice daily 28 days on and 28 days off (currently an off month), and pancrelipase 12,000-unit capsules 3 capsules with meals and 2 with snacks. B.L. reports increased cough and increased sputum production. Past respiratory cultures are positive for P. aeruginosa and MSSA. She states that she seems to feel this way every time she stops her inhaled tobramycin solution but feels good while she is on tobramycin inhaled. Today, her FEV1 is 85% (baseline 97%). Which is the best treatment option for B.L.?
options: A. Discontinue tobramycin nebulized solution, and initiate inhaled aztreonam.
B. Continue tobramycin nebulized solution, and add inhaled aztreonam in the off months.
C. Discontinue tobramycin nebulized solution, and initiate colistin inhaled and aztreonam inhaled alternating.
D. Continue tobramycin nebulized solution, and add inhaled vancomycin in the off months.
questions.explanation: Because this patient is having ongoing symptom control while on inhaled tobramycin and is not experiencing any adverse effects, she should be continued on inhaled tobramycin (Answers A and C are incorrect) as part of her regimen. Because she is having difficulty with tobramycin in the off months, she may benefit from Pseudomonas coverage during those months with inhaled aztreonam (Answer B is correct). Answer D is not the best option because she does not grow MRSA, and from her symptom report, that does not appear to be the issue.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the primary care provider with difficulty breathing and wheezing. Her mother reports that she wakes up at night coughing once or twice a week. In addition, she struggles to keep up with her friends and often has to stop while playing. Which is the best classification for the patient's asthma?
questions.explanation: Her asthma is classified as moderate persistent (Answer C is correct) because she has nighttime awakenings more than once weekly but less than daily. She has some impairment of normal activity because she has to stop while playing with her friends. Answers A and B are incorrect because she has impairment of normal activity. Answer D is incorrect because she is not having daily symptoms.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl presents to the primary care provider with difficulty breathing and wheezing. Her mother reports that she wakes up at night coughing once or twice a week. In addition, she struggles to keep up with her friends and often has to stop while playing. Which is the best medication regimen?
options: A. Budesonide DPI 200 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily and albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing.
B. Fluticasone HFA 110 mcg 1 puff inhaled twice daily and albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing.
C. Beclomethasone HFA 40 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily and albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing.
D. Budesonide 1 mg nebulized twice daily and albuterol HFA 2 puffs inhaled every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing.
questions.explanation: The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute asthma guidelines recommend that patients with moderate persistent asthma be treated with step 3 therapy. Options for step 3 for 5- to 11-year-old patients are the preferred medium-dose ICS; alternatives include a low-dose ICS plus a LABA or montelukast or theophylline, together with a SABA for as-needed use. Answer A, budesonide DPI, is a high-dose ICS, and the DPI will be difficult for a 5-year-old patient to use correctly. Answer C, the beclomethasone dose, is a low dose for this age group. Answer D, the budesonide dose, is high dosing. Answer B is the best answer because the fluticasone dose is a medium-dose ICS, and the SABA as needed is included.

questions.question: H.M., a 10-year-old boy with asthma, is admitted to the hospital for acute shortness of breath and cough. Home medications include fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 1 puff inhaled twice daily, albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours as needed for cough or wheezing, and a chewable multivitamin 1 tablet orally daily. H.M. is being treated for an asthma exacerbation. His mother reports that he is missing his fluticasone twice monthly and that he uses his albuterol inhaler about twice weekly. H.M. had pulmonary function testing done today that showed an FEV1 of 67% and an FEV1/forced vital capacity (FVC) of 85%. Which is the optimal home treatment regimen?
options: A. Fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 1 puff inhaled twice daily.
B. Fluticasone HFA 110 mcg 1 puff inhaled twice daily.
C. Fluticasone/salmeterol HFA 115/21 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
D. Fluticasone/salmeterol HFA 230/21 mcg 2 puffs inhaled twice daily.
questions.explanation: According to the asthma guidelines, this patient's asthma is not well controlled. He has been adherent to his medication, so the recommendation is to increase his therapy 1 step. He is currently at step 2 low-dose ICS; the recommendations for step 3 therapy are a medium-dose ICS. Alternatives include a low-dose ICS plus a LABA or montelukast or theophylline. Answer A is incorrect because this is his current therapy. Answers C and D are incorrect because these ICS plus LABA are not low-dose ICS options. Answer B is the best answer because this is a medium-dose ICS.

questions.question: A 3-year-old girl (weight 12 kg) presents to the ED with increased work of breathing, retractions, and decreased breath sounds. Her medical history is significant for GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) and asthma. She is placed on oxygen, and she is currently receiving three back-to-back treatments of albuterol/ipratropium. She is responding to the albuterol/ipratropium treatments. Which treatment would best be administered next?
options: D. Methylprednisolone 1 mg intravenously every 6 hours.
questions.explanation: Status asthmaticus is caused by inflammation in the airways, and it is necessary to reduce this inflammation to resolve the exacerbation. It is recommended to use corticosteroids orally or intravenously at 1-2 mg/kg/day (max of 60 mg/day) with early administration (Answer C is correct). Because the patient's acute symptoms are covered with the albuterol/ipratropium treatments, the systemic corticosteroids should be administered to the patient next. Answer A is a supplemental treatment option if she does not respond to the albuterol/ipratropium treatments. Answer B is a treatment option, but given its adverse effects and narrow therapeutic index, it should be reserved as a rescue medication. Answer D is the incorrect dose of the corticosteroid at only 0.33 mg/kg/day.

questions.question: An 11-year-old boy (43 kg) with asthma who presented with increased work of breathing and loud wheezing is currently in the pediatric ICU on continuous albuterol 20 mg/hour and methylprednisolone 15 mg intravenously every 6 hours; he has received one magnesium bolus. The patient continues to have a respiratory rate of 29 breaths/minute and an increased oxygen requirement on 3 L of non-rebreather facemask. Which is the best treatment option for this patient?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline (Answer A) is a systemic beta-adrenergic agonist that may help improve gas exchange. Answer B is not the best option given its sedation adverse effects, which may decrease the respiratory drive in this patient, who is not intubated. Answer C, inhaled fluticasone, will not provide much benefit with this patient because he is already taking systemic corticosteroids. Epinephrine (Answer D) can be used nebulized as a bronchodilator; however, it is not recommended for routine use in status asthmaticus.

questions.question: T.Y., a 7-year-old boy who presents to his pediatrician's office with fever and upper respiratory symptoms, receives a diagnosis of pneumonia. Which antibiotic would be best to recommend to treat T.Y.'s pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin is recommended for the treatment of CAP in the outpatient setting, according to the Infectious Disease Society of America guidelines (Answer D is correct). Amoxicillin/clavulanate (Answer A) is an alternative to amoxicillin. Azithromycin (Answer B) is not recommended as first-line treatment, and the patient is not school aged or at risk of atypical pneumonia. Cefdinir (Answer C) is an option for patients with penicillin allergies; however, it has poor bioavailability.

questions.question: T.Y., a 7-year-old boy who presents to his pediatrician's office with fever and upper respiratory symptoms, receives a diagnosis of pneumonia. Which best represents the number of days that T.Y. should take the prescribed antibiotic?
questions.explanation: The CAP guidelines recommend a 10-day course (Answer B) of antibiotics for CAP. Total courses of 10 days are the most studied in this patient population. A shorter course may be sufficient, but 3 days (Answer A) of treatment is not long enough. A longer course is not necessary for the treatment of CAP (Answers C and D).

questions.question: A 2500-g boy is born at 35 weeks' gestational age to a mother whose hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) status is unknown. Which is the best recommendation regarding postexposure prophylaxis for this neonate?
options: A. Give the hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth; administer hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 7 days if the maternal HBsAg is positive.
B. Give the hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of life.
C. Give the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose; HBIG is not indicated.
D. Wait for the results of the maternal HBsAg test before giving the hepatitis B vaccine or HBIG.
questions.explanation: According to the AAP recommendations, a neonate with a birth weight of at least 2000 g who is born to a mother with an unknown HBsAg status should receive the hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth. Administration of HBIG can be delayed for up to 7 days after birth, awaiting the mother's test results. If, at that time, the mother's status is still unknown or is positive, HBIG should be administered (Answers C and D are incorrect). Administration of both agents within 12 hours of birth is recommended if the mother's HBsAg is positive or for neonates with a birth weight less than 2000 g who are born to mothers whose HBsAg status is unknown (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: A 2100-g girl born at 34 weeks' gestational age develops seizures 2 weeks after birth. Serum electrolytes and glucose are normal. Vesicular lesions are noted on the tongue and buccal mucosa. In addition to anticonvulsant therapy, ampicillin, cefotaxime, and acyclovir are initiated for suspected meningitis. Two days later, the herpes simplex virus (HSV) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is positive and the bacterial cultures are negative, so ampicillin and cefotaxime are discontinued. Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) has remained normal. Which is the best recommendation regarding this neonate's antiviral therapy?
options: A. Continue intravenous acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 7 days.
B. Continue intravenous acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 10 days.
C. Continue intravenous acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 14 days.
D. Continue intravenous acyclovir 20 mg/kg/dose every 8 hours for 21 days.
questions.explanation: This neonate's presentation is consistent with disseminated herpes disease because she has lesions in her mouth and positive herpes PCR from the CSF. According to the AAP treatment algorithm, intravenous acyclovir should be administered for at least 21 days for disseminated or localized CNS disease (Answers A, B, and C are incorrect). Near the end of 21 days of treatment, the CSF PCR should be repeated to confirm the clearance of HSV. If the PCR is negative, acyclovir can be discontinued after 21 days of therapy. If the PCR is positive, acyclovir should be continued for an additional 7 days, after which the CSF PCR should be rechecked; acyclovir should be continued until the PCR is negative. Shorter courses of acyclovir are recommended for preemptive therapy without proven disease (10 days) and for SEM disease (14 days).

questions.question: A 450-g boy who was born at 24 weeks’ gestational age received two doses of surfactant for respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). Because of his very low birth weight and severity of RDS, the medical team would like to initiate therapy to prevent progression to BPD. According to clinical trials, which is most likely to prevent BPD in premature neonates at highest risk?
questions.explanation: There are several biologically plausible theories for the prevention of BPD by various drug therapies. Because Ureaplasma spp. have been isolated from the tracheal aspirates of neonates with BPD, it has been theorized that eliminating that organism will decrease the incidence of BPD. Clinical trials have not shown this benefit in all neonates at high risk of BPD (Answer A is incorrect). When examining a specific subset of neonates who were proved to be colonized with Urea plasma, azithromycin initiated within 3 days of birth did reduce the incidence of BPD. A PDA with a left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow and is a risk factor for developing BPD; therefore, theoretically preventing a PDA would decrease the risk of BPD. This has not been shown to be true with indomethacin or ibuprofen prophylaxis or with PDA treatment (Answer B is incorrect). In animal models, inhaled nitric oxide has been shown to reduce lung inflammation and promote lung growth that would theoretically decrease the risk of BPD. Clinical trials of human neonates have not shown this benefit (Answer C is incorrect). Vitamin A has been shown to reduce the incidence of BPD in clinical trials. Although used in some NICUs, vitamin A has not become a standard of care within neonatology, given concerns about frequent intramuscular injections in extremely premature neonates as well as a lack of evidence showing a long-term benefit in improving neurodevelopmental outcomes.

questions.question: When benchmarking against similar NICUs, your unit finds a higher than average rate of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). The medical team would like to develop a protocol to standardize care of neonates at highest risk of developing NEC. Which intervention is most likely to be beneficial in reducing the incidence of NEC in high-risk neonates?
options: A. Initiate trophic feeding at 7 days of age.
B. Administer oral probiotics until 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age is reached.
C. Administer oral antibiotics until full enteral feeding is achieved.
D. Administer histamine-2 receptor antagonists until enteral feeds are initiated.
questions.explanation: Although oral probiotics are not considered the standard of care for preventing NEC, many studies show their efficacy of doing so. The optimal duration is unknown, but a recent study showed a benefit in neonates receiving oral probiotics until 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Other positive studies continued this intervention until the neonate reached term corrected age or until hospital discharge. Delaying enteral feeding has been theorized to reduce the incidence of NEC because it allows for the maturation of the GI tract, and cases of NEC rarely occur in neonates who have not been fed enterally. Overall, clinical studies have not shown this benefit (Answer A is incorrect). Administration of oral antibiotics has been shown to reduce NEC, but the benefit of this intervention is outweighed by the risk of colonization with resistant organisms, which is an outcome that has occurred in clinical trials (Answer C is incorrect). Administration of histamine-2 receptor antagonists has been associated with an increased incidence of NEC. Increasing the pH of the GI tract allows the overgrowth of bacteria, so this intervention should be avoided (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A 39 weeks’ gestational age boy was born to a mother with a history of sickle cell disease treated with chronic hydrocodone plus acetaminophen. He is admitted to the NICU for monitoring for withdrawal symptoms. In the past 12 hours, his Finnegan scores are 10, 8, 9, and 11 (evaluated every 3 hours). Which recommendation would be best for managing this neonate?
options: D. Treatment is not indicated because withdrawal symptoms are not severe enough.
questions.explanation: Three consecutive scores using the Finnegan tool of 8 or higher or two consecutive scores of 12 or higher are indicative of the need for pharmacologic management of withdrawal (Answer D is incorrect). An opioid agent (e.g., morphine, methadone) is the treatment of choice for managing withdrawal symptoms from hydrocodone exposure. Clonidine is generally reserved for adjunctive therapy with morphine (Answer A is incorrect). Phenobarbital monotherapy is not as effective as morphine or methadone for managing opioid withdrawal because it does not treat the GI symptoms or seizures (Answer C is incorrect). Phenobarbital is often used as first-line monotherapy for withdrawal from non-opioid agents.

questions.question: A new drug for the treatment of hypertension was shown to be teratogenic in rat models, but there are no reports of its use in pregnant women. Which characteristic is most likely to allow the drug to cross the placental barrier into the fetal circulation?
options: A. High molecular weight (greater than 500 Da).
questions.explanation: Drug characteristics associated with transport across the placenta include low molecular weight (less than 500 Da), lipophilicity, and low protein binding (Answers A and B are incorrect). A prolonged half-life may increase the time during which the drug can cross the placenta but, without the other characteristics, does not alone promote drug transport across the placenta (Answer D is incorrect). Although transfer across the placenta does not necessarily predict a drug’s teratogenicity, it is required for the drug to cause fetal harm.

questions.question: You are working with the neonatologists in your unit to develop a treatment protocol for NEC. Which organism is it most important to cover with your recommended empiric antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria are all common pathogens causing early neonatal sepsis (Answers C and D are incorrect). C. albicans can cause late-onset neonatal sepsis, especially in neonates with specific risk factors (e.g., history of abdominal surgery, long-term total parenteral nutrition, Candida colonization of several sites) (Answer A is incorrect).

questions.question: A breastfeeding mother presents with newly diagnosed hypertension. The medical team asks you to suggest ways to minimize neonatal risks and exposure from the treatment while still allowing the mother to breastfeed. Which recommendation is most likely to achieve this goal?
options: A. Choose a drug with a relatively long half-life.
B. Choose a drug that is not highly protein bound.
C. Advise the mother to feed when her serum concentrations of the drug are likely to be lowest during the day.
D. Select the lowest effective treatment dose.
questions.explanation: The safest medications during lactation are those with low oral bioavailability, high protein binding, low lipid solubility, and a short half-life (Answers A and B are incorrect). Dosing just after breastfeeding can allow a longer time for clearance before the next feeding and reduce transfer to the infant, but this option is dependent on the medication and the feeding schedule (Answer C is incorrect). Choosing the lowest effective maternal dose is recommended to minimize exposure to the infant.

questions.question: A 660-g boy born by vaginal delivery at 24 weeks’ gestational age had a poor respiratory effort, grunting, and retractions at birth and required intubation with 100% oxygen in the delivery room. Apgar scores were 4 at 1 minute, 5 at 5 minutes, and 8 at 10 minutes. Maternal obstetric history was significant for preterm labor, tobacco smoking, and no prenatal care. Because of the lack of prenatal care and a precipitous delivery, no antenatal steroids were administered. An initial blood gas showed pH 7.1, Pco2 73, Po2 71, and base deficit 11. Ampicillin and gentamicin are ordered for possible early sepsis. A chest radiography is ordered, and the result is pending. After transfer to the NICU at 15 minutes of life, he continues to require 100% oxygen and high peak inspiratory pressures to maintain adequate oxygen saturations. Which is the best recommendation regarding surfactant therapy for this patient?
options: A. Surfactant therapy should be withheld pending radiographic findings confirming RDS.
B. Prophylactic surfactant therapy should be administered because this neonate is at high risk of developing RDS.
C. Early surfactant rescue therapy should be administered because this neonate’s presentation is consistent with RDS.
D. Surfactant rescue therapy should be delayed to avoid overtreatment of the neonate, whose symptoms of RDS may resolve spontaneously.
questions.explanation: Surfactant rescue therapy should be administered early in this case because this neonate’s presentation is consistent with RDS. Withholding surfactant until radiographic confirmation may delay effective treatment (Answer A is incorrect). Prophylactic surfactant therapy is administered in the delivery room before symptoms develop; this neonate already has severe respiratory failure requiring high oxygen and pressures (Answer B is incorrect). Delaying rescue therapy is not recommended in severe cases because it can worsen outcomes (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: The patient in case 1 had a modest response after two doses of surfactant, but he remains intubated and mechanically ventilated, requiring 30% oxygen 24 hours after birth. Because of his prematurity and continued need for invasive respiratory support, the medical team would like to initiate a therapy to prevent the development of BPD. Which medication would be best to recommend?
questions.explanation: Caffeine use in premature infants has been shown to reduce the risk of BPD. In addition, this patient has several risk factors for BPD, including prematurity and continued need for respiratory support, and caffeine has other beneficial effects (e.g., treatment of apnea of prematurity). Dexamethasone can reduce BPD but has potential adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes and is generally reserved for severe cases when extubation is not possible (Answer C is incorrect). Azithromycin may reduce BPD only in a subset of neonates colonized with Ureaplasma (Answer A is incorrect). Poractant is a surfactant preparation and is not used for prevention of BPD at this stage (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: The patient from cases 1 and 2 is now 36 weeks’ postmenstrual age. During his NICU stay, he was treated for RDS and Klebsiella sepsis. He has had several failed extubation attempts and remains intubated, requiring 30%–40% oxygen to maintain adequate oxygenation and prevent frequent desaturations. His chest radiograph reveals diffuse haziness with lung hyperinflation consistent with chronic lung disease. Which is the best treatment to recommend for his severe BPD?
options: A. Albuterol 2 puffs by endotracheal tube every 6 hours.
B. Aldactazide 3 mg/kg/day by mouth divided every 12 hours.
C. Fluticasone 2 puffs by endotracheal tube every 12 hours.
D. Furosemide 1 mg/kg/dose intravenously as needed for signs of pulmonary fluid overload.
questions.explanation: In severe BPD, diuretic therapy can improve pulmonary mechanics in infants with pulmonary edema or fluid overload; furosemide is often used for this purpose (Answer D is correct). Routine use of bronchodilators (Answer A) and inhaled corticosteroids (Answer C) has not consistently shown benefit for all infants with BPD, and they are generally reserved for selected patients. Chronic thiazide/spironolactone therapy (Answer B) may be used in some cases but is not the best immediate recommendation in this scenario.

questions.question: The patient in cases 1–3 is now 37-3/7 weeks’ postmenstrual age. After prolonged intubation and mechanical ventilation, he was extubated 10 days ago to nasal CPAP with 21% oxygen. He has received caffeine since shortly after birth but has had no apneic spells since extubation. Which is the best recommendation regarding his methylxanthine therapy?
options: A. Discontinue caffeine, and monitor the patient for apnea recurrence.
B. Taper the caffeine dose over the next 2 weeks, and discontinue it if no apnea occurs during the taper.
C. Switch to theophylline because its shorter half-life will allow for a faster wean off therapy.
D. Continue caffeine until discharge, and then plan to taper over several weeks as an outpatient.
questions.explanation: Caffeine is typically discontinued when apnea of prematurity has resolved and the infant has been free of apneic events for an appropriate observation period. In this case, the patient has had no apneic spells since extubation; discontinuing caffeine and monitoring is appropriate (Answer A is correct). Tapering is not necessary because caffeine can be stopped without taper (Answer B is incorrect). Switching to theophylline is not recommended (Answer C is incorrect). Continuing caffeine until discharge is unnecessary if apnea has resolved (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A 750-g girl was delivered prematurely at 26 weeks’ gestational age secondary to maternal chorioamnionitis. Soon after birth, she had symptoms of RDS and subsequently received two doses of surfactant. Despite some improvement in her symptoms, she remained intubated and mechanically ventilated. Caffeine was initiated. She also received three doses of indomethacin according to the NICU’s IVH prophylaxis protocol. At 12 days of age, she became tachycardic and had a widened pulse pressure; also, a systolic murmur was heard. She became hypotensive, so a dopamine continuous infusion was initiated, and the dose was titrated to 20 mcg/kg/minute. Her total daily fluid intake was 120 mL/kg/day. Her chest radiograph revealed pulmonary edema, and her ventilator support had to be increased. An echocardiogram (ECHO) was ordered and showed a moderate PDA with left-to-right shunting. Which is the best therapy to recommend for the management of this patient’s PDA?
options: A. Acetaminophen 15 mg/kg/dose intravenously every 6 hours x 3 days because indomethacin failed.
B. Furosemide 1 mg/kg/dose intravenously every 12 hours until pulmonary edema is resolved; then recheck ECHO.
C. Indomethacin 0.2 mg/kg/dose x 1 dose; then 0.25 mg/kg/dose every 12 hours x 2 doses for late symptomatic treatment.
D. Restrict fluid intake to 100 mL/kg/day, and recheck ECHO in 2 days.
questions.explanation: This infant has a symptomatic PDA with pulmonary edema and need for increased ventilator support. Indomethacin is used for PDA closure; late symptomatic treatment dosing is appropriate here (Answer C is correct). Acetaminophen may be used when indomethacin fails, but this patient received indomethacin for IVH prophylaxis, not for PDA closure (Answer A is incorrect). Diuretics and fluid restriction may help symptoms but are not definitive therapy for PDA closure (Answers B and D are incorrect).

questions.question: The patient in case 150 who was born at 26 weeks’ gestational age was treated for a PDA with indomethacin at 12 days of age; a repeat ECHO confirmed closure. Trophic enteral feedings were discontinued when the PDA was diagnosed. Feedings were resumed at 14 days of age with 2 mL every 3 hours (20 mL/kg/day) of preterm formula at 24 kcal/oz. Feedings were advanced by 20 mL/kg every day. At 20 days of age, she developed abdominal distension, bloody stools, and temperature instability. Her feedings were discontinued. An urgent abdominal radiograph was ordered, which revealed dilated loops of bowel and pneumatosis intestinalis with no evidence of free air. Which is the best antibiotic regimen to recommend?
questions.explanation: Initial empiric antibiotic therapy for NEC typically includes coverage for gram-negative and anaerobic organisms; however, many standard regimens include ampicillin plus gentamicin, with anaerobic coverage added based on severity and local protocols. In this scenario, ampicillin plus gentamicin is the recommended regimen (Answer A is correct). The other regimens are broader or include additional anaerobic coverage and are not first-line in all cases (Answers B–D are incorrect).

questions.question: A 4200-g girl is born by cesarean section at 39 weeks’ gestational age to a mother with a history of genital HSV infection and visible genital lesions at delivery. The neonate appears well and begins feeding within a few hours after birth. Surface cultures for HSV are sent at 24 hours of age and are subsequently reported as positive. Intravenous acyclovir is initiated. Cerebrospinal fluid for HSV PCR and serum ALT are sent. The neonate remains asymptomatic. The HSV PCR is negative, and the ALT is within normal limits. Which is the best recommendation regarding this patient's management?
options: B. Continue acyclovir 60 mg/kg/day intravenously in three divided doses to complete 10 days of treatment.
C. Continue acyclovir 60 mg/kg/day intravenously in three divided doses to complete 14 days of treatment.
D. Switch to oral acyclovir 300 mg/m2/dose every 8 hours to complete 10 days of treatment.
questions.explanation: This neonate has positive surface cultures but no evidence of disseminated disease or CNS disease (negative HSV PCR and normal ALT). A 10-day course of intravenous acyclovir is recommended for preemptive therapy without proven disease (Answer B is correct). Shorter courses are not recommended (Answer A is incorrect). A 14-day course is recommended for SEM disease, and 21 days for CNS or disseminated disease (Answer C is incorrect). Oral acyclovir is not recommended for this initial treatment (Answer D is incorrect).

questions.question: A 3900-g boy was born at 38 weeks’ gestational age to a mother with a history of syphilis that was adequately treated 3 months before delivery. The mother has shown no signs of relapse or recurrence since treatment. Maternal syphilis rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is 1:16. In the delivery room, the neonate had some grunting and retractions. He was transferred to the NICU and initiated on ampicillin 100 mg/kg/dose intravenously every 8 hours and gentamicin 5 mg/kg/dose intravenously every 24 hours to rule out sepsis/pneumonia. Syphilis RPR was sent for the neonate, and the result was 1:64. The neonate’s symptoms resolved within 6 hours after birth, and blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours. Which is the best recommendation regarding this patient’s management?
options: A. Discontinue ampicillin and gentamicin. No treatment is indicated for congenital syphilis.
B. Discontinue gentamicin and continue ampicillin to complete 10 days for congenital syphilis.
C. Discontinue ampicillin and gentamicin. Give benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg intramuscularly x 1 dose for congenital syphilis.
D. Discontinue ampicillin and gentamicin. Give aqueous penicillin G 50,000 units/kg/dose intravenously every 12 hours x 10 days for congenital syphilis.
questions.explanation: In this case, maternal treatment for syphilis is unknown (Answer B is incorrect). Benzathine penicillin G is the recommended treatment for neonates born to mothers treated with penicillin more than 4 weeks before delivery but during the pregnancy AND the neonate has a normal physical examination and an RPR/VDRL titer less than 4-fold higher than the mother’s titer (Answer C is incorrect). In this case, the neonate’s initial respiratory symptoms most likely occurred because of transient tachypnea of the newborn rather than sepsis or pneumonia because they resolved quickly; this, in conjunction with blood cultures that are negative at 48 hours, makes it reasonable to discontinue ampicillin and gentamicin.

questions.question: A 2600-g girl was born at 36 weeks’ gestational age to a mother in a methadone treatment program for her heroin addiction. The mother has received methadone 80 mg daily for the past 7 months and has been adherent. The neonate is admitted to the NICU for initial respiratory distress in the delivery room and for monitoring of withdrawal symptoms. Finnegan scores have been assessed every 4 hours since birth. Scores for the first 24 hours are 4, 6, 5, 8, 7, and 8. Which is the best recommendation for the management of this neonate at risk of abstinence syndrome?
options: A. No pharmacologic intervention for withdrawal is currently indicated.
questions.explanation: This infant is at high risk of developing NAS because of in utero exposure to methadone. When using the Finnegan Scoring Tool to assess neonates at risk of withdrawal, three consecutive scores of 8 or higher or two consecutive scores of 12 or higher indicate the need for pharmacologic management of withdrawal. Lower scores may indicate mild withdrawal symptoms that should be managed with non-pharmacologic interventions (e.g., swaddling; minimal handling; reduced environmental noise; subdued lighting; frequent, small feedings). Although this neonate is not currently showing severe signs of withdrawal requiring pharmacologic intervention, she should continue to be monitored because withdrawal from methadone typically manifests on days 2–6 of age (Answer B, C, and D are incorrect). If severe withdrawal does occur, an opioid agent (e.g., morphine, methadone) is the treatment of choice. Clonidine is an effective adjunctive therapy with morphine. Phenobarbital is not as effective for monotherapy as is an opioid agent because phenobarbital does not treat the GI symptoms or seizures.

questions.question: A 2-month-old boy who was born at term and has no significant medical history is being breastfed. His mother is prescribed tobramycin ophthalmic solution 2 drops in both eyes every 4 hours for 10 days for a severe conjunctivitis. Which is the best recommendation regarding breastfeeding during this mother’s treatment?
options: A. Therapy should be switched to an agent with a higher molecular weight.
B. Tobramycin ophthalmic can be used, but breast milk should be discarded during therapy (i.e., “pump and dump”) and formula used.
C. Tobramycin ophthalmic can be used, and breastfeeding can continue without modifications.
D. Tobramycin ophthalmic can be used, breastfeeding can continue, and the infant should receive probiotics.
questions.explanation: When assessing whether a drug is safe for administration during lactation, several factors must be considered the molecular weight, protein binding, half-life, and oral bioavailability of the drug can affect the transfer of the drug into the breast milk and the subsequent oral absorption by the infant; the maternal serum concentration can affect the concentration in the breast milk; potential adverse effects of the drug in the infant; and the risk-benefit of continuing breastfeeding during the therapy. The likelihood of significant maternal serum concentrations of tobramycin after ophthalmic administration is very low. Similarly, tobramycin’s oral bioavailability is very low; therefore, the amount of drug available to the infant and the extent to which it is absorbed will not lead to a significant exposure (Answer A is incorrect). Because tobramycin exposure is likely to be low from breastfeeding, GI flora should not be altered; therefore, probiotics would not be of benefit (Answer D is incorrect). “Pumping and dumping,” which eliminates all the benefits of breastfeeding, is generally not recommended (Answer B is incorrect).

questions.question: R.H. is a 15-year-old female adolescent who presents to the emergency department (ED) with a headache. She describes her headache as a throbbing, pulsing pain in the front of her head. Bright lights seem to make it worse. She has been nauseated since the onset of the headache and has vomited twice in the past hour. Which medication is best, given R.H.’s symptoms?
questions.explanation: Although almotriptan is the only FDA label-approved medication for the acute treatment of migraines in adolescents, this patient has nausea and vomiting (Answer A is incorrect). An alternative dosing form is recommended in this case; therefore, sumatriptan would be the best option (Answer D is correct). Narcotics are not recommended for migraines and should be avoided, if possible (Answers B and C are incorrect).

questions.question: S.K. is a 5-year-old girl (weight 20 kg) with focal (partial onset) seizures. She was placed on carbamazepine 2 months ago. For the first month after the dose was titrated to 200 mg twice daily, she had no seizures. After the first month, however, the seizures recurred. A therapeutic level was drawn, which was 3.5 mg/mL (normal range 4–12 mg/mL). Which is the most likely reason for the low level?
options: A. Carbamazepine binds to protein binding.
B. Carbamazepine has displacement of the freefraction.
questions.explanation: The most likely reason for the patient’s low therapeutic level of carbamazepine is that carbamazepine is an autoinducer (Answer C is correct). After 1 month of treatment, carbamazepine would have reduced itself. The other three choices of protein binding, displacement of the free fraction, and multi-phasal distribution do not explain the patient’s decreasing carbamazepine level (Answers A, B, and D are incorrect).

questions.question: C.F. is a 12-year-old boy (weight 45 kg) who has been having difficulty in school. He has been described as staring off into space and not paying attention. He seems to do this many times a day, but each episode lasts for only a few seconds. Which is the best medication for C.F.?
questions.explanation: Of the possible choices, only ethosuximide is indicated for absence seizures (Answer A is correct). The other three agents are useful for generalized tonic-clonic seizures (Answers B–D are incorrect).

questions.question: M.M. is an 8-year-old boy with cerebral palsy. His primary symptoms are muscle tightness in his arm, a scissored gait, grimacing in his face, and an intermittent tremor. His mother brings a prescription for baclofen 5 mg every 8 hours. Which best reflects the target symptom in M.M. for which baclofen has been prescribed?
questions.explanation: Baclofen is a muscle relaxer indicated for spasticity (Answer D is correct). Although the other three choices are the classic symptoms of cerebral palsy, baclofen is not indicated for these symptoms and may not be helpful in relieving these symptoms (Answers A–C are incorrect).

questions.question: M.P. is an 11-year-old boy with autism disorder. His current symptoms include inability to communicate verbally, inability to follow directions, irritability, self-injurious behavior, flat affect, and aggression. He often gets upset, and if his routine is disrupted, he will start rocking back and forth. Aripiprazole is prescribed. Which of his symptoms is aripiprazole most likely to improve?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is indicated for irritability, aggression, and other tantrum-like behaviors (Answer B is correct). Aripiprazole does not improve communication skills such as following directions and verbal ability (Answers A and D are incorrect). Flat affect is also not an indication for aripiprazole and can be an adverse effect of some antipsychotics (Answer C is incorrect).

questions.question:
Questions 161 and 162 pertain to the following case: T.E. is a 15-year-old female adolescent with bipolar disorder. She presents wi an expansive mood, grandiosity, and flight of ideas. She has not slept for the than 2 hours for at least 1 week.

161. Which would be the most appropriate medication for T.E.?
questions.explanation: of the choices, only olanzapine is indicated for the acute mania phase of bipolar disorder in adolescents (Answer A is correct)[cite: 25]. Lamotrigine may be helpful for maintenance treatment or the depression phase (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 26]. Fluoxetine is an antidepressant and is not effective for mania (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 27]. Methylphenidate, a stimulant, is indicated for ADHD; as such, it could exacerbate this patient's manic symptoms (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 28].

questions.question:
Questions 161 and 162 pertain to the following case: T.E. is a 15-year-old female adolescent with bipolar disorder. She presents wi an expansive mood, grandiosity, and flight of ideas. She has not slept for the than 2 hours for at least 1 week.

162. The physician would like to prescribe lithium for T.E. For which adver effect is lithium most likely titrated with initiation?
questions.explanation: The most common adverse effect related to initial dosing with lithium is nausea and vomiting as well as other GI problems (Answer B is correct)[cite: 29]. Leukocytosis is a potential problem with the long-term use of lithium (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 30]. Pancreatitis and liver enzyme elevation are more likely to occur with valproic acid use (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 31]. Early jitteriness and anxiety are common with SSRIs (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 32].

questions.question: 163. K.C. is a 14-year-old male adolescent (weight 45 kg) who presents to the ED with hallucinations, paranoia, and aggression. On medication reconciliation it is noted that the dose of his attention deficit / hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medication was recently doubled. Of the medications indicated to treat ADHD, which is most likely causing these symptoms in K.C.?
questions.explanation: because methylphenidate increases dopamine in the synaptic cleft, it can cause psychotic symptoms; including hallucinations and paranoia (Answer D is correct)[cite: 33, 34]. Clonidine and guanfacine indirectly affect dopamine and are therefore less likely to cause psychotic symptoms (Answers B and C are incorrect)[cite: 34]. Atomoxetine weakly affects dopamine and is therefore less likely to cause psychotic symptoms (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 35].

questions.question: 164. N.B. is a 12-year-old girl who was given a diagnosis of ADHD. The physician would like to use a methylphenidate product that will last at least 10 hours. Which medication would be best for N.B. because of its longer duration of action?
questions.explanation: The methylphenidate OROS formulation has a duration of action of about 12 hours (Answer C is correct)[cite: 36]. The other three long-acting formulations have a duration of action of 6-8 hours (Answers A, B, and D are incorrect)[cite: 37].

questions.question: 165. L.R. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who binges on junk food and later purges. She is given a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa. Which best depicts the medication that is U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) indicated for bulimia nervosa and may be useful in treating L.R.?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine, an SSRI, is the only medication that is FDA label approved for bulimia in adults (Answer A is correct)[cite: 38]. However, fluoxetine is not indicated in children for bulimia, although it is approved for other anxiety disorders and depression in children[cite: 39]. The other three medications are also SSRIs and are indicated for other types of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents, but not for bulimia nervosa (Answers B-D are incorrect)[cite: 40].

questions.question: 166. R.S. is a 17-year-old male adolescent with a history of alcohol use and binge drinking who received his first DUI (driving under the influence) after his 17d birthday. His parents bring him to the hospital for evaluation as having possible alcohol use disorder. It is determined that he meets the criteria for this disorder, and he is referred to an outpatient treatment center. Given the evidence for treating adolescents with substance use disorders, which would be best to initiate as first-line therapy in R.S.?
questions.explanation: Although medications have been studied in adults that show a reduction in alcohol use, binge drinking, and cravings (naltrexone, acamprosate, and disulfiram) (Answers B-D are incorrect), none is indicated inchildren and adolescents (Answer A is correct)[cite: 41, 46]. Different types of behavior therapy, including family therapy, are recommended[cite: 47].

questions.question: 167. Female adolescent who presents with depressed mood, insomnia, weight loss, feelings of guilt, and suicidal ideation. She has been feeling this way for the past 3 months. Several weeks ago, she almost tried to overdose on her mother's oxycodone but then confessed to her mother her thoughts. At that time, she was admitted to the hospital, but no medications were prescribed. The current presentation began when she notified her mother of her suicidal thoughts, and her mother brought her immediately to the hospital for evaluation. This time, the physician would like to initiate an antidepressant. Which medication is best for K.B.?
questions.explanation: Escitalopram and fluoxetine are the only two antidepressants indicated for adolescent depression (Answer C is correct)[cite: 48]. Venlafaxine, duloxetine, and mirtazapine are not indicated for childhood and adolescent depression, and studies comparing these medications with placebo did not show a significant difference (Answers A, B, and D are incorrect)[cite: 49].

questions.question:
Questions 168 and 169 pertain to the following case: A.M. is a 12-year-old girl (weight 50 kg) with a throbbing headache located the front of her head that has lasted for 2 hours. She has phonophobia, but nausea and vomiting. She describes this as the worst headache she has ever She has had "bad" headaches in the past, when acetaminophen has worked by this headache did not go away with a 650-mg dose.

168. Which would be the next best step for her headache?
questions.explanation: Of the choices, ibuprofen is the only one with clinical trials showing efficacy for acute treatment (Answer A is correct)[cite: 50]. Efficacy evidence for sumatriptan is available for the nasal spray and subcutaneous formulations but not for the oral formulation (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 51]. Prochlorperazine may be beneficial even without nausea and vomiting present, but there is more evidence for ibuprofen (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 52]. Topiramate is useful for prophylaxis but not for acute treatment (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 53].

Questions 168 and 169 pertain to the following case: A.M. is a 12-year-old girl (weight 50 kg) with a throbbing headache located the front of her head that has lasted for 2 hours. She has phonophobia, but nausea and vomiting. She describes this as the worst headache she has ever She has had "bad" headaches in the past, when acetaminophen has worked by this headache did not go away with a 650-mg dose.

169. After a few months, A.M. continues to have migraine headaches, consistin of about four per month. She has missed 1 week of school in the past mont because of her migraines. Although the medications for acute treatment seem be working, her mother is concerned about the amount of medications her daughter is taking and wonders whether there is anything her daughter could take for migraine prevention. Which scheduled medication would be best fre migraine prophylaxis?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is the only agent useful for prophylaxis (Answer D is correct)[cite: 54]. The other three agents are for acute treatment (Answers A and B are incorrect)[cite: 55]. Sumatriptan orally lacks sufficient evidence to support its use in adolescents (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 56].

questions.question: 170. A.K. is a 6-year-old boy who comes to the ED with nausea, vomiting irritability, and restlessness and states that his head hurts. When asked where hurts, he says "all over my head." His mother states he has been acting like this for several hours. She tried acetaminophen several hours ago, but there appeared to be no change in his behavior or complaints. Which medication would best be tried next in A.Κ.?
questions.explanation: Because the patient is vomiting, a non-oral formulation is recommended (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 57]. Sumatriptan nasal spray is the only choice with evidence of efficacy in a non-oral formulation (Answer C is correct)[cite: 58]. Valproic acid is for prophylaxis (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 59]. Opioids should be avoided (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 59].

questions.question:
Questions 171 and 172 pertain to the following case: A.P. is a 13-year-old male adolescent (weight 55 kg) initiated on oxcarbazepine monotherapy for partial-onset seizures. His mother comes to the pharmacy to fill the prescription. His current prescription dose is 200 mg twice daily. His mother says that the physician told her the dose would most likely increase.

171. Which best reflects the max daily recommended dose for this patient?
questions.explanation: The max dosing recommendation according to the manufacturer for a 55-kg child is 1800 mg (Answer C is correct)[cite: 60]. The other doses are either below or above the recommendation (Answers A, B, and D are incorrect)[cite: 61].

questions.question:
Questions 171 and 172 pertain to the following case: A.P. is a 13-year-old male adolescent (weight 55 kg) initiated on oxcarbazepine monotherapy for partial-onset seizures. His mother comes to the pharmacy to fill the prescription. His current prescription dose is 200 mg twice daily. His mother says that the physician told her the dose would most likely increase.

172. A.P.'s mother has heard that antiepileptics have many adverse effects. Which adverse effect would the mother best be cautioned about regarding oxcarbazepine in A.P.?
questions.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism are both common adverse effects of phenytoin (Answers A and B are incorrect)[cite: 62]. Oxcarbazepine, which is hepatically cleared, does not affect renal function (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 63, 68]. Hyponatremia is more common with oxcarbazepine than with carbamazepine (Answer C is correct)[cite: 69].

questions.question: 173. K.W. is a 15-year-old female adolescent (weight 54 kg) with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She has been taking valproic acid 125 mg four times daily. Her serum level is 80 mcg/mL She is still having seizures, but the family does not want to increase the dose because, on higher doses, K.W. becomes very drowsy, uncoordinated, and lethargic. The physician would like to add lamotrigine. Which would be the best initial dose of lamotrigine for K.W?
questions.explanation: The dosage recommendation according to the manufacturer is to initiate lamotrigine with an every-other-day schedule when used concurrently with valproic acid (Answer C is correct)[cite: 70]. A dose of 25 mg/day is for monotherapy (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 71]. Initial 50 mg/day doses are used when lamotrigine is used concurrently with enzyme inducers (Answers B and D are incorrect)[cite: 72].

questions.question: 174. Which best reflects the lamotrigine adverse effect correlated with spe of titration?
questions.explanation: Rash is the main concern with the concomitant use of valproic acid (Answer A is correct)[cite: 73]. The other three types of adverse events are common with valproic acid (Answers B-D are incorrect)[cite: 74].

questions.question: 175. E.E. is a 16-year-old male adolescent who has been prescribed topiram for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Which adverse event is most common associated with topiramate and is the one about which E.E. be counseled?
questions.explanation: Memory and concentration difficulties have been reported with topiramate (Answer D is correct)[cite: 75]. The other three adverse events are more common with other antiepileptics, including valproic acid, lamotrigine, phenytoin, and carbamazepine (Answers A-C are incorrect)[cite: 76].

questions.question:
Questions 176-178 pertain to the following case: J.N. is a 10-year-old girl (weight 28 kg) with cerebral palsy. Her symptoms spasticity (muscle stiffness/tightness) are getting worse and are interfering with daily function. The physician prescribes tizanidine 2 mg at bedtime.

176. On which adverse event would J.N. and her family best receive counseling?
questions.explanation: One of the most common adverse effects of tizanidine is sedation (Answer B is correct)[cite: 77]. It is more likely to cause hypotension than hypertension (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 78]. Renal dysfunction and mania are adverse effects of baclofen (Answers C and D are incorrect)[cite: 79].

177. After several months. J.N. returns to the physician's office with worsening this medication is well tolerated by J.N., the muscle tightness continues in her symptoms. The physician switches the prescription to oral baclofen. Although arms, interfering with writing and other activities. The physician decides to try potentially serious adverse effect would be best to notify J.N. and her family on abotulinum toxin A to be given every 3 months. Although rare, which about?
questions.explanation: although rare, it is possible for the botulinum toxin to become systemic if it spreads from the injection site (Answer C is correct)[cite: 80]. It does not cause direct harm to either the liver or the kidney (Answers A and B are incorrect)[cite: 81]. Tardive dyskinesia is a long-term adverse effect associated with dopamine receptor blockers (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 82].

Questions 176-178 pertain to the following case: J.N. is a 10-year-old girl (weight 28 kg) with cerebral palsy. Her symptoms spasticity (muscle stiffness/tightness) are getting worse and are interfering with daily function. The physician prescribes tizanidine 2 mg at bedtime.

178. After about 1 year of treatment, J.N.'s family continues to report that the medications tried have not been that helpful for J.N.'s spasticity symptoms. The physician decides to try intrathecal baclofen. After 2 months of improved symptom control, J.N. suddenly becomes confused and irritated, with an elevated temperature. J.N. also is having terrible muscle rigidity, and her spasticity symptoms are worse. Which is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
questions.explanation: This scenario probably suggests an abrupt discontinuation, and the family should make sure the pump is not empty (Answer C is correct)[cite: 84]. The symptoms may also reflect an infection but not the return of spasticity (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 85]. Although an inadequate dose may explain the inadequate control of spasticity symptoms, it does not explain the change in the patient's mental status or temperature (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 86, 91]. An overdose ofbaclofen may explain the mental status changes, but not the change in temperature or inadequate control of spasticity symptoms (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 92].

Questions 179 and 180 pertain to the following case: E.A., a 9-year old boy with ASD presents with symptoms of hyperactivity stereotypies, and self-injurious behavior.

179. A physician decides to prescribe risperidone for E.A. For which potent adverse effects would the patient and his family best receive counseling risperidone use?
options: B. Anticholinergic symptoms like constipation, dry mouth, and blurred visior
D. Antipsychotic withdrawal symptoms like seizures.
questions.explanation: Risperidone can increase prolactin because of its dopamine receptor-blocking mechanism (Answer C is correct)[cite: 93]. Other second-generation antipsychotics may also increase prolactin, but not to the same extent as risperidone[cite: 94]. Olanzapine, quetiapine, and ziprasidone have rates of prolactinemia similar to each other, but less than risperidone[cite: 95]. Aripiprazole has the lower rate of prolactinemia[cite: 96]. Antipsychotics are more likely to cause weight gain than weight loss (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 96]. Risperidone has the lower rate of anticholinergic adverse effects compared with other antipsychotics (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 97]. Seizures are not a common withdrawal symptom of antipsychotics (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 98].

180. After several years of improved behavior, E.A. begins to have worsetinng irritability and aggression. The physician would like to change E.A.'s thera Which alternative medication would be the best option?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole is the only other antipsychotic indicated for autism among the choices (Answer A is correct)[cite: 99]. Lurasidone, iloperidone, and asenapine have not been studied in this population (Answers B-D are incorrect)[cite: 100].

questions.question: 181. J.P. is a 12-year-old girl (weight 35 kg) with an ASD. For the past few months, the patient has become more irritable and aggressive, and she is having emotional outbursts. Her parents are frustrated and looking for help. The physician wants to prescribe an antipsychotic. Given J.P.'s diagnosis and symptoms, which is the best option?
questions.explanation: Of the choices, risperidone is the only antipsychotic indicated for this patient's symptoms (Answer B is correct)[cite: 101]. Olanzapine has been studied for this indication, but it lacks an FDA indication for these symptoms (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 102]. Quetiapine and ziprasidone lack sufficient data for recommendation over risperidone and do not carry the indication for autism disorder (Answers C and D are incorrect)[cite: 103].
