Questions 182-184 pertain to the following case: M.W. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who presents to the ED with flight of ideas, rapid speech, irritability, and hyperactivity. She is wearing a silver top with sequins and heavily applied makeup. She flirts with the young male resident covering the ED. Her parents are concerned with her behavior, especially with her overt sexual conduct. This seems to be a new development in the past few weeks, and it has caused marked impairment in her functioning af school. No psychotic symptoms are present. Laboratory tests reveal no abnormalities, and her toxicology screen is negative. She denies using drugs or alcohol. After a thorough workup, M.W. is given a diagnosis of type 1 bipolar disorder, current episode mania.

182. According to the treatment guidelines, which is the most appropriate first-stage recommendation?
questions.explanation: According to the treatment guidelines, monotherapy is recommended for the initial stage when treating mania without psychosis (Answer A is correct)[cite: 104]. Olanzapine may be added to lithium if a partial response occurs with lithium monotherapy (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 105]. Valproic acid plus quetiapine may be tried after other treatment trials have failed (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 106]. Regimens containing two antipsychotics are not recommended (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 107].

183. The physician decides to prescribe lithium for M.W. After a few days, her lithium dose is 600 mg twice daily. A lithium level is ordered after 5 days at this dose. Which most accurately represents the target range for this therapeutic level?
questions.explanation: The recommended therapeutic range for treating mania is 0.8- 1.2 mEq/L (Answer C is correct)[cite: 112]. The therapeutic range of 0.6-0.8 mEq/L is recommended for maintenance therapy (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 113]. The range of 0.2-0.5 mEq/L is too low for an effect to occur (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 114]. Toxic symptoms start to occur when the level rises above 1.2 mEq/L (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 115, 116].

184. After M.W. is stabilized on lithium, she is discharged home with instructions to follow up in 1 month and repeat another lithium level. Two weeks later, during her menstrual cycle, she starts taking over-the-counter ibuprofen and presents to the ED. Which symptom would she most likely present with?
options: A. Ataxia and a coarse tremor.
questions.explanation: Ataxia is a CNS symptom that can occur with moderate toxicity (Answer A is correct)[cite: 117]. Lithium is not metabolized and is therefore unlikely to cause liver or pancreatic problems (Answers B and C are incorrect)[cite: 118]. Hyperactivity is a symptom of mania (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 119]. Toxic symptoms are more likely to be somnolence, syncope, seizures, and coma[cite: 120].

questions.question: 185. L.T. is a 15-year-old female adolescent with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder, current episode of acute depression. She presents to the ED after overdosing or 10 lorazepam tablets. After being medically cleared, she is admitted to th pediatric behavioral health care unit. Which medication may be mo appropriate for L.T. at this time?
questions.explanation: Of these three mediations, lamotrigine is recommended for bipolar depression (Answer B is correct)[cite: 121]. The other three antiepileptics are recommended for mania or mixed episode symptoms (Answers A, C, and D are incorrect)[cite: 122].

questions.question: 186. W.B. is a 5-year-old boy (weight 25 kg) with a diagnosis of ADHD. According to the most recent guidelines published in 2011, which accurately depicts first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) guidelines published in 2011, the first-line treatment for children 4-5 years of age is behavior therapy (Answer A is correct)[cite: 124]. Only methylphenidate is considered a second-line medication (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 125]. The other agents are not recommended in this age group (Answers B and C are incorrect)[cite: 126].

Clonidine XR, guanfacine XR, and atomoxetine are second-line agents (Answers A-C are incorrect)[cite: 128].

188. The physician believes there may be some substance abuse potential with R.K. and wants to prescribe an amphetamine-based product that is a prodrug. Which best reflects the product that is available as a prodrug?
questions.explanation: Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug that converts to amphetamine (Answer C is correct)[cite: 129]. The other three medications are not prodrugs (Answers A, B, and D)[cite: 130].

questions.question: 189. L.F. is a 17-year-old female adolescent with bulimia nervosa and depression. L.F. has tried two SSRIs for her depression, but neither worked. The physician would like to try an antidepressant with a different mechanism. Which best reflects the medication that is contraindicated for L.F.?
questions.explanation: Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with bulimia nervosa and other eating disorders (Answer A is correct)[cite: 131]. In early studies when bupropion was studied for efficacy is this disorder, bupropion increased the risk of seizures[cite: 132, 137]. The other three agents are all appropriate for the treatment of depression, although none has the indication for treating eating disorders (Answers B-D are incorrect)[cite: 138].

questions.question: 190. A.O. is a 16-year-old female adolescent with BED, Which is the best first-line treatment for this disorder?
questions.explanation: Nonpharmacologic treatment is considered first-line therapy (Answer A is correct)[cite: 139]. Although orlistat, atomoxetine, and topiramate have all been studied in adults for symptoms of BED, none has an indication for this disorder (Answers B-D) [cite: 140]; also, none of these medications has been studied in children[cite: 141].

Questions 191 and 192 pertain to the following case: C.V. is a 16-year-old female adolescent who went to a party at her friend's house while her parents were on vacation. At the party, C.V. had 5 drinks over 2 hours. This is not the first time she has had these behaviors. When C.V. arrived home, her parents noticed that she was slurring her words, could not walk straight, and was belligerent. They took her to the ED for further evaluation. In the ED, her blood alcohol level was 150 mg/dL.

191. Which treatment would be best to initiate for alcohol withdrawal?
options: A. No treatment needed at this time.
B. Chlordiazepoxide 25 mg four times daily.
questions.explanation: Adolescents are unlikely to need treatment for alcohol withdrawal because most do not experience severe withdrawal symptoms (Answer A is correct)[cite: 142]. Naltrexone, which is used for treatment of the disorder, may decrease future alcohol consumption (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 143]. Benzodiazepines and supportive care may be used if the adolescent is in severe withdrawal (Answers B and C are incorrect)[cite: 144].

questions.explanation: Family-based therapy has the most evidence for treating adolescents (Answer B is correct)[cite: 145]. Questions 193 and 195 pertain to the following case: B.B. is a 10-year-old boy who says that he is sick and does not want to go to school. On further questioning he is unable to specify his symptoms. He has been irritable, has been throwing temper tantrums, has a low frustration tolerance, and has been drawing pictures of weapons. He has been preoccupied with thoughts of death.

193. He is given a diagnosis of depression. Which antidepressant is best for B.B.?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine is the only FDA-indicated medication for depression in children younger than 12 (Answer B is correct)[cite: 148]. Sertraline has been studied in pediatric patients but does not have the FDA indication (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 149]. Paroxetine was shown to be effective in only one of three studies (Answer A is incorrect)[cite: 150]. Bupropion has not been studied for depression (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 151]. Because no other medications have been prescribed for this patient, it is reasonable to start with the antidepressant having the most evidence, which is fluoxetine[cite: 152].

Questions 196-198 pertain to the following case: A 5-year-old patient with no significant medical history presents to the emergency department in January with tachycardia (120beats/minute), a temperature of 102°F (39°C), and an elevated white blood cell count of 25 x 10^3 cells/mm^3. Both the basic metabolic panel and the liver function tests are normal.

196. Which best describes the patient's stage of sepsis?
questions.explanation: This patient has a fever with a leukocytosis, classifying her as having SIRS (Answer A is correct)[cite: 162]. If there were laboratory abnormalities or the presence of an infection, she would be classified as having sepsis (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 163]. Hypotension would indicate septic shock (Answer D is incorrect)[cite: 164]. Severe shock (Answer C) would be correct if there were other organ system dysfunction[cite: 164].

197. While the team is examining the patient, a nurse notices a warm red area around the child's ankle. On questioning, the mother explains that he was cut in that area 5 days ago and that it did not heal correctly. A BP reading is taken. which is 60/40 mm Hg. Which best represents the patient's stage of sepsis now?
questions.explanation: The child's ankle has a warm area around it now, which appears to be an infection, placing her in sepsis[cite: 165]. She is also hypotensive now, which signifies decompensated septic shock (Answer D is correct)[cite: 166]. Because the patient is thought to have an infection, Answer A is incorrect[cite: 167]. Answer B is incorrect because she has cardiovascular dysfunction[cite: 168]. Answer C would be correct if there were other organ system dysfunction[cite: 168].

198. The team initiates two rounds of normal saline 20 mL/kg and is almost ready to initiate the third when the medical resident hears rales in the lungs. The patient's BP is 65/45 mm Hg, and he has cold extremities. Which is the next most appropriate step for this patient?
questions.explanation: Proper treatment is three boluses of normal saline 20 mL/kg[cite: 169]. The team was able to do only three boluses when water began filling the patient's lungs[cite: 170]. The tank is now full[cite: 171]. Because further fluids would only worsen the pulmonary edema, this therapy is now contraindicated (Answer Dis incorrect)[cite: 171]. A vasopressor is the next treatment modality for her[cite: 172]. Milrinone is patient has decreased SVR, making milrinone incorrect (Answer B is incorrect)[cite: 172, 173]. The patient is in cold shock, making dopamine the drug of choice for her (Answer A is correct)[cite: 174]. Norepinephrine is used for warm shock (Answer Cis incorrect)[cite: 175].

questions.question: 199. A 4-month-old child with no significant past medical history presents with respiratory failure secondary to respiratory syncytial virus. Mechanical ventilation has been maximized, with little improvement in the patient's clinical status. The decision is made to start extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant to use during ECMO?
questions.explanation: During ECMO, blood flow to the gastrointestinal tract is compromised, making the oral route of administration inappropriate for medications, which eliminates warfarin and aspirin as appropriate (Answers B and D are incorrect) [cite: 176, 181]; moreover, warfarin takes days to work, which is another reason not to use this agent in ECMO[cite: 182]. Because there is an extremely fine line between clotting and bleeding in ECMO, an agent that can be easily titrated is best[cite: 183]. Heparin is a continuous infusion that can be titrated easily, especially with bedside testing (Answer A is correct)[cite: 184]. Enoxaparin, which lasts for extensive periods, would not be appropriate in ECMO (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 185].

questions.question: 200. A 7-year-old patient is currently on a fentanyl infusion at 1 mcg/kg/hour and is in the process of being deployed on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Which best describes the pharmacokinetic change that is expected to occur with fentanyl while the patient is on ECMO?
options: D. No changes to fentanyl pharmacokinetics.
questions.explanation: Fentanyl has an increased volume of distribution (Answer A is incorrect), can be adsorbed into the circuit by almost 80% (Answer B is correct), and has decreased clearance (Answer C is incorrect)[cite: 186]. Fortunately, because this is a continuous infusion and the patient is being monitored closely, bolus doses and increases in the drip rate can occur easily when more sedation is needed[cite: 187]. Answer D is incorrect since there are changes as described[cite: 188].
